episodes.title: Indianola post office affair
episodes.lead: The Indianola post office affair was a dispute in Indianola, Sunflower County, Mississippi, in which white citizens pressed Minnie M. Cox, the town's Black postmistress, to resign in late 1902, and the federal government closed the office rather than accept her resignation. President Roosevelt's administration said the resignation had been forced by threats from "a brutal and lawless element," while Cox, her husband and white townspeople denied that she had been threatened. The case was debated in the Senate and credited with aiding James K. Vardaman's campaign for governor; the office reopened in January 1904 under a white postmaster.

episodes.title: Pike County whitecapping campaign of 1903
episodes.lead: The Pike County whitecapping campaign of 1903 was a series of threats and attacks by a band of white men against Black tenants, laborers and churches in the Cross Roads and Linwood beats, about twelve miles north of Troy, Alabama. Notices threatening death drove off the hands of a sawmill and several farms, houses were shot into, a woman and her baby were wounded, and two Black churches were burned. Six white farmers were arrested by federal officers in October 1903, and five were indicted in January 1904 for oppressing Black residents because of their race.

episodes.title: Lynching of Andy Clark
episodes.lead: The lynching of Andy Clark was the hanging of a Black man by a mob at Leeper, a small town in Wayne County, Missouri, on the night of Wednesday, January 21, 1903. Clark, accused of killing a white farmer named James Herman after a quarrel over land, was taken from the village calaboose by a mob of about seventy men and hanged to a tree. The case reached the press through a short Poplar Bluff dispatch and was later counted in the year's lynching tallies in both white and Black newspapers.

episodes.title: Boaz hanging ordeal and expulsion
episodes.lead: The Boaz hanging ordeal and expulsion took place on January 17, 1903, when about a dozen men hanged two Black men from trees in the woods near Boaz, Marshall County, Alabama, after they were accused of stealing meat from a local merchant. The men were cut down alive, confessed, and were driven out of town, and the dispatch reported that the people of Boaz would not tolerate Black residents. The story ran as a short wire item in white papers from Alabama to South Dakota; no Black-press coverage was found.

episodes.title: Intimidation of Charles Jackson at Boeuf River
episodes.lead: The intimidation of Charles Jackson at Boeuf River was a threat made in January 1903 against Jackson, a Black mail carrier in Louisiana, by white men who ordered him not to return with the mail on his route and threatened him with death if he did. The Post Office Department sent an inspector to investigate, but no report of his findings or of any arrest appears in the coverage. The threat drew national notice because it coincided with the closing of the Indianola, Mississippi, post office, and papers treated it as part of a Southern campaign against Black federal employees.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Jefferson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Charles Jefferson took place in Washington County, Pennsylvania, at the end of January and start of February 1903, when crowds in several towns tried to seize Jefferson, a young Black man accused of assaulting the small daughter of Dr. George R. Conger of Taylorstown. Armed officers carried him through the crowds to the jail at Washington, Pa., and he was brought to trial on February 12. A Richmond paper used the episode to argue that lynching was no more a Southern practice than a Northern one.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Charles S. Burns
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Charles S. Burns took place on Fore street in Portland, Maine, on the afternoon of January 15, 1903, when a street crowd pursued Burns, a Black man, shouting "Lynch him" and "Kill him." Burns, who had been accused of chasing a restaurant keeper's wife with knives, took refuge in a drug store and was arrested. He was not harmed, and the next day he pleaded guilty to intoxication and was sentenced to thirty days in jail.

episodes.title: Lynching of Ransom O'Neal and Charles Tunstall
episodes.lead: The lynching of Ransom O'Neal and Charles Tunstall was the shooting of two Black prisoners in their cell in the county jail at Angleton, Texas, late on the night of January 13, 1903, by several unnamed men. The two were awaiting trial on a charge of murdering County Attorney Ed C. Smith, and several white headlines presented the killers as his avengers. The Associated Press dispatch ran across the country, and in the Black press the St. Paul Appeal condemned the killing as "outrageous butchery."

episodes.title: Clinton wash-basin incident
episodes.lead: The Clinton wash-basin incident was a confrontation in late January 1903 at Clinton, Mississippi, in which Isham Peterson, a Black woodcutter, was driven from his white employer A. M. Gill's home after washing in Mrs. Gill's bowl. The local report said only that he was ordered off the premises, but a later Jackson dispatch claimed a hanging had narrowly been prevented. Both reports blamed President Roosevelt's racial policy.

episodes.title: Killing of an unidentified Black man at Cornfield Point, Louisiana
episodes.lead: The killing of an unidentified Black man at Cornfield Point, Louisiana, was a mob killing listed as having taken place on January 19, 1903. It is known only from a single line in a lynching tally that the Sedalia Times printed in August 1903, which gave no name, charge or circumstances.

episodes.title: Red Star whitecap confrontation
episodes.lead: The Red Star whitecap confrontation was an encounter on the night of January 27, 1903, in which two Black tenants, Dan Johnson and Link Hudson, fired on three whitecaps who came to their homes on the Peets place near Brookhaven, Mississippi. The visitors fled; the first report said one or more might have been wounded, while a later account from one of the Black men involved said the shots were fired into the air. The encounter came during a whitecap campaign against Black residents of Lincoln County that state and county officials prosecuted in the following months.

episodes.title: Whipping of Dave Stokes
episodes.lead: The whipping of Dave Stokes was an assault on a Black man by the town marshal of Soperton, Montgomery County, Georgia, around the turn of 1903. Marshal T. H. Blizzard whipped Stokes for taking a drunken man home without his consent, and a few nights later four Black men fired on the marshal in what the white press called an attempted murder. Three Black men were jailed afterward, while Stokes himself was hunted by officers.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black renters from the Tomberlin neighborhood, Lonoke County, Arkansas
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black renters from the Tomberlin neighborhood took place in Lonoke County, Arkansas, in January 1903, when night riders notified every Black renter on lands there to leave at once. The Newport Independent reported that thirty-five families moved away, and Arkansas papers explained the notices as a dispute over rising farm rents.

episodes.title: Whitecapping and Black flight from Amite County, Mississippi
episodes.lead: The whitecapping and Black flight from Amite County, Mississippi, was the departure of Black farm laborers and tenants from Amite County around the turn of 1903, under night raids and threats by bands of white men whom Mississippi papers called whitecappers. Dispatches from New Orleans and Mobile reported that Black residents were leaving "in droves," mostly at night, despite a recent "compromise agreement." The story ran as a wire brief in papers from New York to North Dakota and Vermont, and the Cleveland Gazette reprinted it and later condemned the whitecaps in an editorial.

episodes.title: Threat against a Black rural mail carrier in Lincoln County, Mississippi
episodes.lead: The threat against a Black rural mail carrier in Lincoln County, Mississippi, was a warning by white residents in January 1903 that a Black man employed to carry mail on a rural route would not be permitted to do the work. The same residents told the federal postal inspector that he would be given "a dose of tar and feathers" if he took the carrier's side. Northern and Southern papers ran the item as one step in a spreading "crusade against negro Federal officeholders" in Mississippi.

episodes.title: Lauderdale County whitecapping of 1903
episodes.lead: The Lauderdale County whitecapping of 1903 was a series of attacks by a band of 'whitecaps' on Black tenants in Lauderdale County, Tennessee, in January 1903, in which shots were fired into a cabin, a horse was killed and Black families were ordered to leave. No one was reported hurt, but residents petitioned the governor and a mass meeting at Ripley authorized a $200 reward for the capture of those responsible.

episodes.title: Posse attack on Hal Smith's house, Amherst County, Virginia
episodes.lead: The posse attack on Hal Smith's house was an armed raid by a white man named Martin and a posse he organized on the home of Hal Smith, an elderly Black man in Amherst County, Virginia, shortly before January 24, 1903. Smith, his two sons and a nephew were ready for the posse, which came back to Amherst with about eight of its members wounded. The only known account is a joking paragraph in the Richmond Dispatch, which offered it as an example of the county's violence.

episodes.title: Holdenville hotel dynamiting
episodes.lead: The Holdenville hotel dynamiting was a bomb attack on the quarters of Black hotel workers in Holdenville, Indian Territory, on the night of Saturday, January 24, 1903, after the workers had been ordered to leave the town. No one was reported hurt, but the workers left on the first train out, and the dispatches tied the attack to a local rule that no Black people should live in the town. Papers in Kansas and Indian Territory carried the story within a week, one under the headline "Serious Race Trouble."

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black hotel workers from Holdenville, Indian Territory (1903)
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black hotel workers from Holdenville, Indian Territory, took place in late January 1903, when a dynamite bomb was thrown at the quarters of Black hotel help who had been ordered to leave the town. No one was reported hurt, but the workers left on the first outgoing train. Papers in Kansas and Indian Territory reported it as a case of a town enforcing a rule that no Black people should live there.

episodes.title: Lynching of Huse Thompson
episodes.lead: The lynching of Huse Thompson was the killing of a Black man who was found hanging from a tree near a Black church near Robeline, Natchitoches Parish, Louisiana, on a Sunday morning in early January 1903, after he had been arrested and jailed. A coroner's jury found that he had died by hanging "at the hands of unknown parties." It drew wider notice later that month, when District Judge Porter called it murder in a charge to the Natchitoches grand jury that papers from New York to Richmond quoted.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Isaac Jones
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Isaac Jones took place on the night of January 10, 1903, when a mob of about two hundred people went to the village jail in Tarrytown, New York, intending to hang Jones, a Black man accused of attempting to assault a young white woman. The crowd dispersed after police said Jones had been moved to the county jail, and he was later sentenced to four and a half years in Sing Sing. The mob itself drew only brief notice in the New York press, mentioned in passing in a story about a second accusation against a Black man in the same village.

episodes.title: Warnings against Black mail carriers in Jackson and Lincoln County, Mississippi
episodes.lead: In January 1903 white residents of Mississippi warned postal officials to stop employing Black mail carriers, serving notice on the postmaster at Jackson and threatening a post-office inspector in Lincoln County with tar and feathers. No violence was reported, but the dispatch was printed in papers from Washington to Minnesota and Texas as evidence of a spreading "crusade against negro Federal officeholders."

episodes.title: Stoning of the Jas. Grimes house in Boone
episodes.lead: The stoning of the Jas. Grimes house in Boone was a night attack in which a group of white men pelted the home of Jas. Grimes, a Black resident of Boone, North Carolina, with stones on a Thursday night in late January 1903, most likely 22 January. The stones broke many windows and frightened the occupants, and the house's owner offered a reward for the attackers' conviction. The town's weekly, the Watauga Democrat, condemned the attack in two items of its local column.

episodes.title: Libby whitecap attacks
episodes.lead: The Libby whitecap attacks were assaults in early 1903 by a masked band, called "Kuklux" or "whitecaps" in the press, on a colony of Black landowners near Libby in eastern Nacogdoches County, Texas. On the night of January 28, the band fired into the home of a Black man, named Jim Pleasant, Jim Morris or Jim Martin, and carried him off; he was not found and was supposed murdered. Dispatches said the colony was "terror stricken" and leaving, and Black papers called it a "reign of terror."

episodes.title: Lynching of John Thomas
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Thomas took place on 26 January 1903 near Luling, St. Charles Parish, Louisiana. Within hours of the shooting of Sheriff Lewis Oury, hundreds of armed white men chased down Thomas, a Black man accused of the killing, shot him to death and burned his body. The New-York Tribune called it the 'Horrible Revenge of a Louisiana Mob'. The story ran in papers from Louisiana to Minnesota and in one Black weekly.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Hollins
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Hollins took place near Drew, Mississippi, on the night of January 9, 1903, when a mob of masked men took Hollins, a Black man, off a train two miles south of the town and shot him to death. He had been charged with attempting a criminal assault upon a white girl. An Associated Press dispatch carried the killing to newspapers across the country, and Black weeklies later counted it in their records of the year's lynchings.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Lloyd Boyd
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Lloyd Boyd took place at Annapolis, Maryland, in January 1903, when sailors and marines from the Naval Academy set out for the jail to lynch Boyd, a Black man held on a charge of shooting a navy sailor. Officers moved Boyd by train to the Baltimore city jail. The Baltimore Afro-American credited armed Black men who guarded the jail overnight and praised them in an editorial.

episodes.title: Macon Western Union messenger strike
episodes.lead: The Macon Western Union messenger strike was a walkout by white telegraph messenger boys at Macon, Georgia, in early January 1903, after which the company hired Black messengers in their place and the strikers threatened to mob them. No attack was reported, but several hundred of the company's patrons petitioned for the Black messengers' discharge.

episodes.title: Macon lynch crowds after the killing of Thomas J. Conrad
episodes.lead: The Macon lynch crowds of January 1903 gathered in Macon, Georgia, after Thomas J. Conrad, a baggage agent at the Union depot, was shot and killed on January 5, and a young Black employee, Oscar Shiver, was accused of the shooting. A crowd shouted threats at Shiver's arrested brother, and crowds later assembled to take a Black man arrested on a train from officers and lynch him. The man proved not to be Shiver, no prisoner was brought back, and no one was killed.

episodes.title: Clubbing of Mr. Hill by Officer Palmer in Tarrytown
episodes.lead: The clubbing of Mr. Hill by Officer Palmer was a police beating in Tarrytown in about mid-January 1903, reported in a dispatch dated January 26 as having occurred "about a week ago." The correspondent called the clubbing "unnecessary" and reported that the Black residents of "both villages" secured a lawyer for Hill, presenting the case as part of a wider demand for their rights.

episodes.title: Demands for the resignation of Black railway mail clerks (1903)
episodes.lead: The demands for the resignation of Black railway mail clerks were a series of notices that white residents along several Southern railroads served on Black postal clerks in early January 1903, ordering them to quit their runs. The earliest report said clerks on the Alabama and Vicksburg railroad in Mississippi were threatened with death, while later dispatches said no violence had been reported. Newspapers treated the demands as a spread of the dispute over the Indianola, Mississippi, post office, which President Roosevelt had closed after its Black postmistress resigned.

episodes.title: Whitecap notice to remove telephones from Black homes at Osyka and Magnolia
episodes.lead: The whitecap notice to remove telephones from Black homes at Osyka and Magnolia was a demand, reported in January 1903, that the manager of the Cumberland Telephone Company in the two Mississippi towns take all telephones out of Black households. The manager refused and offered a $100 reward for the arrest of the senders, and a Jackson dispatch presented the notice as the latest act of a whitecap campaign it said was nearly over.

episodes.title: Killing of Philip Johnson
episodes.lead: The killing of Philip Johnson took place at Campti, in Natchitoches Parish, Louisiana, around January 12, 1903, when two deputy sheriffs shot to death a leader of a Black religious group, the Church of God, as they tried to arrest him. Johnson had been ordered out of Campti by a committee of citizens and was killed after he returned. Two weeks later the parish's district judge cited deaths at Campti in a widely reprinted grand jury charge against mob violence.

episodes.title: Killing of a railroad survey superintendent near Spring Hill, Louisiana
episodes.lead: The killing of a railroad survey superintendent near Spring Hill, Louisiana, took place in early January 1903, after whitecaps had repeatedly ordered his surveying corps to discharge its Black cooks or leave the parish. The superintendent, who was not named, was found dead, killed by what the report called "party or parties unknown." The only account found is a short Marshall, Texas, dispatch in the Houston Daily Post that relayed a letter from a member of the crew.

episodes.title: Burning of Squire Williams's house at Johnston Station
episodes.lead: The burning of Squire Williams's house at Johnston Station was a whitecap attack on the night of January 10, 1903, near Summit, Mississippi, in which a band of "white caps" burned the home of Williams, a Black man, after posted notices had ordered him to leave. The same night the band fired guns on the nearby premises of Sam Caruth, evidently to frighten his Black tenants; no one was reported hurt. First reported in a special to the New Orleans Picayune, the burning ran in wire briefs from Texas to Maryland, and a Jackson dispatch treated it as one of the last acts of a whitecap campaign in southern Mississippi.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Stoney Ball
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Stoney Ball took place at Belen, Valencia County, New Mexico Territory, on January 27, 1903, when a crowd seized Ball, a Black man from Albuquerque accused of assaulting a girl, and began hanging him from a telegraph pole before Sheriff Baca and a posse arrived by special train and took him away. Ball had been shot and beaten during his capture, and the Santa Fe New Mexican later reported that he died of those injuries in the Los Lunas jail. New Mexico papers in English and Spanish presented the accusation against Ball as fact.

episodes.title: Killing of Tom Irvin
episodes.lead: The killing of Tom Irvin was the shooting death of a Black man by a sheriff's posse at Alpine, Texas, reported in a dispatch dated January 11, 1903. Irvin had been accused of killing a Mexican man at a dance, and the posse killed him at a house where, by the officers' account, he had barricaded himself and refused to surrender.

episodes.title: Whipping of Tom Jefferson
episodes.lead: The whipping of Tom Jefferson was an attack by a crowd of white citizens on a Black man at Graniteville, South Carolina, on the night of January 11, 1903. Jefferson, accused of assaulting a crippled white boy at Aiken, was given more than fifty lashes and ordered to leave the community. An Associated Press dispatch from Augusta carried the story to papers across the South and beyond, and a one-sentence version reached the Richmond Planet through a syndicated news digest.

episodes.title: Averted lynching at Victoria, Mississippi
episodes.lead: The averted lynching at Victoria, Mississippi, took place on January 20, 1903, when a crowd of about 500 people gathered as two Black men suspected of murdering Oneal Jones were brought to Victoria for a preliminary hearing. No attack was made, and the prisoners were returned to jail at Holly Springs; a dispatch carried under the headline "Lynching Averted" said that a lynching had been expected.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of W. P. Richardson
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of W. P. Richardson took place on a Sunday afternoon in early January 1903 at a street car crossing in Tampa, Florida, where a crowd of white bystanders threatened to kill Richardson, a Black butcher, as a deputy sheriff arrested him. The deputy calmed the crowd and took Richardson to jail, and the only surviving report, a Tampa Herald item reprinted in Savannah, ran under the headline "ESCAPED A LYNCHING."

episodes.title: Pfeiffer Quarry spur camp shooting
episodes.lead: The Pfeiffer Quarry spur camp shooting was an ambush in February 1903 in which unknown gunmen fired into the camp of a newly hired Black grading crew about seven miles north of Batesville, Arkansas. No one was reported hurt, but the ten or twelve workers abandoned the camp and fled to Batesville on their first night there. A Batesville paper headed its account "Inexcusable Lawlessness" while making light of the workers' flight.

episodes.title: Lynching of Cornelius Lee
episodes.lead: The lynching of Cornelius Lee took place at or near Plaquemine, Iberville Parish, Louisiana, in February 1903, when a crowd of men took Lee, a Black man, from his bed and hanged him. Lee had been shot on January 25 during a street fight in which, according to white papers, a crowd of Black men beat Andre Gourrier, assistant cashier of the Bank of Plaquemine. Wire reports called him a "dying" man, since gangrene had set in from his wound, and Black weeklies entered him in their lists of the year's lynchings.

episodes.title: Reported expulsion of Black residents from Eldorado, Illinois
episodes.lead: The reported expulsion of Black residents from Eldorado, Illinois, is known only from a remark by Senator Tillman that the people of the town had "recently chased every negro out of the town," printed in a Washington dispatch of February 26, 1903. Tillman offered it as evidence that white northerners were as hostile to Black people as white southerners, and no other report of the episode was found.

episodes.title: Fayette whippings (1903)
episodes.lead: The Fayette whippings were the night flogging of a Black man and two or three Black women by a citizens' committee at Fayette, the seat of Howard County, Missouri, in early February 1903. The women were ordered out of town, at least twenty-five Black residents left within a day, and two of the women were whipped again near Myers about ten days later. A wire report of a "race war" ran nationally, while Missouri papers disputed that description and largely approved.

episodes.title: Forest parlor assault
episodes.lead: The Forest parlor assault was an attack on an unnamed Black man at Forest, Mississippi, in about late January or early February 1903, after he sat down in the parlor of Capt. S. B. Fairchild and refused to leave. Friends summoned by telephone handled him roughly and took him to jail, and the account says he came near being hanged before the sheriff interfered. The incident is known only from a press dispatch that presented it as a consequence of the "Roosevelt-Hays policy".

episodes.title: Horsewhipping of Frank Allen
episodes.lead: The horsewhipping of Frank Allen was an attack on a Black man from Gainesville, Georgia, who was whipped at gunpoint by two white men at Demorest, Georgia, in early February 1903 and then driven out of town. The attackers, C. L. Adams and Edgar Taylor, were said to be avenging an insult Allen had allegedly offered their orphan niece months before. The episode reached print as a short wire item in two Georgia dailies, which gave only the attackers' grievance.

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank Brown
episodes.lead: The lynching of Frank Brown, called Jim Brown in Bossier Parish papers, was the hanging of a Black plantation worker by a posse of white men near McDade station in Bossier Parish, Louisiana, on the morning of February 24, 1903. Brown was accused of shooting the overseer Harvey Connell, who was not seriously hurt, and of firing at the plantation's owner, McDade, during a dispute over work. A brief Shreveport dispatch carried the killing to papers across the country, while the Caucasian printed a long account that defended the lynchers.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Fred Jackson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Fred Jackson took place at Oxford, Connecticut, on the night of February 25, 1903, when woodchoppers beat Jackson, a Black man, in a hotel barroom and hunted him through the woods threatening to lynch him. Jackson had just been released by the coroner, who found insufficient evidence that he had killed a French Canadian woodchopper, Henry Resnet. He escaped, and the New-York Tribune reported the coroner's finding under the headline "Mob's Verdict Not Sustained."

episodes.title: Averted lynching of George Washington, Fayette County, Pennsylvania
episodes.lead: The averted lynching of George Washington took place in Fayette County, Pennsylvania, in February 1903, after Washington, a Black man, was accused of shooting Constable Isaac Hostetler on a passenger train out of Uniontown. Washington was arrested and taken to jail, and a lynching was reported to have been narrowly averted on the way. The only coverage found is a short item in a Morgantown, West Virginia, newspaper.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Webrum, Pennsylvania
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black residents from Webrum, Pennsylvania, took place on February 23, 1903, when white residents of the town pulled down the shacks of its Black residents with ropes and poles and drove out about twenty people. It followed a shooting about ten days earlier in which a Black man, Sterling Aiken, was reported to have wounded a white bookkeeper and escaped. The displaced residents left on a freight train for Vintondale, and Southern papers reprinted the wire story as evidence that the North treated Black people no better than the South.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jake Hines
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jake Hines was the fatal whipping of a young Black man, named in the papers as Jake Hines or Jake Haines, by a band of white men near Young's Island in Colleton County, South Carolina, in February 1903. Suspected of stealing hogs or meat from a neighbor, he was taken from his house and flogged, and he died of his wounds several days later. South Carolina weeklies and papers in Georgia, Florida and Arkansas carried the story under headlines about "whitecaps," and a Columbia dispatch noted that the local magistrate was himself in jail on a murder charge. The Colored American reported it as a killing "on the mere suspicion of stealing."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Johnson Reed
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Johnson Reed was a gathering of crowds near the county jail at Pikeville, Kentucky, on a Sunday night in February 1903, with the aim of hanging Reed, a Black prisoner charged with assaulting a white girl. Officers deputized special guards, citizens urged the crowd to give up the plan, and it dispersed without harming Reed. Papers reported it as a lynching narrowly checked; Reed was later convicted and sentenced to death.

episodes.title: Franklin County whitecapper arrests
episodes.lead: The Franklin County whitecapper arrests took place in February 1903 in Franklin County, Mississippi, when white neighbors of a Black farmer warned in writing to leave the county lay in wait at his house and captured eight members of a mounted band. The eight were bound over at $2,000 each for intimidating Black residents to make them leave, and days later the circuit judge and district attorney announced a wider campaign of arrests. Mississippi papers praised the capture, one editor calling it proof that "the white southern man is the best friend the negro has."

episodes.title: Killing of Lafayette Sims
episodes.lead: The killing of Lafayette Sims was the shooting of a Black lodger by New Orleans police early on February 20, 1903, after a siege of several hours at a Rampart Street boarding house. Police set his room on fire and shot him as he came out. The Associated Press story ran nationwide; Southern papers likened it to the Robert Charles riot of 1900, while a Mississippi editorial and the Black St. Paul Appeal questioned the police.

episodes.title: Kansas City Southern train riot (1903)
episodes.lead: The Kansas City Southern train riot was an attack by a crowd of intoxicated white men on the coach for Black passengers of an incoming Kansas City Southern train bound for Lake Charles, Louisiana, on the night of February 22, 1903. According to the Associated Press dispatch, a Black passenger was shot to death and three white men were seriously injured, one of them probably fatally. The dispatch ran in white newspapers from Georgia to North Dakota, several times under headlines that named the white men as the aggressors.

episodes.title: Lynching of Lee Hall
episodes.lead: The lynching of Lee Hall took place early on February 7, 1903, when a mob took Hall, a Black man accused of shooting Sheriff D. A. Crawford, from the jail at Wrightsville, Johnson County, Georgia, and hanged and shot him. A coroner's jury attributed his death to "unknown persons," and the sheriff died of his wound four days later. Many white papers carried the story, some reporting that the mob took Hall's ears and fingers as souvenirs; Black weeklies printed brief notices and later counted him among the year's lynching victims.

episodes.title: Killing of Melvin Fair
episodes.lead: The killing of Melvin Fair took place in early February 1903 near Luverne, Crenshaw County, Alabama, when constable James Stallings and John Lawson shot a Black man they had come to arrest for leaving a labor contract. The two men said he had fired on them first, but a grand jury indicted both for first-degree murder in March and a judge refused them bail.

episodes.title: Killing of Charles Potter
episodes.lead: The killing of Charles Potter was the fatal shooting of Potter, a Black former farm hand also reported as Charles Porter, by the farmer Isaac Chase at Chase's farm in Portsmouth, Rhode Island, near Newport, on February 20, 1903. Chase said he fired in self-defense after Potter had shot at him that morning; he was charged with manslaughter, but a Newport grand jury declined to indict him. Black residents of Newport and Portsmouth raised a fund to bury Potter and investigate, saying they doubted Chase's account.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of D. R. Stokes
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of D. R. Stokes took place on the night of February 25, 1903, in Gregg County, Texas, when a large body of white men seized Stokes, a Black preacher from Dallas who had been speaking against prohibition, and prepared to hang him across the Sabine River. By Stokes's account, he was spared after he made the Masonic sign of distress and a white leader who had urged the lynching demanded his life, on condition that he never return to the county. The story became public about two weeks later through a federal official in Dallas and ran in white dailies across the country and in two Black weeklies, chiefly as a tale of a life saved by Freemasonry.

episodes.title: Beach's Still dance shooting
episodes.lead: The Beach's Still dance shooting took place on the night of February 7, 1903, when two white men fired into a Black dance near Beach's Still and McDonald in Coffee County, Georgia, killing two turpentine workers, Sam Bell and Aleck Mervin, and wounding nine or more others. The attackers reportedly tied survivors to the dead and robbed them, and though they were said to be locally known, a coroner's jury blamed "unknown parties" and no arrest was reported. Georgia papers and the Black Savannah Tribune condemned the inaction, and Governor Terrell offered a $250 reward per killer.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black pipe line workers from Sour Lake, Texas (February 1903)
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black pipe line workers from Sour Lake took place in early February 1903, when white men at the Texas oil field ordered the Black employees of a pipe line contractor to leave under threat of being driven away or killed. All twenty-five Black workers left, most of them for Beaumont, and the one who spoke to a reporter said he saw no motive, since the Black men were paid more than the whites.

episodes.title: Stanaford City killings
episodes.lead: The Stanaford City killings took place at daybreak on February 25, 1903, when joint posses under Deputy U.S. Marshal D. W. Cunningham and Sheriff Harvey Cook shot and killed three Black men in the house of Stonewall Jackson at Stanaford City, Raleigh County, West Virginia, during a battle with striking coal miners. A coroner's jury found that one of the dead, William Clark, had been feloniously shot by men under Cunningham's direction. A union investigator said the men were shot in their beds without warning, but a federal grand jury exonerated the officers and indicted miners, Jackson among them.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Tom Manns, Ed Morris and Charles Sanders (February 1903)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Tom Manns, Ed Morris and Charles Sanders took place at Maysville, Kentucky, on February 3, 1903, when several hundred men followed the three Black prisoners from the jail to the railroad depot as officers moved them to Covington. The three were accused of robbing and shooting John B. Farrow, an aged farmer near Mt. Gilead, and officers held the crowd back with pistols. No one was hurt, and Kentucky papers reported the removal as a lynching prevented.

episodes.title: Tryon manhunt of 1903
episodes.lead: The Tryon manhunt of 1903 was an armed search for a Black man near Tryon, Polk County, North Carolina, in February 1903, after he was accused of raping and beating an 18-year-old white girl. Searchers fired on a man they took for the culprit, and the papers reported that he would be lynched if caught. Four days later officers at Forest City arrested Solon Jackson, who denied the assault, and held him for the county authorities.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Fambro
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Fambro was the killing of Will (William) Fambro, a Black man, by a party of about fifteen white men who fired into his home near Griffin, Spalding County, Georgia, early on February 24, 1903. Fambro had already pleaded guilty and been fined for an offense committed weeks earlier, described as insulting a white woman and her child or as an indecent exposure while drunk. The Governor offered rewards for the killers, and Georgia papers and Black weeklies alike called the killing unjustified.

episodes.title: Death of William Rice
episodes.lead: The death of William Rice occurred at Lawrenceville, Virginia, in late February 1903, when the body of the Black hotel worker was found beneath a railroad trestle over Rose creek. The local Brunswick Gazette, reprinted by the Richmond Planet, reported that several white men had beaten and whipped him, while a Washington paper reported that the coroner's jury found he died from a fall. An investigation at the county court in May found nothing.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Adam Stewart
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Adam Stewart took place near Ridgely, Caroline County, Maryland, in March 1903, after Stewart, a Black farm hand, was accused of shooting his employer, John H. Imler. Facing calls to lynch him, the sheriff moved Stewart from the Denton jail to Baltimore, where he was held until his trial. Imler died on April 3, and Stewart, tried in Queen Anne's County after his lawyer sought to move the case, was sentenced to 15 years.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Ben Riley
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Ben Riley took place in Grafton, West Virginia, in March 1903, when Riley, a Black day cook at the Painter boarding house, was accused of assaulting a chambermaid there. He was arrested, jailed and held for the grand jury, and the Wheeling Sunday Register reported that public anger was such that "a lynching was scarcely avoided." No violence against Riley was reported, and the threat appears in only one of the two papers that covered the case.

episodes.title: Cross County whitecapping and killing of John H. Brown
episodes.lead: The Cross County whitecapping and killing of John H. Brown was a campaign of night raids by a masked band, the "Smith's Chapel Club," against Black tenants near Wynne, Arkansas, in early 1903, in which Brown, a white Memphis detective, was shot dead on March 9. More than 200 Black families were reported to have fled the county, and eight local white men were held for the murder; federal charges against eleven men were dismissed a year later.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Carrel Alexander
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of Carrel Alexander was an incident at Sealy, Texas, in late March 1903, in which a jailed Black man accused of attempted assault was, according to a wire dispatch, taken by a mob after officers removed him. The dispatch ran under the headline "Probably Lynched" but did not say that Alexander was killed, and a separate Texas report the same day placed the accused man in jail at Bellville.

episodes.title: Caruthersville jail whipping
episodes.lead: The Caruthersville jail whipping took place at Caruthersville, Missouri, around midnight on March 13-14, 1903, when citizens took three Black men and one Black woman from the jail and whipped them with leather thongs. The four, held on a charge of pilfering during a flood, were then ordered to leave the vicinity. A brief wire dispatch about the whipping ran in papers from Georgia to Arizona, usually as an item in flood news.

episodes.title: Flogging of Charles Johnson
episodes.lead: The flogging of Charles Johnson was the whipping of a Black man by a posse in Monroe County, Mississippi, in March 1903, after he was accused of stealing the horse of Hutch Walton, the farmer who had paid him out of jail. Johnson was captured near Amory and returned to the county jail. The flogging became known through a short state-news paragraph headed "Flogged the Negro" that ran in several Mississippi weeklies.

episodes.title: Whitecap whipping of Black women near Myers, Missouri
episodes.lead: The whitecap whipping of Black women near Myers, Missouri, was an attack in February 1903 in which a band the papers called "whitecaps" took Black women from a Black man's home near Myers, in eastern Howard County, whipped them, and ordered them to leave. The women had already been whipped and driven out of the town of Fayette, and after the second whipping they left the neighborhood the next day. Newspapers in St. Louis and Indianapolis carried it as a sequel to the Fayette whipping, and a Chariton County weekly reported it with approval.

episodes.title: Greenwood County church burning (1903)
episodes.lead: The Greenwood County church burning was the burning of a Black church ("a negro church") in the backwoods of Greenwood County, South Carolina, reported in a single state-news item in April 1903. The same item said that three white men were shot and wounded that night and refused to say how; it named no one responsible for the fire and did not say how the two incidents were connected. A month earlier, three white farmers of the county's Phoenix section had been reported shot from ambush in an attack rumored to have been made by Black men, though none of those reports mentions a church.

episodes.title: Dynamiting of Fannie Robinson's house
episodes.lead: The dynamiting of Fannie Robinson's house was an attack on the home of a Black woman in Christiansburg, Virginia, at about 2 a.m. on March 20, 1903. Dynamite placed on the front door step partly demolished the house, but Robinson and her children, asleep inside, escaped unhurt. No one was identified as responsible, and the attack was reported only briefly in two white newspapers.

episodes.title: Whipping of a Black witness at Fort Myers
episodes.lead: The whipping of a Black witness at Fort Myers was an assault on an unnamed Black man by several white men at Fort Myers, Florida, shortly before March 21, 1903. The only account comes from George L. Battersby, a deputy sheriff of DeSoto county, who said the man was punished for lying under oath at the inquest into the murder of the Punta Gorda marshal. No arrests were reported, and the deputy's explanation was printed as the story.

episodes.title: Averted lynching of Frank Brown
episodes.lead: The averted lynching of Frank Brown took place at Checotah, Indian Territory, on the night of March 11, 1903, when white residents talked of lynching a Black prisoner charged with killing a white youth and Black residents armed themselves to prevent it. Deputy marshals guarded the prisoner and took him to the jail at Muskogee the next morning, after a special officer and a group of armed Black men exchanged shots in which no one was reported hurt. The killing ran as a short wire item in Texas and Kansas papers, while a Muskogee dispatch headlined "Officers Prevent Lynching" described the standoff.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Frank Brown
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Frank Brown took place in Muscatine, Iowa, on the night of March 28, 1903, when a crowd chased, beat and tried to lynch Brown, a Black man who had shot a white man who struck him. Police and an armed guard held off the crowd on the street and at the jail. The wounded man recovered, and in late April Brown was released when the county attorney moved to dismiss the charge as self-defense.

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank Robertson
episodes.lead: The lynching of Frank Robertson took place at Bradley, in Lafayette County, Arkansas, near the Louisiana line, in late March 1903, when a party of about twenty-five men overpowered the jailer and carried off Robertson, a Black prisoner charged with arson. Robertson was reported lynched, although the first dispatches said his body had not been found and a Shreveport paper said it was found hanging from a tree. The case ran as a short wire item across the country and later appeared in lynching tallies kept by both white and Black papers.

episodes.title: March 1903 Bungaloo attacks in Indianapolis
episodes.lead: The March 1903 Bungaloo attacks in Indianapolis were pursuits of Black men through downtown Indianapolis, Indiana, on the night of Sunday, March 8, 1903, by white youths known as the "Bungaloos." The crowd, which grew to nearly five hundred, chased at least five men with cries of "Kill the niggers!"; all escaped, and no injuries or arrests were reported. The Indianapolis Freeman wrote that the city had "narrowly escaped a lynching scene."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Harvey Williams
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Harvey Williams took place at Bramwell, West Virginia, on March 27-28, 1903, when a crowd gathered to lynch Williams, a Black coal miner jailed on a charge of assaulting a 13-year-old white girl. Officers took him out of the jail in plain clothes and moved him to Princeton, and the crowd then tore the Bramwell jail apart and fired hundreds of shots into the air. The story ran as a wire item across the country, and a list of the year's mob cases later recorded a hanging at Bluefield on March 29.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Thomas
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Thomas was the hanging of a Black man near Parish, Manatee County, Florida, on the night of Sunday, March 8, 1903, after citizen posses captured him on an accusation of attempting to criminally assault the ten-year-old daughter of Porter Keene. An Associated Press dispatch from Tampa said he was hanged to a tree after the girl identified him and after he "admitted his guilt," a claim that rests on that account alone. White newspapers across the country carried the dispatch within days, and two Black weeklies later included Thomas in a published record of the year's lynchings.

episodes.title: Armed seizure and expulsion of a Black depot worker in Kansas (1903)
episodes.lead: The armed seizure and expulsion of a Black depot worker took place in a Kansas town in late March 1903, when a townsman held an unnamed Black man at revolver point and marched him to the lockup after he was accused of following two women on the street. The man was held for two days, fined $10 and told to leave town, and he left. The only known account, a short local item in the Chanute Times, presented the episode as a lighthearted success.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of James Beran
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of James Beran took place in March 1903 at North Royalton, Ohio, where a crowd of villagers gathered at the place Beran was held on a charge of assaulting a school teacher, Gertrude Money. Officers took Beran out through a rear door and lodged him in the county jail at Cleveland on March 18, and no harm to him was reported. A single Cleveland dispatch carried the story to newspapers across the country the next day under headlines such as "Lynching Feared in Ohio" and "Ohio Mob Seeks Revenge."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John Broadnax
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of John Broadnax occurred in March 1903 in Rockingham County, North Carolina, after Broadnax, a Black youth of sixteen, was accused of killing the farmer Sidney Blair and wounding his niece, Sallie Walker, near Reidsville. Talk of lynching among the neighbors who caught him, and later reports of armed men from Rockingham, led officials to move him to Greensboro and then to Raleigh while National Guard companies stood ready. No attack on him took place; he was convicted at a special term of court and hanged at Wentworth on May 22, 1903.

episodes.title: Barwick whitecap raid
episodes.lead: The Barwick whitecap raid was a night attack by a band of disguised whitecaps on Black residents near Barwick, Georgia, on or about Friday, March 6, 1903. The band beat two men and ordered them out of the state, chased a third, and fired into a house, fatally wounding a boy. The reports stressed that the victims were "respectable negroes" and that no reason for the attack was known.

episodes.title: Attack on the "Our Kids" troupe at Home City, Kansas
episodes.lead: The attack on the "Our Kids" troupe at Home City, Kansas, was an assault in March 1903 by white townspeople on members of a touring company of six Black vaudeville performers, followed by its rejection by hotels at Marysville. Threatened with being followed, the performers cancelled their next date and were turned away by four Marysville hotels. The Topeka State Journal ran the story as "This Was in Kansas," and the Savannah Morning News used it to taunt Kansans about Black "rights."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Paul Doe
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Paul Doe took place at Brackettville, Texas, in March 1903, when about 150 soldiers gathered at the town jail with picks and crowbars to take out and lynch Doe, a Black youth accused of stabbing a cavalry private. Major Kendall of Fort Clark dispersed the soldiers with a strong guard, and military guards were then posted at the jail. Headlines in papers from Texas to Rhode Island stressed that the would-be lynchers were soldiers, and the Richmond Planet, a Black weekly, reprinted the story.

episodes.title: Killing of Robert Stroud
episodes.lead: The killing of Robert Stroud took place near Lake Village, Arkansas, in late March 1903, when a posse of fifteen men shot Stroud, a Black man accused of murdering a woman who lived with him, as he fled from his cabin. Struck by five bullets, he was taken by boat to jail and died there. Arkansas papers carried the story as a short state-news item, most often under the headline "Murderer Meets Speedy Death".

episodes.title: Beating of Sanders at the Atlantic Coast Line shops, Wilmington
episodes.lead: The beating of Sanders at the Atlantic Coast Line shops in Wilmington, North Carolina, was an assault on a Black railroad shop worker by a crowd of his fellow workmen in the spring of 1903, after he was said to have cursed one of them. Sanders was beaten but not seriously hurt, and the Black workers at the shops, numbered at 500, walked off the job in response. The walkout and a company investigation carried the story to papers in North Carolina, Georgia and South Carolina.

episodes.title: Harassment of Black pedestrians by white boys in Savannah (1903)
episodes.lead: The harassment of Black pedestrians by white boys in Savannah was a series of incidents in which groups of white boys in parts of Savannah, Georgia, interfered with Black passersby, culminating on a Sunday afternoon in March 1903 when several women were "mistreated." The boys responsible were placed on a court docket and punished by their parents, and the Savannah Tribune warned that the practice could lead to "serious trouble."

episodes.title: Mob attack on William Jackson in the Tenderloin, New York
episodes.lead: The mob attack on William Jackson in the Tenderloin took place on the afternoon of 1 March 1903 on Seventh Avenue in Manhattan, New York, when a crowd of white boys and young men chased and beat Jackson, a Black man, after he tried to stop them tormenting an elderly Black man. Police drove the crowd back and arrested Charles Staub, whom Jackson named as the ringleader, on a charge of disorderly conduct. Two New York papers headlined the episode as a near "race riot" and a "little race war."

episodes.title: Banishment of Aaron P. Prioleau from Eutawville
episodes.lead: The banishment of Aaron P. Prioleau from Eutawville was the flight of Aaron P. Prioleau, a Black Republican politician, from his home in Eutawville, South Carolina, in April 1903, which he said he made to escape being lynched after a "pretended arrest." Prioleau described it in a letter asking Governor Heyward for protection, and the governor declined to act on what he called meagre facts.

episodes.title: Lynching of Alexander Thompson
episodes.lead: The lynching of Alexander Thompson took place at Gurdon, Arkansas, early on April 23, 1903, when a disguised mob took Thompson, a Black lumber-mill worker, from the town calaboose and hanged him from a railroad trestle. He had been held on a charge of cutting a physician, Dr. J. H. Guffman, in a dispute over a medical bill. A coroner's jury blamed unknown parties, and the local lumber plant shut down when its Black laborers quit work. Wire reports stressed that the lynching was done quietly, which some headline writers turned to irony.

episodes.title: Lynching of Andrew Rainey
episodes.lead: The lynching of Andrew Rainey took place near Bainbridge, Georgia, on the night of April 20, 1903, when a mob took Rainey, a Black man charged with arson, from a constable who was bringing him to jail and beat him so badly that he died the next morning. The officers recognized none of the attackers, and a coroner's inquest failed to learn who they were. An Associated Press dispatch carried the killing to papers in many states, and Black weeklies later counted it among the year's lynchings.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Arthur Robinson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Arthur Robinson took place on the night of April 12, 1903, in Bloomington, Illinois, when a crowd of several hundred people pursued Robinson, a Black depot porter, with threats of lynching after he struck a baseball excursionist on the head. Police reached the barn where he had been cornered and saved him, and he was jailed.

episodes.title: Assault on Bill Barker at Selma
episodes.lead: The assault on Bill Barker was an attack on a Black man by five or six young white men on the river bank opposite Selma, Alabama, on the afternoon of April 8, 1903. The men struck him, took his money and threw him into the river, but he survived; two Alabama dailies reported it the next day, one of them as a joke.

episodes.title: Shooting of John Taylor at Castle Haynes
episodes.lead: The shooting of John Taylor at Castle Haynes was the killing of a Black convict by guards who fired on twelve prisoners escaping from the New Hanover County chain-gang stockade, six miles from Wilmington, North Carolina, early on April 20, 1903. Two other escapees, a white convict, J. P. Hughes, and a Black convict, Forney George, were reported wounded. The break came shortly after a grand jury described the camp as infested with vermin, and an opposition paper in Clinton used it to attack the county's Democratic administration.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Clifford Bell
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Clifford Bell took place in Indianapolis, Indiana, on the evening of April 11, 1903, when a crowd of about a hundred men chased Bell, a young Black man, through the streets with cries of "lynch him." Policemen with drawn revolvers stopped the pursuit, and Bell escaped. A wire dispatch that called the episode a "race riot" carried the story to papers in Kentucky, Indiana and Wisconsin.

episodes.title: Cleves town hall attack and threatened attack on Coal City
episodes.lead: The Cleves town hall attack and threatened attack on Coal City was a racial clash at Cleves, Ohio, early on April 9, 1903, in which a band of nearly fifty Black men was reported to have stoned and fired on a hall where young white people were dancing, white men chased them with revolvers, and a patrol was posted to keep "indignant whites" from attacking "the negro settlement at Coal City." Several white dancers and one Black man were slightly hurt, and no attack on Coal City was reported. The story spread as a short wire item under headlines that called the Black attackers a "mob" and "toughs," while the threatened white reprisal appeared only as its last sentence.

episodes.title: Killing of Dan Washington
episodes.lead: The killing of Dan Washington was the shooting death of Washington, a Black man, by Constable DeBerry in the court house at Fairfield, Texas, on the morning of April 6, 1903. The constable fired five times, and the one detailed report said Washington had threatened him but did not fire himself. The killing ran as a brief item in several Texas papers and one Louisiana paper.

episodes.title: Daytona peninsula manhunt and lynching threats (1903)
episodes.lead: The Daytona peninsula manhunt was a search by officers and a crowd of white citizens for an unnamed Black cyclist near Daytona, Florida, on 26 April 1903, during which open threats of lynching were made. The man was never found, and a suspect was released; the Daytona Gazette-News said the incident "came near precipitating mob violence."

episodes.title: Killing and cremation of Albert Washington
episodes.lead: The killing and cremation of Albert Washington was the shooting of a Black man by two police sergeants near Shreveport, Louisiana, on April 11, 1903, and the burning of his body by a mob early the next morning, after he was suspected in the ax murder of Mrs. Alice Matthews. First reported as Ed Porter, he was shot in the back as he ran, and about 100 men later burned his body on a pyre. Within days a coroner's jury attributed the murder to a person unknown, his employers placed him miles away, and papers in both presses reported that an innocent man had been killed.

episodes.title: Assault on Frank Holland and Nelson Peters
episodes.lead: The assault on Frank Holland and Nelson Peters was an attack by striking teamsters on two Black non-union coal drivers at Chestnut and Point streets in Providence, Rhode Island, on the morning of April 18, 1903. After both were beaten and stoned, Holland fired into the crowd and wounded the striker Edward Baxter; a second striker, William O'Neil, was hurt when the discarded revolver went off. The Providence News put the shooting on its front page, and wire reports carried it to New York, Portland, Maine, and Manchester, New Hampshire.

episodes.title: Expulsion of George Brown from Salem, Nebraska
episodes.lead: The expulsion of George Brown from Salem, Nebraska, took place in April 1903, when residents of the town, acting through a citizens' meeting, forced Brown, a Black man from Falls City, to give up a house he had rented there and leave. Brown left after a committee ordered him out, and the dispatches noted that Salem had never had a Black resident. Editors in Iowa, Mississippi and Georgia used the episode to charge Northern Republicans with hypocrisy on race.

episodes.title: Memphis manhunt for George Morgan
episodes.lead: The Memphis manhunt for George Morgan was a search by posses of German residents in Memphis, Tennessee, on April 15, 1903, for Morgan, a Black man accused of shooting and killing a German brewery worker, Adolph Heinz, with the stated aim of lynching him. The posses did not find him, and three months later he was arrested in St. Louis, where he denied the shooting. An Associated Press dispatch about the hunt ran in white newspapers across the South and Midwest.

episodes.title: Lynching of Hensley Johnson
episodes.lead: The lynching of Hensley Johnson was the hanging of a Black man by a mob on the public square of Carthage, in Panola County, Texas, on the night of April 25, 1903. Johnson had been jailed on a charge of assaulting a four-year-old white girl and released on bond, and his body was found the next morning hanging from a telephone pole. A dispatch from Longview carried the story to papers across the country, while a correspondent to the Black paper Western World reported it under an editor's note calling the charge "a lie on its face."

episodes.title: Hutchinson near-lynching (1903)
episodes.lead: The Hutchinson near-lynching was a racial confrontation in Hutchinson, Kansas, reported in April 1903, in which a Black man who stepped on a white man's foot was attacked and, according to a Wichita paper, 'nearly' lynched. No one was reported killed, and the trouble ended when the white man left. The episode is known only from two jesting items in Kansas state-news columns, one of which likened it to the Joplin riot.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching in Indianapolis (April 1903)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching in Indianapolis took place in April 1903, when a crowd of white men sought to kill an unnamed Black man in Indianapolis, Indiana, and the city police called out an alarm to stop them. No death was reported, and the incident survives only in brief comments in Southern white papers, which cited it as proof that lynching was not confined to the South.

episodes.title: Dynamiting of the James store at Beggs, Indian Territory
episodes.lead: The dynamiting of the James store at Beggs, Indian Territory, took place on the night of 25 April 1903, when unidentified whites described as whitecaps blew up the new store of a Black family from Alabama. The blast followed nightly posters showing a Black man hanged and also wrecked a neighboring white-owned drug store, though no one was hurt. The family said it would stay, and several Black editors condemned the attack as an assault on Black business.

episodes.title: Henderson circus shooting
episodes.lead: The Henderson circus shooting was an exchange of gunfire on the night of April 9, 1903, in Henderson, North Carolina, between James Bruce, a young Black man, and two white policemen, John W. Robertson and R. A. Crockett, after the officers moved Bruce out of a white reserved seat at John Sparks' circus. Robertson and Bruce both died in a Raleigh hospital, and Crockett was slightly wounded. White papers blamed Bruce, and a Black paper's letter saying the officers attacked him drew calls that its author leave town.

episodes.title: Whitecapping of Joe Shively and the Stevens women
episodes.lead: The whitecapping of Joe Shively and the Stevens women was a night attack in which white men broke into a house at Bloomington, Indiana, early on April 26, 1903, and whipped Joe Shively, a Black man, and white women of the Stevens family. Governor Durbin threatened to have the State University moved unless the attackers were punished, which made the case a statewide story. Seven men were arrested, but the prosecution stalled, and by October Shively was said to have repudiated his account.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John D. Tross
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John D. Tross took place on the West Side of New York City on the evening of April 15, 1903, when a crowd of two to three hundred men and boys chased Tross, a Black man, into a grocery store and fought the police to take him. Police had charged Tross with shooting and seriously wounding Otto Richter, a picture frame maker. Officers held the store until reserves dispersed the crowd, and wire reports carried the episode across the country as a lynching that police had prevented.

episodes.title: Assault on John Logan
episodes.lead: The assault on John Logan was an attack by three white men on John Logan, a Black hotel bellboy, on South Meridian street in Indianapolis, Indiana, on the night of April 28, 1903. It drew notice because Logan said two patrolmen had used him as a decoy against the "bungaloo" rowdies and then left him, a charge that led the mayor to order an inquiry.

episodes.title: Killing of John Swancey
episodes.lead: The killing of John Swancey was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Mark Crumpley, a man acting as a deputy, at Waverly, Missouri, on the night of the town's city election, Tuesday, April 7, 1903. The shooting came as officers tried to break up an election-night disturbance among Black residents in which the city marshal was beaten. A wire paragraph calling it an election riot started by 'blacks' ran in papers across the country, while Lafayette County papers added a self-defense claim and the visit of the sheriff and coroner.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Turner
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Turner was the hanging of a Black man by a mob at Warren, Arkansas, shortly after midnight on the night of April 5-6, 1903. He had been jailed on a charge of assaulting a white woman, Mrs. W. H. Neely, and was taken from the county jail and hanged in front of the court house. A coroner's inquest attributed the killing to unknown parties, and Black newspapers later entered the case in their lists of the year's lynchings.

episodes.title: Killing of Sarah Nealy
episodes.lead: The killing of Sarah Nealy was the death of a Black woman held as a laborer on Fletcher Turner's plantation about seven miles west of Dadeville, in Tallapoosa County, Alabama, after she was whipped, hung by the wrists and struck with a pistol, according to an affidavit of six Black witnesses. The account surfaced in June 1903 during a federal peonage inquiry and was printed across the country, while Turner said the woman died of disease.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at the Grayson County jail, Texas
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching at the Grayson County jail was a confrontation in Grayson County, Texas, reported in April 1903, in which an armed mob of about a thousand men twice demanded a Black prisoner held on an assault charge. Sheriff Lee McAfee refused to give him up, and the mob turned away. The story ran in the press as a tribute to the sheriff.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Sol Butcher
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Sol Butcher took place near Dresden, Tennessee, in the spring of 1903, when a crowd hunted a Black man accused of cutting the Weakley County sheriff while resisting arrest. Butcher escaped, and the local paper predicted he would be lynched if caught. He was later arrested in Illinois, where he fought extradition on the ground that he would be lynched, but Illinois granted Tennessee's requisition after Weakley County officials gave assurances.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Solomon Glasgow and Charles Strickland
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Solomon Glasgow and Charles Strickland took place at Holly Springs, Marshall County, Mississippi, on the night of April 11, 1903, when a mob came to the jail to hang two Black prisoners who were under sentence of death. Sheriff McWilliams disguised the two men and got them away through the crowd, and the mob found only the sheriff's son, whom it forced to give up the keys. Both men were hanged legally at Holly Springs on June 30, 1903.

episodes.title: Texarkana pest house whitecap raid
episodes.lead: The Texarkana pest house whitecap raid was an attack in early April 1903 by a band of "whitecappers" on the Texarkana pest house, whose only occupant was a lone Black man. Armed citizens met the raiders with a volley and they dispersed; no one was reported hurt. The episode drew notice chiefly because townspeople organized to defend the occupant, which the San Antonio Daily Light praised in an editorial.

episodes.title: Thebes lynching and attack on Black construction camps
episodes.lead: The Thebes lynching and attack on Black construction camps took place on April 26, 1903, near Santa Fe and Thebes in Alexander County, Illinois, when a mob of white farmers took a Black youth of about seventeen from officers and hanged him. The mob then shot into and burned a camp of Black bridge workers. Indictments and trials followed in Cairo without a reported conviction.

episodes.title: Lynching of Thomas Gilyard
episodes.lead: The lynching of Thomas Gilyard took place in Joplin, Missouri, on the evening of April 15, 1903, when a white mob of several hundred broke into the city jail, took out Gilyard, a 20-year-old Black man charged with killing a policeman, and hanged him two blocks away. The mob then burned houses in the Black district and drove Black residents from the city. The man named as its leader was sentenced to ten years and later acquitted on retrial.

episodes.title: Assault on Will Baker at Selma
episodes.lead: The assault on Will Baker at Selma was an attack on a Black man by five or six young white men on the river bank opposite Selma, Alabama, on the afternoon of April 8, 1903. The men struck him, threw him into the river and threatened to cut his throat with a razor, but he survived.

episodes.title: Whipping of Will Sewell
episodes.lead: The whipping of Will Sewell was an attack on a Black farm hand in Pike County, Alabama, one night in April 1903, in which he was tied and beaten with a wagon whip by attackers the reports do not name. He was hurt badly enough that he could not work for three weeks. The whipping became public only in October 1903, as government testimony against six white men charged with whitecapping in the Cross Roads and Linwood beats, where Black residents had been ordered to leave, churches burned and a woman and her baby shot.

episodes.title: Lynching of Amos Randall, Dan Kennedy and Henry Golden
episodes.lead: The lynching of Amos Randall, Dan Kennedy and Henry Golden was the killing by a mob of one white man and two Black men at Mulberry, Polk County, Florida, early on May 20, 1903. Accused of murdering Barney Brown, a white prohibition worker, they were shot by armed men described as unmasked and prominent in the county, and a coroner's jury blamed "persons unknown." Editors remarked chiefly on a white man being lynched with two Black men.

episodes.title: Killing of Andrew Render
episodes.lead: The killing of Andrew Render was the fatal shooting of Andrew ("Andy") Render, a Black man, by town marshal R. L. Paris on the night of May 16, 1903, during the street fair in Hartford, Ohio County, Kentucky. Paris said Render had defied and advanced on him, and five days later a grand jury declined to indict the marshal. The first dispatch drew notice by describing armed Black and white crowds and a vow by white citizens that every Black person in the county would be "exterminated" if anyone tried to take Paris.

episodes.title: Texas, Maryland, dynamite explosions (1903)
episodes.lead: The Texas, Maryland, dynamite explosions were two blasts set off by unknown persons near the village of Texas, on the "N. C. R. R.," on the night of 5-6 May 1903, one of them at the house of a Black man, Arch Wye. Damage was slight and no one was reported hurt, but the local paper said the blasts were rumored to be aimed at intimidating Black and foreign laborers who had come to work at the area's quarries.

episodes.title: Attempted expulsion of Black residents from Ballinger, Texas
episodes.lead: The attempted expulsion of Black residents from Ballinger, Texas, took place in May 1903, when whitecaps signing themselves the "Clearing Committee" posted notices ordering all Black people to leave the town by June 1 or "suffer the consequences." Mayor John Hoffer answered with a proclamation that Black residents should not be molested and deputized citizens to protect them, a response that most of the coverage emphasized. No violence was reported, and the coverage does not show whether any families left.

episodes.title: Beaumont refinery notices
episodes.lead: The Beaumont refinery notices were threats posted in May 1903 at the oil refineries in the South End of Beaumont, Texas, ordering Black workers to leave under threat of death. No attack, arrest or departure of workers was reported in the coverage found. The episode drew comment mainly in the Black press, where a Dallas Express editorial reprinted by the Colored American treated the notices as the work of "whitecaps" trying to drive Black men from their jobs.

episodes.title: Lynching of Benjamin Gorman
episodes.lead: The lynching of Benjamin Gorman took place in Webster County, Georgia, on the evening of Friday, May 29, 1903, when a crowd described as friends of Shelley Kent hanged Gorman, a Black man accused of killing Kent, a young white farmer, with a hoe the day before. According to the Dawson News, the crowd took Gorman from a bailiff who was trying to bring him to jail. An Associated Press dispatch carried the story widely, and Gorman's name later headed lists of June lynchings in white and Black papers.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bob Bryant and Will Morris
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bob Bryant and Will Morris took place before daylight on Sunday, May 3, 1903, when a crowd of armed farmers took the two Black prisoners from sheriff's deputies and hanged them from the Yazoo bridge at Haynes Bluff, near Vicksburg, Mississippi. The men were accused of shooting the planter W. H. Legg, and Bryant was said to have confessed. Within two days dispatches reported that Morris's rope had broken and that he had escaped, a story a Mississippi paper later called untrue.

episodes.title: Pursuit and capture of Calvin Baker
episodes.lead: The pursuit and capture of Calvin Baker was a May 1903 manhunt for a 15-year-old Black boy accused of attempting to assault a five-year-old girl near Phenix City, Alabama. A Columbus, Georgia, dispatch said he would "very likely be lynched on the spot" if the posse caught him. He was instead captured by a ruse and carried to Opelika, the Lee county seat.

episodes.title: Bombing of Ebenezer A.M.E. Church, Evanston
episodes.lead: The bombing of Ebenezer A.M.E. Church in Evanston was a dynamite attack on the night of Friday, May 15, 1903, on the African Methodist Episcopal church of a Black congregation in Evanston, Illinois, a suburb of Chicago. The explosion, set off under the pulpit after the congregation had left, wrecked the interior and front of the building. Papers presented it as the second church bombing in the Chicago area that month and ascribed it either to policy gamblers angered by the pastor's preaching against the game or to Black residents offended by his sermon declaring this "the white man's country"; no one was identified as the bomber.

episodes.title: Warning notices to Black residents of Colorado, Texas (1903)
episodes.lead: The warning notices to Black residents of Colorado, Texas, were notices placed on the town's Black churches in the spring of 1903 warning "the colored people" to leave. The episode is known only from a one-sentence news brief in a Waxahachie paper of 11 May 1903, which gave no author, date or outcome.

episodes.title: 1903 whitecap attacks in Franklin and Amite counties, Mississippi
episodes.lead: The 1903 whitecap attacks in Franklin and Amite counties, Mississippi, were night assaults by bands of "whitecaps" on Black residents of the two counties in late May 1903. In Franklin County the band fired fifty shots into the house of a Black man named Dillon, and in Amite County it shot a Black man who broke away when they tried to whip him. Mississippi papers reported the attacks as a renewal of "whitecapping outrages" that circuit courts had already tried to suppress.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Fremont, Ohio
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black residents from Fremont, Ohio, was the departure of about two dozen Black men and their families from Fremont, Sandusky County, in May 1903, after striking workers of the Clauss Shear Works stormed a Black family's house on the night of May 11. It followed the killing of a striker, Otto Mischke, in a clash involving Black workers hired to replace the strikers, and those who left included long-time residents as well as strikebreakers. Mobs stoned the homes of Black men in Fremont again on May 19.

episodes.title: Killing of George Vann
episodes.lead: The killing of George Vann was the fatal shooting of a Black man during his arrest aboard an excursion train near New Bern, North Carolina, on the night of May 4, 1903. Vann died instantly in a volley of shots as Officer C. Lupton tried to take him off the train, and a deputy, J. B. Dixon, was wounded. Wire reports said officers shot him after he resisted, while a New Bern newspaper and a coroner's jury attributed the fatal shot to persons unknown.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Dearborn County, Indiana
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black residents from Dearborn County, Indiana, took place in late May 1903, after the murder of Rosa Kaiser near Manchester Station was blamed on Black men and a Black suspect, Louis Everson, was threatened with lynching at Lawrenceburg. Everson was released and stoned out of town by a mob, and farmers then ordered Black families and workers out of the county, about 100 by one estimate. The murder remained unsolved in September.

episodes.title: Shooting and attempted lynching of Henry Johnson
episodes.lead: The Kaufman County posse shooting and attempted lynching of Henry Johnson took place in Kaufman County, Texas, in May 1903, when a posse shot a Black man accused of assaulting a white farmer's wife near Kemp and a mob then tried to take him from the Kaufman jail to burn him. Officers and militia sent by the governor kept him from the mob, and within five days he was tried, sentenced to death and hanged in public at Kaufman on May 30. The case drew notice beyond Texas because the speed of the legal hanging led New York papers and a Black columnist to call it 'railroaded'.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of James T. Quarles and Henry Williams
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of James T. Quarles and Henry Williams took place at Nampa, Idaho, shortly after midnight on May 25, 1903, when a crowd broke into the jail to seize the two Black men from Boise after Quarles was accused of shooting a Nampa officer at a baseball game. Officers kept the mob from the prisoners, and Governor Morrison took them to Boise by special train. The attack ran in wire reports as far as Atlanta and Maine, while Idaho papers outside Boise called it exaggerated; Quarles was later convicted of assault with a deadly weapon and fined $150.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Archie Hill
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Archie Hill was a mob's effort to lynch a Black man in Pasadena, California, after he was accused of fatally shooting streetcar conductor Will Carlton in a fare dispute at the end of May or start of June 1903. Hill was lodged in the Los Angeles county jail, and according to the Sedalia Times the 'hoodlum element' of Pasadena then turned on the city's Black residents. Hill was later convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life, an outcome white papers in Kansas and Colorado reported as hometown news about Carlton without any mention of a mob.

episodes.title: Lenox Hotel shooting
episodes.lead: The Lenox Hotel shooting took place on the night of May 2, 1903, in New York City, when three off-duty policemen beat Jefferson Sanders, a Black waiter, with their revolvers in the "black and tan" saloon where he worked, and Sanders shot all three. Patrolman Ernest O. J. Peters and Sergeant Thomas Gilhooley died, while Patrolman Joseph Russo survived. Witnesses said the policemen began the attack, a grand jury declined to indict Sanders, and Black newspapers held up his act as justified self-defense.

episodes.title: Lowrysville lynching threat of 1903
episodes.lead: The Lowrysville lynching threat of 1903 was a reported move by a crowd at Lowrysville, Chester County, South Carolina, to lynch a Black man named Jim Montgomery, later called Jim Gilmore, in early May 1903. Governor Heyward sent the Lee Light Infantry from Chester by special train, and the sheriff took the prisoner to jail without resistance. Papers disagreed over how near a lynching had come, and the man drew renewed notice when he broke out of the Chester jail a month later.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Jim Montgomery
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Jim Montgomery occurred at Lowrysville (also spelled Lowryville), Chester County, South Carolina, on the night of May 4, 1903, when a crowd was reported gathering to lynch Montgomery, a Black man arrested on the accusation of threatening an aged widow with a pistol. Governor Heyward sent the Lee Light Infantry by special train, and the sheriff took the prisoner to the Chester jail without resistance. A Columbia dispatch credited the militia with probably preventing a lynching, while a Chester correspondent called the report "greatly exaggerated"; later reports named the man Jim Gilmore.

episodes.title: Whipping of Jim Pruitt
episodes.lead: The whipping of Jim Pruitt was an attack by a band of white men, called "white cappers" in the press, on a Black man in the Cross Anchor section of Spartanburg County, South Carolina, on a Tuesday night in late May 1903.
