The men took Pruitt from his house, whipped him severely and threatened him and his wife with death if they spoke of it. The case became known when the couple complained to a magistrate in Spartanburg, and a dispatch about it ran in several South Carolina weeklies.

episodes.title: Intimidation of John C. Allgood
episodes.lead: The intimidation of John C. Allgood was a hold-up on May 6, 1903, in which armed, masked men stopped Allgood, a Black rural mail carrier, near Gallatin, Sumner County, Tennessee, and told him he would be killed if he kept the job. Postmaster General H. C. Payne suspended the route, and Northern papers likened the case to the Indianola, Mississippi, post office affair. Local whites denied the hold-up had happened, but a federal inspector found that two men had carried it out; Allgood resigned and the route reopened with a new carrier.

episodes.title: Expulsion of John Dixon from Fremont, Ohio
episodes.lead: The expulsion of John Dixon from Fremont, Ohio, took place on May 19–20, 1903, when a mob stoned the home of Dixon, a Black ("colored") worker at the Clauss shear plant who had not gone out with its strikers, and drove him from town. His wife and children took refuge in the jail, while Dixon hid overnight and escaped to Norwalk. A short dispatch about the attack ran in papers across the country, and two Southern papers later held it up as evidence of mob violence against Black people in the North.

episodes.title: Braggs race riot of May 1903
episodes.lead: The Braggs race riot of May 1903 was an armed confrontation between Black and white residents of Braggs, Indian Territory, eighteen miles northeast of Muskogee, in which a Black man, John Silk, was shot in the back from ambush on May 3. Deputy marshals found the settlement armed but quiet, and on May 5 brought seventeen men, fourteen white and three Black, to Muskogee charged with rioting. An early report of six white men killed ran under the headline "Killed in Race Riot," but later reports named only Silk and a white man, John McBloom, as hurt.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Wood
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Wood took place at Yates Center, Woodson County, Kansas, on the night of May 27-28, 1903, when a mob of about 300 made three attempts on the county jail to seize Wood, a Black man charged with assaulting a farmer's wife, Mrs. Lind. Officers held off the mob and took Wood to Wichita; he was later convicted. The Topeka Plaindealer, a Black weekly, used the episode to explain Kansas's new anti-lynching law.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Johnson at Kaufman, Texas
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Johnson at Kaufman, Texas, took place on May 26, 1903, when a mob tried to take a wounded Black prisoner from the Kaufman County jail in order to burn him. Johnson, accused of assaulting a white farmer's wife, was guarded by the sheriff and by militia. He was tried on May 29 and hanged in public the next day, a speed that several Northern papers and a Black weekly called "railroading."

episodes.title: Killing of the Laurant family near Florenville, Louisiana
episodes.lead: The killing of the Laurant family was the shooting of four Black men of one family, and the wounding of two others, by white men at a logging settlement near Florenville in St. Tammany Parish, Louisiana, on May 9, 1903. The trouble was traced to a white store clerk striking one of the family with an axe handle for failing to address him respectfully. Wire services reported it across the country as a "race riot" or "pitched battle," and the deputies who arrived afterward were reported to have arrested only Black men.

episodes.title: Hunt for a Black suspect in the Seward murder, Putnam County, Indiana
episodes.lead: The hunt for a Black suspect in the Seward murder was a manhunt in Putnam County, Indiana, after Mrs. Henry Seward was beaten to death in her farmhouse near Fern station, west of Greencastle, on May 16, 1903. Searching parties hunted a Black tramp seen boarding a freight train near the house, and a widely reprinted dispatch said they threatened to lynch him if caught. No Black suspect was reported caught, and within days suspicion turned to the woman's husband, who was jailed in July and held for the murder.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Leroy Gibbons
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Leroy Gibbons took place in east Georgia in late May 1903, when white men searching for a missing white farmer, Dupree Holmes, seized Gibbons, an elderly Black man accused of killing him, and whipped his wife until she named him as the killer. Gibbons broke away and surrendered to the sheriff, and Holmes came home alive on May 31, saying he had been ill at a sawmill. Early wire reports said Gibbons had probably been lynched; after Holmes reappeared, Georgia papers and the Black press cited the case against mob law.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Lewis Hubbard
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Lewis Hubbard took place in Ridgely, a village adjoining Springfield, Illinois, in early May 1903, when posses hunted Hubbard, a Black man accused of shooting and killing the village constable, Peter Heck. Wire reports said that if the village posses captured him he would be "summarily dealt with," but he was arrested the next day and said he had fired in self-defense.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Louis Everson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Louis Everson took place in Dearborn County, Indiana, on 23-25 May 1903, when crowds of farmers threatened to lynch Everson, a Black man known as "Black Ponto," held in the Lawrenceburg jail on suspicion of murdering Rosa Kaiser. No witness identified him; after his release a mob stoned, beat and fired at him; one report said a mob tried to lynch him near Aurora. Black papers reported the murder and the drive against Black residents that followed it, but did not name him.

episodes.title: Killing of Mose Hart
episodes.lead: The killing of Mose Hart was the shooting of a Black man by officers and armed citizens in Corinth, Mississippi, on May 20, 1903, after he opened fire in the mayor's court during his trial for carrying concealed weapons. Hart wounded his wife, fled, and barricaded himself in a house, which the crowd set on fire; when he ran out he was shot many times and killed. A wire story about a "posse of citizens" ran nationally, and Black papers later listed the case among the year's lynchings under the name "Mrs. Hart."

episodes.title: Attack on Moses Banks
episodes.lead: The attack on Moses Banks was the beating and pursuit of a Black man by a crowd of white men and boys at a baseball game in Woodstock, Virginia, on 20 May 1903. Banks escaped to a house, where the police chief and the mayor took him to jail. The local Shenandoah Herald, its only known reporter, called it "a small taste of race riot" and urged young Black residents to leave town.

episodes.title: Mount Vernon trolley strike and coercion of Black replacement workers
episodes.lead: The Mount Vernon trolley strike and coercion of Black replacement workers took place on May 5, 1903, when striking Italian laborers in Mount Vernon, New York, drove a gang of Black workers from their trenches and compelled them to join the strikers' union. No one was reported killed or injured, and the strike was settled ten days later on the strikers' terms. New York papers headlined that the Black workers had joined the union "in Terror of Death," while wire copy said they had been "persuaded."

episodes.title: Smith County, Mississippi, attacks on Black residents (1903)
episodes.lead: In May and June 1903, white men in northern Smith County, Mississippi, near Burns, attacked Black residents after a white farmer named Craft was shot from ambush in a dispute over a Black farmhand who had left a crop. After a second white man, James Boyles, was shot on June 5, four Black men and one Black woman were reported killed, eight or ten beaten and most of the Black community ordered to leave. White papers nationwide called it a “race war,” while the Black press carried only short reprinted items.

episodes.title: Bronx asphalt workers incident (1903)
episodes.lead: The Bronx asphalt workers incident took place on 29 May 1903, when a crowd of about 300 Italian union men surrounded 26 Black laborers of the Uvalde Asphalt Company at 175th Street and Grand Concourse in The Bronx, New York City, and frightened them off the job. Police arrested four of the Italians, and the Black workers went back to work under police guard the same day. The episode is known from a single brief item in The Sun of New York.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Newark (May 1903)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching at Newark was an incident on a Sunday in May 1903, probably May 17, in which the people of a town named Newark "started to lynch" an unnamed Black man. It is known from a single editorial paragraph in the Raleigh News & Observer, which reports no outcome and treated the case chiefly as a quarrel among North Carolina newspapers over where the man came from.

episodes.title: Fremont riot (1903)
episodes.lead: The Fremont riot was a clash on the night of May 9, 1903, in Fremont, Ohio, in which Otto Mischke, a white man, was shot dead in a street fight with Black workers hired to replace strikers at the Clauss shear works, after which a crowd surrounded the jail demanding the three Black men arrested. Sheriff Mason held the crowd off, and Wheeler Kimbro, Lorenzo Martin and Walter Stratton were indicted for murder; Martin was convicted of manslaughter in 1904. White papers told it as a lynching averted, while the Cleveland Gazette defended the three as men who had fought off a strikers' mob.

episodes.title: Sixth and Broadway street fight, Paducah (1903)
episodes.lead: The Sixth and Broadway street fight was a brief clash in Paducah, Kentucky, on the late afternoon of 22 May 1903, in which a number of white people joined a fight between white and Black boys and drove off the Black boys and a Black cyclist who had come to their aid. No one was reported hurt, and the only known account is a short item in the Paducah Sun that treated the affair as one of two "lively altercations" without bloodshed.

episodes.title: Threats against Rev. Charles H. Thomas
episodes.lead: The threats against Rev. Charles H. Thomas were anonymous letters sent in May and June 1903 to the pastor of the African Methodist Episcopal church at Belleville, Illinois, ordering him to leave town on penalty of personal injury. The first letter, by Thomas's account, reached him about two weeks before a Black schoolteacher named Wyatt was lynched at Belleville, and it prompted Thomas to warn Governor Yates. The threats drew notice after the governor's office denied receiving that warning and the letter was found in state files.

episodes.title: Killing of Richard Smith
episodes.lead: The killing of Richard Smith took place on May 23, 1903, at the Mobile Lumber Company's mill outside Mobile, Alabama, where Smith, a Black employee, was cut to death after a dispute over his pay with the company's white owner, Marion L. Daugherty, and an employee, H. Ross Rogers. Daugherty and Rogers were charged with murder, and Black co-workers testified that Daugherty had called for Smith's death and fired a pistol at him as he fled. A grand jury did not indict Daugherty, and in July a jury acquitted Rogers of manslaughter on a plea of self-defense.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Riley Park
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Riley Park took place at Clarendon, Arkansas, on the night of May 22, 1903, when about twenty-five men came into town intending to lynch Park, a Black man accused of shooting a white farmer named Fowler. Sheriff Milwee had already sent Park away to Little Rock, and the mob went home without violence. The case drew notice again a month later, when a Clarendon dispatch cited the mob's failure to reach Park as a reason for the lynching of Jack Harris in the same neighborhood.

episodes.title: Posse shooting of an escaped convict near Roanoke, 1903
episodes.lead: The posse shooting of an escaped convict near Roanoke took place in Virginia in May 1903, when a posse of 12 men pursued a Black man accused of fatally wounding a white man and shot him in the face with buckshot. The man escaped the posse but was later arrested at Roanoke by a policeman named Rigney, who stood to collect a $50 reward. The episode is known from a single unsourced paragraph in a Virginia weekly's column of state news.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Dearborn County, Indiana
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black residents from Dearborn County, Indiana, was a campaign by white farmers and crowds in late May 1903 to drive Black families and laborers from the county after Rosa Kaiser, a white girl, was killed and her father beaten near Manchester station. Black residents were ordered out on penalty of death, families were driven from their homes, and the suspect, Louis Everson, was stoned and chased from Lawrenceburg by a mob. Within days the girl's family and the marshal said the killer may have been white.

episodes.title: Milltown, Georgia, committee beating of 1903
episodes.lead: The Milltown, Georgia, committee beating of 1903 was a week of racial conflict in Milltown, Berrien County, in mid-May 1903, in which white residents hunted a Black railroad engineer, Seab Sharp, and a 'committee' beat an unnamed Black man. Sharp escaped, and white citizens petitioned the railroad's owner to stop employing Black engineers. The episode is known from a single Valdosta dispatch printed in the Savannah Morning News.

episodes.title: Columbia circus lynching attempt (1903)
episodes.lead: The Columbia circus lynching attempt took place on the night of May 11, 1903, at a circus in Columbia, Missouri, when a mob of University of Missouri students tried to seize a Black circus employee to hang him from the tent's center pole. The employee, accused of striking a student, escaped under the tent and was not found. Newspapers across the country carried the story under headlines such as 'Race Riot at a Circus', while Columbia's Black weekly blamed the students for the trouble.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Thomas Vaughn
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Thomas Vaughn occurred in Swedesboro, New Jersey, on May 7, 1903, after Vaughn, a Black man from Philadelphia, was accused of shooting his wife on the town's main street. Townspeople threatened to lynch him on the spot, but the threats were discouraged and he was taken to jail at Woodbury.

episodes.title: Union gambling raid killing
episodes.lead: The Union gambling raid killing was the fatal shooting of a Black man named Washington or Columbus Jay by a policeman during a raid on a gambling party in Union, South Carolina, on Saturday night, May 2, 1903. A coroner's jury found that policeman William O'Shields had fired the fatal shot, and he was jailed and tried for murder, but a jury acquitted him in June after deliberating seven minutes. The case drew most comment for the acquittal, which the Abbeville Press and Banner headlined "Acquitted, of Course."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Vine Bryant
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Vine Bryant took place on May 15, 1903, in the Fulton circuit court at Hickman, Kentucky, when spectators rushed a Black defendant on trial for shooting a young white man. Sheriff Carpenter held the crowd back while deputies took Bryant out of the courthouse and on to the Eddyville penitentiary, where he was to serve a five-year sentence. Kentucky papers reported it as a lynching averted only by the officers' quick action, and the story was reprinted as far away as Wichita.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Wheeler Kimbro, Walter Stratton and Lorenzo Martin
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Wheeler Kimbro, Walter Stratton and Lorenzo Martin took place at Fremont, Ohio, early on May 10, 1903, when a crowd surrounded the jail demanding the three Black men, who were charged with killing a white man, Otto Mischke, during a strike at the Clauss shear works. Sheriff Mason threatened to shoot the first man who broke in, the crowd dispersed, and the men were later tried, Martin being convicted of manslaughter in 1904. White papers told it as a sheriff's stand against a mob; the Cleveland Gazette argued that the three had fired in self-defense.

episodes.title: West Liberty ball-ground riot
episodes.lead: The West Liberty ball-ground riot was a clash on May 31, 1903, at the High Bridge baseball ground in West Liberty borough, adjoining Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, in which a white crowd pursued Black men described as gamblers, killed Charles Kelly and dragged William Davis to a tree with a rope on his neck. Sandy Garrett, a Black man who had ordered the gamblers away, died of his wound three days later. Wire reports called it a lynching narrowly averted, Southern editors counted it a Northern lynching, and the Cleveland Gazette denied it was a race riot.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Hickson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of William Hickson took place on the evening of 12 May 1903 on Whisky Chute in East St. Louis, Illinois, when a crowd of residents with a rope chased Hickson, a Black man, through several blocks. Alderman Frank Holten and a police roundsman stopped the mob and took Hickson to the police station, where he was locked up. It is known from a single report in the St. Louis Republic.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Hopkins
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Hopkins took place on the night of May 21, 1903, at White's Mill, Georgia, where a mob shot to death a Black man who was being taken to jail by train. Hopkins had been charged with outraging his nine-year-old stepdaughter at Babcock in Miller County. An Associated Press dispatch from Bainbridge carried the news to papers from Georgia to Maine and Minnesota, several of which headlined the charge against him rather than the killing.

episodes.title: Martin's Ferry mob of May 1903
episodes.lead: The Martin's Ferry mob of May 1903 was a gathering of several hundred people around the building in Martin's Ferry, Ohio, where two Black men suspected of attacking a young white woman were held on the night of 9 May 1903. The crowd made no attempt to take the prisoners and dispersed in about an hour, and the main suspect, William Thompson, could not be identified.

episodes.title: Lynching of an unidentified man near Woodville, Mississippi (1903)
episodes.lead: The lynching of an unidentified man near Woodville, Mississippi, took place in late May 1903, when, according to a wire report, citizens of Wilkinson County lynched a Black man described as a burglar who had confessed to setting fire to a store in Woodville. The victim's name was never given in the coverage found, and the case survives mainly as a one-line news item and as an entry in white and Black lynching tallies for 1903.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Adam Jackson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Adam Jackson took place in Washington County, Tennessee, in June 1903, when a mob caught Jackson, a Black man from Charlotte, North Carolina, accused of assaulting a white woman, and put a rope around his neck. Jackson survived and was bound over to court and jailed at Jonesboro, though the local paper and the wire disagreed on how he was spared. Wire headlines such as "Mob Halts in Lynching" made the rescue the news, and a Virginia editorial cited it as proof that Southern authorities protected accused men.

episodes.title: Lynching of Andrew Diggs
episodes.lead: The lynching of Andrew Diggs was the hanging of a Black man by a masked mob at Scottsboro, Jackson County, Alabama, on the night of June 29–30, 1903, after the mob shot down Sheriff D. O. Austin and took Diggs from the county jail. Diggs had been jailed the day before, accused of attempting to assault the daughter of a Larkinsville physician. Five young white men were arrested, but the county grand jury found no evidence to indict, and Alabama papers treated the case as the state's only lynching of 1903.

episodes.title: Whipping of Henry Meredith
episodes.lead: The whipping of Henry Meredith was an attack on a Black youth at Armstrong, Missouri, on the night of Saturday, June 13, 1903, when a group of townspeople broke open the city jail, took him out of town and whipped him. Meredith, described as "a negro boy," was being held on a charge of cutting another Black youth, and he was given 150 lashes with a harness tug. The St. Louis Republic presented the attack as the work of citizens who had tired of "disregard for the law," and a short digest of it ran in papers in several states.

episodes.title: Wilmington City Hall mob (1903)
episodes.lead: The Wilmington City Hall mob was a crowd of thousands that surrounded the City Hall and police station of Wilmington, Delaware, on June 24, 1903, demanding the release of Arthur Corwell, the only man arrested in the burning of George White, a Black man, two nights earlier. While it waited, the crowd jeered streetcars carrying Black passengers, and according to the New-York Tribune its members dragged Black men and children from the cars and beat them. Officials released Corwell on $5,000 bail that night, after a coroner's jury found that White had been burned by persons unknown, and a magistrate dismissed the case two days later.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Arthur Reese
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Arthur Reese occurred in Moundsville, West Virginia, on the evening of June 27, 1903, when a crowd in the mayor's office cried for the lynching of Reese, a Black coal miner accused of cutting a white painter, Pat Rowan. No attempt was reported; Reese was jailed and held for the grand jury.

episodes.title: Atlanta messenger boys' attacks on Black telegraph messengers
episodes.lead: The Atlanta messenger boys' attacks on Black telegraph messengers took place in Atlanta, Georgia, on June 27 and 28, 1903, when white messenger boys discharged by the Western Union and Postal Telegraph companies beat and stoned the Black men hired to replace them. Several messengers were reported badly bruised or hurt, and police repeatedly scattered the boys, but no deaths or arrests were reported. New York papers carried the story as a messenger boys' "riot," while Black weeklies reprinted it as evidence that Black workers were winning employers' confidence.

episodes.title: Lynching of Banjo Peavy
episodes.lead: The lynching of Banjo Peavy took place at Fort Valley, Georgia, on the night of June 8, 1903, when a crowd of armed men took Peavy, a Black man, from a sheriff's guard and hanged and shot him for the killing of W. Cope Winslow Jr. earlier that day. An Associated Press dispatch carried the story nationally, a coroner's jury found that Peavy died at the hands of "unknown parties," and Black papers noted it only in briefs and lynching lists.

episodes.title: Lynching of Case Jones
episodes.lead: The lynching of Case Jones was the killing of a Black man by a mob at Elk Valley, Tennessee, on the morning of June 24, 1903. Jones was accused of assaulting a young white girl, Margaret Bruce, the day before, and was hanged after being taken from a deputy sheriff. An Associated Press brief carried the story to papers across the country, and Black weeklies reprinted it and listed Jones among the month's lynchings.

episodes.title: Pursuit of a Black strikebreaker on the Alton railroad, Chicago (1903)
episodes.lead: The pursuit of a Black strikebreaker on the Alton railroad was an incident in Chicago, reported in June 1903, in which union men hunted a Black non-union freight unloader employed by the Alton road. Believing that the whites meant to lynch him, the man fled and jumped into the river, and police kept him from drowning. The only account found is a short item in the Polish-language Dziennik Chicagoski, which told it as an aside in its local labor news.

episodes.title: Anonymous letters to Black tenants near Clarendon, Arkansas
episodes.lead: The anonymous letters to Black tenants near Clarendon, Arkansas, were warnings sent in late June 1903 to the Black residents of the Fowler-Coburn neighborhood, a plantation district outside the town, telling them that "the quickest way out of the country was the best." A general departure of the Black farm workers seemed imminent until white landowners who lived in Clarendon visited the district on June 30 and promised protection, after which the tenants agreed to stay. A Clarendon dispatch in the Newport Daily Independent presented the letters as the "financial side" of troubles in the neighborhood that had included a killing and a lynching.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Cliff Weeden
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Cliff Weeden was a near-lynching of a 13-year-old Black boy at Canton on a Monday evening in late June 1903, after he was accused of attempting to assault a 7-year-old white girl. Weeden escaped, and the episode is known only from a three-line item in the Savannah Morning News.

episodes.title: Cooper whippings
episodes.lead: The Cooper whippings were floggings of Black men at Cooper, Delta County, Texas, in June 1903, after which the men were driven from the county. According to a Dallas dispatch, three Black "leaders" were taken from their homes and flogged on a Wednesday night, three others had been whipped a week earlier, and notices posted around the town warned Black residents to leave. Papers carried two differing accounts, one calling the victims criminals, the other tying the floggings to criticism of a Black man's prison sentence.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Henry Washington and Cora Bolen
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Henry Washington and Cora Bolen took place in Sharon, Pennsylvania, in early June 1903, when a crowd made threats of lynching against the two Black prisoners, who had been jailed over the death of Washington's six-year-old son. The crowd "lacked a leader" and no attack followed; both prisoners were tried later that month, convicted and sentenced.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Dan Hinds
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Dan Hinds took place on the afternoon of June 5, 1903, at a button factory in Madison, Indiana, where young men employed at the factory seized Hinds, an 18-year-old Black man, put a rope around his neck and threatened to hang him. They accused him of attempting to assault a white girl who worked there, but held him until the sheriff arrested him, and he was kept for the grand jury. A brief wire account circulated nationally, and two papers printed it as an instance of "mob law".

episodes.title: Beating of Dillard Freeman
episodes.lead: The beating of Dillard Freeman was an assault on a Black worker in Lowndes County, Alabama, by three members of the Dixon family, whose brother, the county sheriff, was accused of holding Freeman and others as peons. By his own account to federal prosecutors in June 1903, he was dragged seven miles by a rope around his neck and whipped with a gin strap for visiting his mother without permission, then threatened with death if he testified truthfully. Carried in a Montgomery dispatch by white weeklies and Black papers, the case was offered as proof that peonage amounted to slavery.

episodes.title: Killings of Ned Roberts and Elijah Anderson
episodes.lead: The killings of Ned Roberts and Elijah Anderson were the shootings of two Black levee workers by levee guards in East St. Louis, Illinois, on the night of June 9-10, 1903, a few hours before a flood broke through the city's Illinois Central embankment. According to the most widely reprinted wire report, seven men fired on Roberts after he demanded his pay and threatened to break the dike, and a guard killed Anderson for refusing to work. The two deaths ran as a few lines inside national flood coverage, in two conflicting wire versions and a brief item in the St. Louis Palladium, and no inquest or arrest was reported.

episodes.title: Enigma shooting into Black shanties
episodes.lead: The Enigma shooting into Black shanties was a night attack on 11 June 1903 at Enigma, Georgia, in which unknown parties fired into the homes of Black residents of the town's still quarter. No one was killed, and warrants were said to have been issued for some of the leaders. The episode is known from a single paragraph in a Tifton correspondence column of the Savannah Morning News.

episodes.title: Killing of Eugene Burke
episodes.lead: The killing of Eugene Burke was the fatal shooting of Eugene Burke (also spelled Burk), a Black hotel worker, by a white pursuer after a crowd chased him from near the Kingan packing plant in Indianapolis, Indiana, on June 9, 1903. Burke had been accused of insulting a thirteen-year-old white girl, and the man who fired, Meade Barr, was later convicted of manslaughter. Editors North and South called it a lynching.

episodes.title: Pursuit of a Black man in Chester County, Pennsylvania (1903)
episodes.lead: The pursuit of a Black man in Chester County, Pennsylvania, was a manhunt by a crowd of white residents in about June 1903 after the man was said to have shot and killed a farmer. No report of its outcome appears in the coverage, and the episode is known only from a Maryland editorial that cited it as evidence that lynching had spread to the North.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black workers from the Evansville and Princeton traction line
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black workers from the Evansville and Princeton traction line took place on June 3, 1903, when white workers drove thirty Black laborers from a construction job on the company's traction line in Gibson County, Indiana. The Black men were ordered out of the county and were allowed back only under an arrangement with the contractor that barred them from any work white men wanted. Southern papers picked up the Indianapolis dispatch and used it to argue that the North was hostile to Black workers.

episodes.title: Whipping and expulsion of Black residents of Cooper, Texas
episodes.lead: The whipping and expulsion of Black residents of Cooper, Texas, was a pair of night floggings in June 1903 in which six Black men in Cooper, Delta County, were whipped a week apart and the men flogged were compelled to leave the county. A Dallas dispatch said the men were charged with criticizing the life sentence given a Black man for attempted assault, while a New Orleans dispatch described those whipped as loafers and petty criminals driven out by "the Regulars." Northern and Southern papers carried the story as part of a reported Southern drive to push "disorderly" Black people north.

episodes.title: Whitecap shooting on the Day place, Amite County, Mississippi
episodes.lead: The whitecap shooting on the Day place was an attack in June 1903 in which unidentified men described as whitecaps fired into the homes of two Black families on the Day place in Amite County, Mississippi, wounding an elderly Black man. No arrests were reported, and Mississippi papers carried the attack as a sign that whitecapping had "again broke loose" in the county.

episodes.title: Keysville white cap notices (1903)
episodes.lead: The Keysville white cap notices were written threats posted in June 1903 near Keysville, in Charlotte County, Virginia, ordering an unnamed Black woman to leave within ten days or be "roughly handled." The authors, who called themselves white caps and claimed fifteen members, were not identified, and the only known report is a short item in the Richmond Times-Dispatch.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching at the McDonald colliery, Fayette County, West Virginia
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching at the McDonald colliery was an averted lynching of an unnamed Black striker in Fayette County, West Virginia, on June 3, 1903, after a shot he fired killed a company guard, William Mann. He was taken from a crowd of 'angry men' to the county jail, and two West Virginia papers reported the case as an episode of the New River coal strike.

episodes.title: Whitecapping of Fleming Brown
episodes.lead: The whitecapping of Fleming Brown was a night visit by a neighbors' "committee of safety" to the home of Fleming Brown, a Black man living near Ashby in the Cumberland, Virginia, neighborhood, in late spring 1903. The band, which a Washington paper called "Whitecaps," reportedly made Brown "pay well" for allegedly beating his young ward after a court had declined to take her from his care.

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank Dupree
episodes.lead: The lynching of Frank Dupree took place near Forest Hill, Rapides Parish, Louisiana, in June 1903, when a mob took Dupree, a young Black man, from the officer carrying him to jail and hanged and shot him. Dupree had been arrested on the accusation that he killed J. M. Ditter, a white carpenter, at the Long Leaf mill on June 11. The case ran as a short wire story across the South and later appeared in the monthly lynching lists of both white and Black papers.

episodes.title: Lynching of Garfield McCoy, Wiley Anette and George McKinney
episodes.lead: The lynching of Garfield McCoy, Wiley Anette and George McKinney took place early on June 26, 1903, when a mob took the three Black men from the jail at Newton, Baker County, Georgia, hanged them from one tree a mile west of town and fired hundreds of shots into their bodies. They were awaiting trial for the murder of F. S. Bullard, a white farmer shot at a dance on his farm the previous Saturday. Editors in and outside Georgia noted that the men had not been lynched for the "usual crime" and that their trial had never been in doubt.

episodes.title: Mobbing of George Jerome and expulsion of Black men from Howell, Indiana
episodes.lead: The mobbing of George Jerome and expulsion of Black men from Howell, Indiana, took place on June 16, 1903, when white townsmen at Howell, near Evansville, forced a Black streetcar conductor off his car and that night beat three other Black men and drove them out of town at revolver point. No arrests were reported, and Southern editors took up the case as evidence of Northern hostility toward Black workers.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Kincaid
episodes.lead: The lynching of George Kincaid was the killing of a Black man whose body was found hanging in a swamp near Cleveland, Mississippi, in late June 1903, days after a mob gathered at Ruleville to lynch him. Kincaid was accused of having seriously wounded two white men, John Brock and George Stoakley, five years earlier. Wire reports said a deputy sheriff had surrendered him on a written order to a man named Jackson, and the New York Sun reported that no one knew who killed him. Papers in the North headlined the five-year gap between the alleged shooting and the hanging, and the case was carried in the year's lynching lists.

episodes.title: Eighth Avenue crowd pursuit of George Smith
episodes.lead: The Eighth Avenue crowd pursuit of George Smith took place in Manhattan on the night of about 11 June 1903, when white men chased Smith, a 19-year-old Black man accused of insulting a woman and slashing her escort with a razor. Police arrested Smith, and he was held on a charge of felonious assault. The Evening World put the crowd at about 500 and described the episode as "almost a race riot."

episodes.title: Lynching of George White
episodes.lead: The lynching of George White took place on the night of June 22-23, 1903, when a crowd of several thousand broke into the New Castle County workhouse near Wilmington, Delaware, and burned White, a Black man charged with killing Helen S. Bishop, at a stake in a nearby field. A boy in the attacking crowd was fatally shot, and in September a grand jury declined to indict anyone.

episodes.title: Whipping of Henry Meredith
episodes.lead: The whipping of Henry Meredith took place on the night of Saturday, June 13, 1903, at Armstrong, Missouri, when a group of citizens broke open the city jail, took out Meredith, a Black youth held on a charge of cutting another Black boy, and gave him 150 lashes with a harness tug. Meredith was not killed, and no arrests of the men who whipped him were reported. Missouri and Kansas papers carried the story as a short item, and the fuller accounts presented the whipping as a community's answer to lawlessness.

episodes.title: 1903 Smith County, Mississippi, mob killings and expulsion
episodes.lead: The 1903 Smith County, Mississippi, mob killings and expulsion were an attack by armed white men on a Black settlement near the Smith–Scott county line in early June 1903, in which four or five Black people, one a woman, were killed and eight or ten were beaten. The raid followed the ambush killing of a white man named Craft and the wounding of another, Boyle, which white reports attributed to Black men. The surviving Black residents were ordered out, and lynching lists in both presses counted the dead.

episodes.title: Riverside Park attack (Indianapolis, 1903)
episodes.lead: The Riverside Park attack was an assault by a gang of white youths known as the "Bungaloos" on Black visitors to Riverside Park in Indianapolis, Indiana, on the night of Sunday, June 7, 1903. Gang members picketed the street-car lines, kept Black passengers on the cars and stoned Black people who took refuge in them, striking several people. No arrests were reported, but the attack led city park and police officials to post patrolmen in the parks, and both the white Indianapolis Journal and the Black Indianapolis Freeman called for action against "Bungalooism."

episodes.title: Lynching of Jack Harris
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jack Harris was the hanging of a Black man by a mob at Clarendon, Arkansas, shortly after midnight on June 25, 1903. Harris, accused of assaulting his white landlord John Coburn, was taken from a guard with whom the sheriff had hidden him in a barn. Arkansas papers described the sheriff's failed ruse in detail, and a week later Black tenants near Coburn's farm received anonymous letters telling them to leave.

episodes.title: Stoning of Jacob Clarkson
episodes.lead: The stoning of Jacob Clarkson was a street attack on 29 June 1903, at the corner of Fifth and Franklin streets, evidently in Wilmington, Delaware, in which three youths shouted "Lynch the nigger" at Clarkson, a Black man, and threw stones at him. The three were convicted of disorderly conduct in City Court the next day and fined $5 and costs each. The case survives only as a short item in the Wilmington Evening Journal's court column.

episodes.title: Beating of James Gale
episodes.lead: The beating of James Gale was a mob assault on the night of 24 June 1903, in which a crowd knocked down and severely beat Gale, a Black man of 716 Wilson Street, at Fifth and King streets, apparently in Wilmington, Delaware. Gale escaped to the police station, where his injuries were dressed. He was one of a number of Black people attacked in the streets that night, and the only one named in the reports.

episodes.title: Lonoke whitecapping shooting
episodes.lead: The Lonoke whitecapping shooting was a night attack in June 1903 in which masked white men with shotguns fired into a camp of three Black timber cutters about five miles from Lonoke, Arkansas. One of the men, called Bob Anderson in the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic and Bob Armstrong in a later state news item, was reported killed, though the first briefs said only that he was thought or believed to have died. Three white farmers were arrested on a charge of white-capping and held to the grand jury, and Arkansas papers presented the case as an effort by Lonoke's "better element" to end whitecapping.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Dennis
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Dennis was the hanging of a Black man, also reported as Robert Denis or Robert Dennis, by a mob in Greenville, Washington County, Mississippi, on the afternoon of June 4, 1903. Accused of attempting to assault a white woman who worked at the telephone exchange, he was taken from the county jail and hanged in front of the exchange before hundreds of onlookers. Northern papers seized on a baseball game postponed so the crowd could watch, and J. K. Vardaman later praised the lynching while campaigning in Mississippi.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Tom Manns, Ed Morris and Charles Sanders
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Tom Manns, Ed Morris and Charles Sanders was a series of mob gatherings in Maysville, Kentucky, from February to June 1903 against three Black men accused of robbing and shooting John B. Farrow, an elderly farmer. On June 16, 1903, the three were tried under the guard of state troops with a Gatling gun and a Hotchkiss gun. No lynching took place; all three went to the penitentiary, and wire reports of the military guard ran across the country.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of dining-car porters at Raton
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of dining-car porters at Raton was an attack by a mob of nearly two hundred men on the Colfax County jail at Raton, New Mexico Territory, on the night of June 11, 1903, aimed at five Black porters held for the fatal shooting of Night Marshal John Jones. The sheriff had already removed the prisoners, who reached the Las Vegas jail unharmed, and New Mexico editors cited the case, and the jailing of two mob leaders, as proof of fitness for statehood.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John McCray
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John McCray took place in Peoria, Illinois, on June 23-24, 1903, when crowds of a thousand or more besieged the jails to seize McCray, a Black man accused of killing Detective William E. Murphy. Police and deputies held the crowds off, and the sheriff secretly moved McCray to Galesburg. McCray was later convicted and hanged legally on December 11, 1903, still denying the killing, after a reprieve that a Peoria judge said fed "the spirit of mob law."

episodes.title: Lynching of Lamb Whitely
episodes.lead: The lynching of Lamb Whitely was the killing of a Black man by a mob on the Smithland plantation near Monterey Landing, Concordia Parish, Louisiana, reported from Jonesville on June 26, 1903. According to the dispatch, Whitely was accused of assaulting a white man, and the mob took him to the woods and "riddled his body with bullets." The brief wire report ran in white papers across the country and in the Baltimore Afro-American, and the case was entered in monthly and year-end lists of lynchings, but no follow-up report was found.

episodes.title: Ninth Street riot (Wilmington, Delaware, 1903)
episodes.lead: The Ninth Street riot was a gunfight between an armed crowd of Black men and a party of white men in Wilmington, Delaware, on the night of June 25, 1903, three days after a white mob burned George White at the stake. Two policemen and at least two Black men were wounded, and two Black men were clubbed, arrested and sentenced the next day. A Black man, William Kramer, was fatally shot nearby the same night in a killing a coroner's jury laid to another Black man.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Ben Lee
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Ben Lee took place on the night of June 12, 1903, when a crowd broke into the jail at Greenville, Illinois, to seize Lee, a Black prisoner accused of assaulting a white woman. Sheriff Floyd had driven Lee away hours earlier, and the mob found the jail empty. Newspapers across the country carried the story as 'a second attempt at lynching in Illinois within a week.'

episodes.title: Killing of Ned Roberts
episodes.lead: The killing of Ned Roberts was the fatal shooting of a Black levee worker by armed men guarding a dike in East St. Louis, Illinois, on the night of June 9, 1903, a few hours before the Illinois Central embankment broke and flooded much of the city. Wire reports said he had demanded his pay and threatened to break the dike, and that seven men fired on him at once. The shooting was reported as a paragraph inside national flood coverage, and several papers paired it with the killing of a second Black worker, Elijah Anderson, by a guard for refusing to work.

episodes.title: Whipping of Ned Sparkman
episodes.lead: The whipping of Ned Sparkman was an attack by a crowd of masked men on a Black preacher at his house near Bethune, South Carolina, in late June 1903. The attackers whipped him, fired into his house, wounding him in the face, and ordered him to leave the community. The papers disagreed on whether the attackers were white or Black.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Mat Kimble
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Mat Kimble took place at New Braunfels, Texas, in early July 1903, when armed posses and then a crowd of several hundred people sought a Black man accused of attacking Mrs. Emil Gronle, a farmer's wife, on June 30. Kimble was captured on July 4 and, after a crowd at New Braunfels demanded him the next day, was taken to San Antonio in a woman's dress under militia guard. Papers across the country ran a wire report predicting a lynching, while later San Antonio reports raised doubts about Kimble's guilt.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Oscar Franklin
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Oscar Franklin took place in Manhattan, New York City, on the night of 28 June 1903, when a crowd that had followed a policeman chasing Franklin, a Black waiter, yelled for him to be lynched as he was dragged from a cellar. Franklin had been accused of stabbing the hand of a Chinese restaurant keeper, Loo Sung. The officer drove the crowd back and took Franklin to the station.

episodes.title: Attack on Peter Stark by militiamen at Griffin, Georgia
episodes.lead: The attack on Peter Stark by militiamen at Griffin, Georgia, took place on the afternoon of June 29, 1903, when soldiers of the Second Regiment, encamped in the town, rushed Stark, a Black man, on Hill street after a dispute with one of their sergeants. Citizens and police rescued him, and the mayor dismissed the cases against all parties. The Savannah Morning News reported that a clash between soldiers and townspeople had been narrowly averted.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black workers from the Raton round house
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black workers from the Raton round house took place in June 1903, when white employees of the Santa Fe railway round house at Raton, New Mexico Territory, drove their Black co-workers off the job with picks and shovels. It followed the killing of a Raton marshal by a Black train porter, and it was reported in a single item in the Santa Fe New Mexican.

episodes.title: Lynching of Reuben Elrod
episodes.lead: The lynching of Reuben Elrod was the shooting death of an elderly Black man by a band of white men at his home near Piedmont, Anderson County, South Carolina, on the night of June 30, 1903. The men also beat the Black women who lived in the house and ordered them to leave, and an inquest found that Elrod had died at the hands of parties unknown. South Carolina papers reported that the killing was condemned around Piedmont, and the Black press later counted it among the lynchings of 1903.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Sherman Stevens
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Sherman Stevens took place in Randolph County, Alabama, in the summer of 1903, when a crowd planned to take Stevens, a Black prisoner accused of killing his father, from the jail at Wedowee. Sheriff Kent and a deputy moved him to Opelika before the crowd assembled, and the Montgomery Advertiser headed its report "Lynching Prevented." Open lynching threats were made again at his trial in August, and he was convicted, sentenced to death and legally hanged at Wedowee in September.

episodes.title: Snyder hotel crowd of 1903
episodes.lead: The Snyder hotel crowd of 1903 was an incident in Snyder, reported in late June 1903, in which a crowd went to a hotel to demand a Black man who had come to town as a traveling man's packer. The man was not found, and the only report described the town as determined to let no Black person remain there.

episodes.title: Manhunt for the assailant of Florence Bruno and Annie Green
episodes.lead: The manhunt for the assailant of Florence Bruno and Annie Green was an armed search by hundreds of farmers, police and deputies east of East St. Louis, Illinois, begun on June 23, 1903, for an unidentified Black man accused of assaulting a white girl and a Black woman. Dispatches predicted he would be lynched or shot on sight, but no report shows the searchers seizing or harming anyone. Bruno died the next day; Green survived and later identified James Cross, who as James Northcross was sentenced to forty years for assaulting her.

episodes.title: Notices ordering Black residents out of the Egypt community, Kaufman County, Texas
episodes.lead: In early June 1903, notices ordering all Black residents to leave the Egypt community in Kaufman County, Texas, "under penalty of their lives" were reported posted there, signed "Mobbers." A Terrell dispatch linked the notices to the place where a white woman, Mrs. Whitworth, had been assaulted the week before, a crime for which a Black man had been hanged at Kaufman on May 30. No report of who posted the notices or whether anyone left has been found.

episodes.title: Killing of an alleged looter in the 1903 Topeka flood
episodes.lead: The killing of an alleged looter in the 1903 Topeka flood was the shooting of an unnamed Black man by a volunteer rescue party from St. Joseph, Missouri, in flooded Topeka, Kansas, in the days before June 3, 1903. The rescuers reported that they had caught him 'in the act of looting deserted houses' and shot him dead. The killing was known only from the rescuers' own report, which a wire dispatch carried to papers across the country and to at least one Black weekly as a sentence in a story about rescued schoolchildren.

episodes.title: Lynching of David Wyatt
episodes.lead: The lynching of David Wyatt took place at Belleville, St. Clair County, Illinois, on the night of June 6, 1903, when a crowd broke into the county jail, took out Wyatt, a Black school teacher held for shooting County School Superintendent Charles Hertel, and hanged and burned him on the public square. Hertel survived, and the burning drew comparisons with the Kishineff massacre and protest meetings among Black Chicagoans. Eleven men later pleaded guilty to rioting and were fined $50 each.

episodes.title: Belleview Lake revolver threat (Waterbury, 1903)
episodes.lead: The Belleview Lake revolver threat was an incident near Waterbury, Connecticut, about June 3, 1903, in which eight strike-breakers working the city's trolley lines drew revolvers on an unnamed Black man they believed had insulted them. No one was reported hurt, and the only known account came from the striking trolley men's executive committee, which used it to press the police and the company to rein in the strike-breakers.

episodes.title: Warning notice to Black residents of Waxahachie, Texas
episodes.lead: The warning notice to Black residents of Waxahachie, Texas, was an anonymous hand-lettered notice, found posted near the Central passenger station on the morning of 27 June 1903, that ordered all Black residents to leave the town within four days. The local daily that reported it supposed the notice to be a boy's prank, and no departures, violence or follow-up were reported.

episodes.title: Peonage of Will Waters
episodes.lead: The peonage of Will Waters was the seizure, whipping and forced return to work of Waters, a Black farm laborer, by three young white farmers of Jasper County, Georgia, in 1903, after he left his employer while in debt. William Shy, Arthur Glawson and Robert Turner pleaded guilty in the federal court at Macon on June 24, 1903, and Judge Emory Speer fined each $1,000 but suspended most of the fine. Speer called it the first such crime he knew of in Georgia, and papers often printed the case beside the Alabama peonage conviction of J. W. Pace.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Spencer
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of William Spencer occurred on June 15, 1903, in the Criminal Courts Building in New York City, when a crowd of men tried to take Spencer, a Black man, from a detective minutes after he shot and killed Charles F. McFarlane of the Anti-Policy Society. Police held the crowd back, and Spencer was indicted for first-degree murder within about two hours. He was convicted and sentenced to death the next month, and the Court of Appeals confirmed the conviction in November 1904. Wire stories outside New York presented the episode as a near-lynching in a northern courthouse, under headlines such as "Tried to Lynch the Murderer."

episodes.title: Whipping of Williams in Lee County, Georgia
episodes.lead: The whipping of Williams in Lee County, Georgia, was an attack in about June 1903 in which a committee of white farmers whipped a Black preacher from Columbus and ordered him to leave the county. The farmers blamed Williams for a wave of quitting and wage demands among Black servants and field hands, and the only known report, in the Americus Times-Recorder, treated the whipping as a deserved rebuke to a "walking delegate."

episodes.title: Whipping of Lorenzo Williams
episodes.lead: The whipping of Lorenzo Williams was an assault on a Black man by two sons of John T. Phillips near Norway, South Carolina, on Saturday, June 27, 1903, after Williams was accused of swearing at one of them. The Columbia State's correspondent presented it as the start of the trouble that ended four days later in the lynching of Charles Evans, a friend of Williams who had protested the whipping.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Abner Debleu from Chinook
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Abner Debleu from Chinook took place on July 31, 1903, when residents of Chinook, a small river town reached by steamer from Astoria, Oregon, ordered Debleu, a Black man, to leave over what they called his laziness. After weighing whether to lynch him or tar and feather him, they paid $2.75 to have him shipped to Astoria, where police jailed him and then put him aboard a boat for Portland. The Morning Astorian followed the case in three mocking items and reported that Debleu soon returned to Chinook to show he was not afraid.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Bill Grant
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Bill Grant took place at Bainbridge, Georgia, on the night of July 16, 1903, when a group of men held up a deputy sheriff, demanded the keys to the county jail and gathered with threats near the railroad depot. Grant, a Black prisoner, had been sentenced to hang for the murder of a white man and had just been granted a new trial. The sheriff called out the local military company, which guarded the jail with sworn deputies, and Grant was not harmed.

episodes.title: Attacks on Black sailors at Bar Harbor
episodes.lead: The attacks on Black sailors at Bar Harbor were a series of assaults in July 1903 in which white enlisted men from a fleet of United States warships drove Black crewmen out of a naval YMCA tent and beat and chased them through the streets of Bar Harbor, Maine. No one was reported killed, and after the night of the attacks Black sailors were reported to stay off the shore after dark. Northern papers reported the clash as a "race war" in the navy, and Southern editorials later used it to argue against the enlistment of Black men.

episodes.title: Barbourville posse fight (1903)
episodes.lead: The Barbourville posse fight was a gunfight on the night of July 12, 1903, near Barbourville, Kentucky, between deputy sheriffs of Barbourville and a band of eight Black men from Clay county whom the deputies were pursuing. About twenty shots were fired and one of the men was dangerously wounded, while the rest escaped into Clay county. The only account is a short Associated Press dispatch, which ran in at least sixteen white papers across the country.

episodes.title: Bartlesville vigilance committee ultimatum (1903)
episodes.lead: The Bartlesville vigilance committee ultimatum was an attempt in July 1903 by white union men in Bartlesville, Indian Territory, to drive Black laborers out of the town. Angered that a local man had hired Black workers, they formed a vigilance committee, ordered the Black men out, and threatened one at gunpoint; some fled on foot toward Kansas.

episodes.title: Thomasville posse shooting of Bill Davis
episodes.lead: The Thomasville posse shooting of Bill Davis took place on Sunday night, July 5, 1903, when a marshal and five other men exchanged gunfire with Davis, a Black man, while trying to arrest him at a cabin in Thomasville. Davis escaped under fire, two posse members were slightly wounded, and whites afterward "chastised" some Black onlookers. The only known report, in the Montgomery Advertiser, called it a "battle with posse."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Bud Scipio
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Bud Scipio was a pursuit in July 1903 by a posse of citizens of Coffeyville, Kansas, who said they would lynch Scipio, a Black man accused of assaulting Mrs. Maud Walker, a white woman, on July 15. Scipio escaped into Indian Territory and was captured a week later at Nowata, then returned to Coffeyville, where no mob demonstration was reported and he was committed to jail to await a preliminary hearing. Kansas papers carried the pursuit under headlines such as "Are Bent on Lynching," and the wire version ran as far as Missouri and West Virginia.

episodes.title: Bath Beach manhunt for Calvin R. Ferguson
episodes.lead: The Bath Beach manhunt for Calvin R. Ferguson took place in Brooklyn, New York, on July 4, 1903, when armed citizens, train passengers and police hunted a Black man accused of cutting a conductor and a guard with a razor, and members of the search party threatened to lynch him. Ferguson was captured after a seven-hour search and taken to the Bath Beach police station unharmed, and was held for felonious assault. New York's Evening World headlined the capture as a crowd that "Sought to Lynch Negro," while other New York papers reported it as a man hunt without mention of lynching.

episodes.title: Cambridge Uncle Tom's Cabin disturbance
episodes.lead: The Cambridge Uncle Tom's Cabin disturbance was a disorder in Cambridge, Maryland, in early July 1903 or shortly before, following a traveling company's performance of "Uncle Tom's Cabin." A Montgomery, Alabama, editorial said it ended with "a number" of Black residents beaten, though no attackers were named. The episode reached the press only as a reason Maryland officials gave for barring the same play from two other Eastern Shore towns.

episodes.title: Killing of Richard Dukes
episodes.lead: The killing of Richard Dukes was a night attack in early July 1903 near River Junction in which a party of Black and white men tried to kill Cebe Dukes, a Black man, and then shot his father, Richard Dukes, to death and burned his house. Cebe Dukes escaped with a shoulder wound, and the only report found, a brief item in the Savannah Morning News, gave no motive and named no attackers.

episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Evans
episodes.lead: The lynching of Charles Evans took place at Norway, Orangeburg County, South Carolina, early on July 1, 1903, when a white crowd took Evans, a Black man described as a "mulatto," from the town guardhouse, hanged him and shot his body. Evans was suspected of shooting John T. Phillips, a white Confederate veteran, at his supper table, and before the lynching the crowd whipped three or four other Black men. It drew notice because the Columbia State's correspondent said it came close to justifying lynching, and because Black residents' later gathering brought militia to the town.

episodes.title: Lorain mob attack on Charles Hall and Robert Pleasant
episodes.lead: The Lorain mob attack on Charles Hall and Robert Pleasant took place on the night of 28 July 1903 in Lorain, Ohio, when a crowd of about 300 white men chased two Black men through the south end of the city, threatening to lynch them. The crowd stoned a saloon where one of the men hid and fired shots, but no one was killed; Pleasant was jailed and the mayor persuaded the mob to disperse. Because one wire copy carried a Lawrence, Massachusetts dateline, some southern papers treated the episode as proof that lynching had reached New England.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Lockett
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Charles Lockett took place in Atlanta, Georgia, on the afternoon of July 13, 1903, when a large crowd gathered at a house on Central Street where Lockett, a Black man, had been seized after being accused of attacking Mrs. Susie Wells. Despite "many threats of lynching," patrolmen removed Lockett by a back street and lodged him in the Tower. The incident is known from a single telegraph dispatch printed in the New-York Tribune under the headline "Negro Saved from Atlanta Mob."

episodes.title: Warning to Black residents of Bloomfield, Indiana (1903)
episodes.lead: The warning to Black residents of Bloomfield, Indiana, was a letter received in mid-July 1903 by Charles Shelton, a Black resident of the Greene County town, ordering all Black people to leave the county by July 25. The letter claimed to come from a "committee" of citizens of nearby Linton and threatened that those who stayed would "receive a visit." Papers treated it as an outgrowth of anti-Black feeling at Linton, where a mob had just driven out a group of Black waiters.

episodes.title: Suspected lynching of Cleveland Kelly
episodes.lead: The suspected lynching of Cleveland Kelly was the disappearance of Kelly, a 19-year-old Black man, in July 1903 while a posse pursued him into a swamp near Newborn, Newton County, Georgia. The posse returned saying it had lost him, but a dispatch from Madison, Georgia, reprinted widely in the white press, said it was "almost absolutely certain" that he had been captured and lynched. No report of a body, an inquest or arrests appears in the coverage, and the killing was never confirmed beyond that belief and a later news digest's statement that he "was lynched near Madison, Ga."

episodes.title: Lynching of Crane Green
episodes.lead: The lynching of Crane Green was the hanging of a Black mill worker by a mob near Warren, Arkansas, on the night of Sunday, July 19, 1903. Accused of assaulting a 13-year-old white girl, Green was taken from officers who were bringing him to jail and hanged from a tree beside the Kingsland road. The lynchers were not identified, and the Associated Press carried the event to papers across the country in a single sentence datelined Pine Bluff.

episodes.title: Mob attack on Daniel Lewis
episodes.lead: The mob attack on Daniel Lewis took place in July 1903 near Ninety-fourth Street and First Avenue in New York City, when a crowd of men chased Lewis, a Black man, shouted "Lynch him!" and, by one account, beat him after an encounter with two girls carrying ice. Police took him from the crowd, and a magistrate sent him to Bellevue to be examined as to his sanity. Outside New York the incident circulated as a single paragraph in wire reports of a deadly heat wave, under headlines saying he had narrowly escaped lynching.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Daniel Reed
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Daniel Reed took place in Alexandria, Indiana, on the night of July 26, 1903, when a mob pursued a Black saloon porter accused of assaulting a man and a woman. The porter escaped in the darkness, and the episode was reported in two special dispatches the following day.

episodes.title: Attack on Deb Flynn in Marinette
episodes.lead: The attack on Deb Flynn in Marinette was a mob assault on a Black hotel porter at a street carnival in Marinette, Wisconsin, on the night of July 9, 1903, after white men objected to his walking with a white girl. Flynn escaped a crowd armed with hammers, was hidden overnight and was taken out of town the next day. The Associated Press carried the story nationally, and Southern papers used it to mock the North and to say the white girl deserved punishment.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dennis Head
episodes.lead: The lynching of Dennis Head was the killing of a Black man by a party of white men searching for a murder suspect near Chinquepin, Aiken County, South Carolina, in the night of July 15–16, 1903. The searchers were hunting George Edwards, a Black man accused of shooting William Hall, the white postmaster at Chinquepin, the previous afternoon. Early dispatches reported a "double lynching" that also killed Jesse Butler, but later reports said Butler escaped, and Governor D. C. Heyward called Head's killing an "inhuman outrage."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Dock Bacon and Anderson Finch
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Dock Bacon and Anderson Finch took place at Chase City, Mecklenburg County, Virginia, early on July 24, 1903, when armed white men gathered to take summary action against two Black prisoners accused of attempting to assault a white woman. The crowd desisted, and both men were convicted within a week and legally hanged, Finch on September 2 and Bacon on October 3, after Finch recanted his testimony against Bacon. The Richmond Planet called Bacon's execution "a judicial murder."

episodes.title: Lynching of an unidentified man near Eastman, Georgia
episodes.lead: The lynching of an unidentified man near Eastman, Georgia, took place on July 14, 1903, when a mob of about fifty men hanged and shot a Black man in southern Dodge County, believing him to be Ed Claus, accused of assaulting a white woman near Darien Junction. Late-July wires from Atlanta and Savannah reported that the dead man was innocent and that Claus had been found alive, and papers North and South and in the Black press then treated it as a mob killing the wrong man.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Ed and Rosa Hutcheson
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Ed and Rosa Hutcheson took place at Stevenson, Jackson County, Alabama, on July 19, 1903, when about fifty men closed around the Black couple as an officer hurried them onto a train after their arrest. The couple, charged with writing an obscene letter to the daughter of a prominent Stevenson man, were jailed under armed guard at Scottsboro and later fined $500 and sentenced to six months' hard labor. Rosa Hutcheson escaped with her infant after sentencing and was recaptured soon afterward.

episodes.title: Lower Merion manhunt for Elias Williams
episodes.lead: The Lower Merion manhunt for Elias Williams was a search by an armed citizens' posse in Lower Merion township, Pennsylvania, on 29 July 1903 for a Black man thought to be Williams, who was accused of killing Percy White. Residents had shot at the man two days earlier without hitting him, and the local police chief concluded that he was an escaped convict, "Cracker" Crummity, not Williams. Williams himself was arrested in Maryland on 31 July, amid reports that threats to lynch him were frequent.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Ernest Blakeney
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Ernest Blakeney occurred on July 9, 1903, near O. K. in Lancaster County, South Carolina, when a crowd gathered to hunt down a 19-year-old Black farm hand accused of climbing into the bedroom window of his employer's daughter. After the crowd agreed that he ought to be killed, men among it, including the young woman's father and brother, persuaded it to hand him to the sheriff. South Carolina papers praised the county for letting the law take its course, and in October Blakeney was sentenced to life imprisonment for burglary.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Esau Lovely
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Esau Lovely took place on the night of July 12, 1903, when a crowd of 200 to 400 men gathered at the St. Mary Parish jail in Franklin, Louisiana, to lynch Lovely, a Black prisoner accused of robbing a white woman that morning. U.S. Senator Murphy J. Foster, two judges and the sheriff persuaded the crowd to disperse by promising a speedy trial, and the next morning Lovely pleaded guilty and was sentenced to thirty-four years in the penitentiary. Papers nationally credited Foster and treated the case as a sign of a turn against lynching.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Eugene Smith
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Eugene Smith took place in Liberty, Sullivan County, New York, on the night of Sunday, July 12, 1903, when a crowd beat Smith, a Black porter accused of assaulting a young girl in a boarding house. Citizens took him from the crowd to jail, and he was given a hearing before a judge.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black telephone workers from Madison County, North Carolina
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black telephone workers from Madison County, North Carolina, took place on July 17, 1903, when armed white men ordered a camp of about fifty Black employees of the Southern Bell Telephone and Telegraph Company out of the Doggett section of the county and fired a volley of shots as they left. No one was reported killed or injured, and no report of arrests appears in the coverage. An Associated Press dispatch from Asheville carried the story to papers from Vermont to Alabama, and North Carolina Democratic papers used it to point out that the county was a Republican stronghold and the home of Senator Pritchard.

episodes.title: Nutbush township whipping (1903)
episodes.lead: The Nutbush township whipping was an attack in late July 1903 in which about forty masked men beat and whipped a Black man in Nutbush township, apparently in Warren County, North Carolina. The victim had been charged with burning the Kimball stables that spring, but a grand jury had declined to indict him, and he was not expected to recover.

episodes.title: Barbour County whitecapping (1903)
episodes.lead: The Barbour County whitecapping was a campaign of threats and night attacks by a band of white men, called whitecaps, against Black residents of one part of Barbour County, Alabama, in the summer of 1903. Reports said Black laborers were driven off several large plantations and warned to leave under penalty of death, and a federal prosecutor described one man being beaten and lashed. The case led to arrests by federal officers, guilty pleas to assault and battery in the county court, and six federal conspiracy indictments in January 1904.

episodes.title: Barbour County whitecapping (1903)
episodes.lead: The Barbour County whitecapping of 1903 was a campaign of threats and night violence by bands of white men, called "whitecaps," against Black farm laborers in Barbour County, Alabama, in the summer of 1903. Black laborers were reported driven off several plantations under threat of death, and federal officers arrested seven Barbour men in September. In January 1904 a federal grand jury indicted six of them for conspiring to intimidate four named Black residents.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Frank Clark
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Frank Clark was a manhunt in late July 1903 in which several hundred armed farmers around Kahoka, Clark County, Missouri, hunted Clark, called a "negro" in most reports, vowing to lynch him for an alleged assault on a white girl, Ollie Hess. Wire reports from Farmington, Iowa, said he was surrounded and would soon be lynched, but the man surrounded was someone else and the mobs dispersed without catching him. Arrested in Illinois in September, Clark was convicted at Kahoka and legally hanged there on November 25, 1903, two hours early because officials feared a mob.

episodes.title: Lynching of Cato Garrett
episodes.lead: The lynching of Cato Garrett took place on July 7, 1903, when masked men stopped a passenger train at Stout's Crossing, a flag station south of Vicksburg, Mississippi, took Garrett, a 17-year-old Black youth, from the officer escorting him, and hanged him from a bridge. A special grand jury had indicted him that morning for the killing of Harry Stout, a white farmer, and he was being returned to Vicksburg for trial. The Associated Press carried the story nationally, and the Seattle Republican, a Black weekly, later entered Garrett's name in a list of the year's lynchings headed "Mobocracy's Bloody Reign."

episodes.title: Mutilation of George Houston
episodes.lead: The mutilation of George Houston was an attack on a Black hackman by a mob of about 100 masked, armed men in Tampa, Florida, on the night of July 30, 1903. The mob took Houston from a city detective who was taking him to the county jail, drove him outside the city limits, and mutilated him, but left him alive. A second masked mob shot a Black tailor the next night, and within weeks Houston had left the city.

episodes.title: Killing of George Johnson in Ensley
episodes.lead: The killing of George Johnson in Ensley was the fatal shooting of a Black drayman by Special Officer Williams, Ensley's sanitary inspector, on the morning of July 28, 1903, during a quarrel over a tax. Williams gave himself up, and the only report found presented his claim that Johnson had been about to strike him with a chair.

episodes.title: Posse pursuit of Gus Epps
episodes.lead: The posse pursuit of Gus Epps took place near Huntington, West Virginia, on July 19, 1903, when about twenty armed young men chased Epps, a Black man accused of stabbing William Vinson, and fired an estimated fifty shots at him. A wire dispatch reported that Epps drowned under fire in Twelve Pole river, and one Illinois paper headed the story "Mob Kills Another Negro." Local papers reported instead that he escaped across the creek, was arrested in Ironton, Ohio, that night, and was later sentenced to two years in the state penitentiary.

episodes.title: Killing of Henry Small
episodes.lead: The killing of Henry Small was the shooting of a Black man by a Chesterfield County constable and two other men on a farm near Jarratt, Sussex County, Virginia, on Sunday, July 26, 1903. The men were seeking the attacker of three white women near Centralia five days earlier and shot Small as he ran from them; a coroner's jury called the killing justifiable homicide. Richmond papers had followed the armed manhunt day by day, and the killing was reported as far away as New York.

episodes.title: Whipping of Herman Morrison
episodes.lead: The whipping of Herman Morrison was an assault on July 16, 1903, near Bedford, Indiana, in which a group of white boys tied Morrison, a fifteen-year-old Black boy, to a tree or bush and whipped him. Mayor Smith fined each of the white boys $10.50, then fined Morrison and a white companion the same for an earlier whipping of another boy. The Indianapolis Journal called the boys "youthful whitecappers" imitating whitecappings in nearby counties.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Isaac Ford
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Isaac Ford took place in July 1903 in Grayson County, Texas, after Ford, a young Black man, was arrested near Sherman and charged with criminal assault on a seven-year-old girl. Officers moved him in secret to the Fort Worth jail, and on July 23 he hanged himself there. The Associated Press reported that mob violence had been threatened, and papers outside Texas headlined the death as a suicide to avoid lynching.

episodes.title: Lynching of J. D. Mayfield
episodes.lead: The lynching of J. D. Mayfield took place in Danville, Illinois, on the night of July 25, 1903, when a white mob seized a Black man held for the fatal shooting of Henry Gatterman, a white butcher, hanged him from a pole and burned his body before the county jail. The mob then besieged the jail to lynch a second Black prisoner, James Wilson, until Sheriff H. H. Whitlock and his deputies fired into it. A coroner's jury blamed persons unknown, but twelve members of the jail mob went to prison, and both presses held up the sheriff as a model.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of James Little
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of James Little took place in Greene County, New York, on July 14 and 15, 1903, when crowds of farmers, striking moulders and river men sought to lynch Little, a 19-year-old Black man accused of criminally assaulting 11-year-old Emma Cole near New Baltimore. Deputies moved him from the Coxsackie lockup to the Catskill jail before the crowd acted, and the next day disarmed the girl's father, who drew a revolver when Little was brought back for arraignment. Wire dispatches carried the case nationally, and Southern papers cited it as a Northern instance of the "usual crime" and the mob.

episodes.title: Leesburg lynching tree incident
episodes.lead: The Leesburg lynching tree incident took place near Leesburg, Virginia, at the end of July 1903, when Black members of the District of Columbia National Guard's First Separate Battalion were accused of cutting down the tree from which a Black man named Craven had been lynched the year before. Cavalrymen fired on the fleeing guardsmen, townspeople talked of lynching them, and the mayor of Leesburg fined one of them, Private James Poe. The Evening Star and a brigade officer called the conviction a travesty of justice, and the affair led to a libel suit against the Washington Evening Star.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of James Taylor
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of James Taylor took place in New Rochelle, New York, on July 14, 1903, when a crowd surrounded Taylor, a Black assistant to the city poundkeeper, after he shot a fox terrier, and shouted "Lynch him." A policeman arrested Taylor, who was fined $3 and held for trial on a charge of cruelty to animals. The New York Evening World carried the only known report, as a comic item under the headline "Wanted to Lynch the Dog-Catcher."

episodes.title: Dynamiting of Jasper Smitherman's house
episodes.lead: The dynamiting of Jasper Smitherman's house was an attack in July 1903 in which a number of white men at Brookside, a mining camp in Alabama, blew up the home of Smitherman, a Black man, expecting to find him inside. Smitherman was not at home, and both he and the white woman whose friendship with him had set off the attack left Brookside for an unknown destination. The Montgomery Advertiser carried the episode in two short items based on the account of the town's mayor, Wiley Burton.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jennie Steer
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jennie Steer was the killing of a Black woman by a mob on the Beard plantation near Shreveport, Louisiana, in late July 1903. Accused of poisoning sixteen-year-old Lizzie Dolan with lemonade, Steer was pursued by a posse, hanged from a tree, and shot, while denying the charge to the end. Papers across the country carried the story, and two papers called it the first lynching of a Black woman in that part of the state or anywhere.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Jim Stevens
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Jim Stevens took place in Charlottesville, Virginia, in the early morning of July 4, 1903, when about forty persons came close to lynching Stevens, a young Black man accused of robbing a trunk in a private residence. The threat arose from a rumor that he had attempted an assault, a charge the women of the house rejected. Stevens was later convicted of the robbery and sentenced to two years in the penitentiary.

episodes.title: Cole City convict mine shooting
