episodes.lead: The Cole City convict mine shooting took place on July 24, 1903, when state guards at the Dade County coal mines at Cole City (also spelled Coal City), Georgia, fired on Black convicts who had refused to come out of the mine at the change of shifts. Early wire reports said two convicts were fatally wounded, but a later Atlanta account named three wounded men, Joe Beck, "Snaps" Jordan and an unnamed convict, and reported no deaths. Newspapers across the country carried the story as a convict "mutiny," and the Savannah Tribune printed a version of it on its front page.

episodes.title: Flogging of John Brown
episodes.lead: The flogging of John Brown was an attack by a posse of local citizens on a Black man near Fort Madison, South Carolina, on the night of Thursday, July 2, 1903. Accused of attempting to assault a white woman, Brown was tied to a trestle, whipped, and released on a promise to leave South Carolina for good. The only account, a Seneca dispatch, presented the flogging as an alternative to lynching.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John Coppedge
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of John Coppedge took place in Nashville, Nash county, North Carolina, in July and September 1903, when local talk of lynching followed his arrest and later his sentencing for breaking into a widow's house. Officers moved him to the Wilson jail and, after his trial, guarded him overnight and took him to the state penitentiary, and no attack on him was reported. North Carolina papers covered the case chiefly as a story of the woman's courage, and the trial judge praised the county for letting the law take its course.

episodes.title: Portsmouth lynching threats of 1903
episodes.lead: The Portsmouth lynching threats of 1903 were threats of mob violence in July 1903 against George Washington Griggs, a young Black man held in the jail at Portsmouth, Virginia, on a charge of assaulting the four-year-old daughter of a Port Norfolk dairyman. A group of men from Port Norfolk came to the jail soon after his arrest, but the sheriff's armed guard kept the prisoner and no violence followed. Griggs was convicted and sentenced to eighteen years in the penitentiary, and a Richmond paper reported that lynching had also been threatened against John Edwards, a Black man tried in the same court for assaulting an eleven-year-old Black girl.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Gilbert
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Gilbert was the hanging of a Black man by neighbors of a wounded white planter near Pinckney Landing, Arkansas, about thirty miles south of Memphis, in July 1903. Gilbert, charged with being implicated in the shooting of the planter H. J. Hubert, had been bound over by a magistrate when a mob took him from the officers and hanged him to a tree. The story ran as a wire item in more than two dozen white papers, while a second Black man, Jim Hawke, was named as the actual shooter and became the subject of a governor's reward.

episodes.title: Evansville mob assault on John Hawkins
episodes.lead: The Evansville mob assault on John Hawkins took place on the evening of July 28, 1903, when a mob chased and assaulted Hawkins, a Black man, on the streets of Evansville, Indiana. The next morning a city judge fined one participant, Jacob Keil, and two other young men were arrested as members of the mob, one of whom, Albert Merkel, was later tried for assault and battery. Papers noted the case for the judge's declaration that Black people had the same rights as whites under the law, and as one of a series of 'race outbreaks' in the city after rioting earlier that month.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Osborne
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Osborne took place on the night of July 2, 1903, when a crowd of several hundred people took Osborne, a young Black man, from two officers on a road near Indian Trail in Union County, North Carolina, and hanged him from a tree. Osborne had been charged with assaulting and robbing Mrs. Lizzie Wentz, an elderly white widow, and had been bound over for trial hours earlier. The Associated Press carried the story nationally, while North Carolina papers presented the hanging as deserved and reported no move to prosecute the mob.

episodes.title: Expulsion of John Johnson from Decatur, Indiana
episodes.lead: The expulsion of John Johnson from Decatur, Indiana, occurred on Friday evening, July 3, 1903, when a mob attacked a Black man from Wren, Ohio, who had come to town to trade, and chased him out. Two policemen clubbed members of the mob and saw Johnson off by the Erie railroad, but the mob achieved its purpose of banishing him. The only person punished, Will Foreman, was fined one dollar and costs, a sentence carried by wire across the country and called "a travesty of justice" by the Indianapolis Journal.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Joseph Johnson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Joseph Johnson was a mob attack on a Black man in the quarry district north of Lemont, Illinois, reported in a Joliet dispatch dated July 1, 1903. A crowd of nearly 300 Slavs and Poles chased, beat and fired at Johnson after he was found asleep in a woman's bedroom, but he escaped alive. The dispatch credited his survival to his "fleetness of foot" and added that he was later adjudged insane.

episodes.title: Shooting of Lazard James
episodes.lead: The shooting of Lazard James took place in the Plaquemine Point section of St. Landry Parish, Louisiana, in late July 1903, when Deputy Sheriff Robert Milsted shot James, a Black landowner, through the eye during a dispute at James's home. James was badly wounded but was expected to recover. The only known account, in the Opelousas St. Landry Clarion, gave the deputy's version and presented the case as evidence of rising defiance among Black residents of the parish.

episodes.title: Evansville race riot of 1903
episodes.lead: The Evansville race riot of 1903 was a series of white mob attacks in Evansville, Indiana, on July 5 and 6, 1903, first on the county jail to lynch Lee Brown (Robert Lee), a Black man accused of killing a policeman, and then on Black residents. On July 6 militia guarding the jail fired into the crowd, killing ten by the coroner's count, while many Black residents fled. Black papers stressed that no white woman figured in the case and saw mob violence spreading north.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black waiters from Linton, Indiana
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black waiters from Linton, Indiana, occurred on July 6, 1903, when a crowd in the mining town drove out eight Black men from Terre Haute who had come to serve an Elks banquet. The crowd threatened to dynamite the hall unless the men were sent away, and they were hurried out of town; no one was reported hurt. Coming in the week of the Evansville riot, it was cited by editors as evidence that mob action against Black people was spreading in the North.

episodes.title: Exclusion of Wallace circus's Black workers from Linton, Indiana
episodes.lead: The exclusion of Wallace circus's Black workers from Linton, Indiana, took place on July 13, 1903, when residents of the coal-mining town barred the circus's Black employees from entering. The circus left its Black workers, about sixty by one account, outside Linton and gave its show without them, and no violence was reported. The threat followed by a week the expulsion of Black waiters from the town, and the governor held a militia company ready. Southern papers later used the story to answer Northern criticism of the South's treatment of Black people.

episodes.title: Logansport manhunt
episodes.lead: The Logansport manhunt was an armed pursuit in late July 1903 by farmers of Harrison township, near Logansport, Indiana, of an unidentified man accused of attacking Mrs. Joseph Watts near her home, which wire reports said would likely end in a lynching. After a chase with bloodhounds on July 28, the posse concluded that the man had escaped by train, and no capture was reported. Dispatches called the armed crowd a "posse" "intent on lynching," a usage the Baltimore Sun mocked and the Baltimore Afro-American put in quotation marks.

episodes.title: Killing of Louis Hogan
episodes.lead: The killing of Louis Hogan was the death of a Black youth of about nineteen, beaten and stamped upon by white men on the night of July 4, 1903, near a saloon at Oxon Hill, Prince George's County, Maryland. A coroner's jury that included five Black members held three white men, Ernest Allen and Joseph and Jesse Sansbury, for trial. Only Allen was indicted and tried; he was convicted of manslaughter in April 1904 and pardoned by the governor that December.

episodes.title: Whitecap attack on Lucius Brownlee
episodes.lead: The whitecap attack on Lucius Brownlee was a night shooting in Monroe County, Georgia, in July 1903, in which a band the Tribune called 'whitecaps' fired on Brownlee, a Black man who had testified in federal court in a moonshine case, and ordered him to leave the county. Five Monroe County men were charged in federal court with conspiring to drive him out to prevent his testimony, and all were acquitted at Macon in June 1904.

episodes.title: Mob attack on M. M. Wadkins
episodes.lead: The mob attack on M. M. Wadkins took place in Tampa, Florida, on the night of July 31, 1903, when masked men surrounded the house of Wadkins, a Black tailor, and shot him twice as he fled. Wadkins survived by taking refuge on the roof of another house, and police then guarded him. Wire reports presented it as the second mob attack in Tampa in two nights.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Knightsville, Indiana
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching at Knightsville, Indiana, was a pursuit on the night of Friday, 10 July 1903, in which a posse of men tracked an unnamed Black man to his home after Mamie Goodhue accused him of trying to break into her room. The man and his family escaped before the posse could take him, leaving their belongings behind. A Brazil dispatch described the episode as a lynching "narrowly averted."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Marion, Ohio (1903)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching at Marion, Ohio, was a mob's effort to lynch an unnamed Black man on a Sunday evening in mid-1903, known only from a passing reference in an Atlanta Constitution editorial. The editorial gave no outcome, accusation or name, and used the episode to rebuke a Northern critic of Southern lynching.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Andrew Gilford
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Andrew Gilford took place in Mendota, Illinois, in early July 1903, when crowds talked of lynching Gilford, a Black man from Princeton jailed for stabbing a white man, Albert Kane. Mayor Brown swore in special police, who dispersed a mob at the jail and kept it under heavy guard. A wire dispatch carried the story under the headline "Another Outbreak of the Mob Spirit."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Minnie Pearl
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Minnie Pearl took place in Peoria, Illinois, on the night of Sunday, July 5, 1903, when a mob of white people went to the home of Minnie Pearl, a Black woman, intending to kill her. Police had already arrested her, and the mob instead tore down her house and threw her furniture into the river. Wire reports of the averted lynching ran in white papers across the country and were reprinted in two Black weeklies.

episodes.title: Attempted lynchings of Joe Scott and expulsion of Black residents from Montevideo, Minnesota
episodes.lead: The attempted lynchings of Joe Scott were two attempts by armed crowds in Chippewa County, Minnesota, in July 1903 to take Scott, a Black man accused of an axe assault on a white woman, from officers; Black residents were also driven from Montevideo. Officers held off several hundred men at the Montevideo depot on July 19 and outran a second mob from Minnesota Falls on July 22. Scott pleaded guilty in November and was sentenced to thirty years.

episodes.title: Killing of Mooney Allen
episodes.lead: The killing of Mooney Allen was the shooting of a Black man by a crowd of armed citizens in the streets of Beaumont, Texas, on July 23, 1903, after he was accused of shooting Policeman Walter Skensbury. Pursuers fired on Allen until he fell dead, with Sheriff Landry joining the chase; one account put the crowd in the hundreds. The Associated Press story ran across the country within a week, some papers calling the killing a lynching, and two Black newspapers later listed Allen among the year's lynching victims.

episodes.title: New Bern State Guard chase of 1903
episodes.lead: The New Bern State Guard chase of 1903 occurred on the morning of July 28, 1903, when soldiers of the Second Regiment of the North Carolina State Guard, passing through New Bern on their way home from encampment, chased a young Black boy until he fell on the railroad track and broke his leg. No one was identified or punished, and the Charlotte Observer later called such conduct "a reproach to the State Guard."

episodes.title: Attempted expulsion of Black residents from Orchard Park, Oklahoma City
episodes.lead: The attempted expulsion of Black residents from Orchard Park was a 1903 campaign by armed white men to drive Black families out of Orchard Park, a residence suburb of Oklahoma City, Oklahoma Territory. It began around July 30 with a masked night visit that gave a Black household twenty-four hours to leave and turned officers away at rifle point, and on August 8 a house being built for a Black woman named Warner was dynamited. The Black residents refused to leave and armed themselves, and papers across the country reported a threatened "race war".

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Ore Brown
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Ore Brown took place in Madison, Wisconsin, on July 2, 1903, when railroad men threatened to lynch Brown, a young Black man accused of attempting to assault two little girls near the State Capitol. Police captured and guarded him, no mob formed, and he later pleaded guilty and was sentenced to six years in state prison. The New-York Tribune presented the episode as a lynching prevented by prompt police action, while a wire version circulated in Midwestern papers under headlines about lynching talk and a "foul crime."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Willie and Otho Green
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Willie and Otho Green was a pair of mob actions in western Virginia in July and August 1903, in which armed men tried to seize two Black prisoners accused of shooting Harry Rudisill, first by firing into a train near Clifton Forge and then by threatening the jail at Covington. No one was hurt, and troops escorted the two men by special train to Lynchburg and then to Bedford City. Wire services carried the train shooting nationally; the Covington standoff was reported mainly in Virginia.

episodes.title: Pell City mob attack
episodes.lead: The Pell City mob attack occurred on Saturday, July 18, 1903, near Pell City, St. Clair County, Alabama, when a crowd of thirty or more white men chased a Black man to his home, fired on it, and that night burned a neighboring Black family's dwelling. The man and a child were wounded, two of the white pursuers were shot, and the burned-out family was left homeless. It drew notice because Judge A. H. Alston summoned a special grand jury and denounced the burning, a charge two Alabama dailies reprinted and praised.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Perry Griffin
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Perry Griffin took place on 13 July 1903 in Mount Vernon, New York, when a crowd surrounded Griffin, a 23-year-old Black coachman, crying "Lynch him" after he shot and killed another Black coachman, Eli Brown, in front of the City Hall. Six policemen escorted Griffin through the crowd to the station house, and he was later held in the White Plains jail to await trial for murder. The story ran in New York dailies and, through a short wire report, in papers in other states, with headlines that credited the police with keeping the crowd from the prisoner.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Peter Gillette
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Peter Gillette took place at Whitehall, Washington County, New York, on July 16, 1903, when a crowd threatened to lynch Gillette, a Black man held on a charge of assaulting a fifteen-year-old girl. The Whitehall chief of police removed him by train to the county jail at Salem, and no lynching occurred. Papers from New York to South Carolina carried the story, most as a lynching narrowly averted in a northern state, one as a lynching that had taken place.

episodes.title: Radford Fair Grounds lynching threat
episodes.lead: The Radford Fair Grounds lynching threat was an episode on July 4, 1903, at the races in Radford, Virginia, in which a crowd cried for the lynching of an unnamed Black man accused of striking a white man with a whip. A former United States marshal quieted the crowd and a sergeant took the man to jail, and no injury to him was reported. Richmond and Washington papers reported it as violence narrowly averted.

episodes.title: Red Bank lynching threat (1903)
episodes.lead: The Red Bank lynching threat of July 1903 was a threatened lynching in Red Bank, New Jersey, on July 14, 1903, when a crowd gathered at the town lockup after Thomas Thomas, alias Thomas Drum, a Black ex-convict, was arrested on charges of burglarizing the home of Mayor O. E. Davis and attempting to assault his daughter, Grace Davis. Police hurried the prisoner to the county jail at Freehold, and no attempt was made to seize him. He was indicted two days later and convicted within a week, and several white papers held up the case as an example of law prevailing over mob violence.

episodes.title: Whipping of a Black woman at Blue Ridge Springs, Virginia
episodes.lead: The whipping of a Black woman at Blue Ridge Springs, Virginia, took place on a Saturday night in late July 1903, when a party of white men beat an unnamed Black woman accused of insulting the wife of a local physician, Dr. Early. The papers treated it as notable less for the whipping than for what followed: Black residents were reported buying guns and ammunition in Roanoke, whites armed, and dispatches warned of a threatened race riot.

episodes.title: Killing of Robert Good (John Goodwin)
episodes.lead: The killing of Robert Good, also reported as John Goodwin, was the shooting death of a Black man by pursuing white citizens near McGehee, Arkansas, on 3 July 1903, hours after he was accused of firing the shot that killed railway conductor B. L. Wright. Wire reports said a posse killed him while he resisted arrest, but the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic, citing sheriff's officers, said two unidentified men ambushed him with shotguns before any officer arrived. No arrest was reported, and the story ran widely in white papers as the killing of a conductor by a 'boisterous negro'.

episodes.title: Shanghaiing of eight Black men from Savannah
episodes.lead: The shanghaiing of eight Black men from Savannah was the shipment of eight Black laborers from Savannah, Georgia, aboard the Russian bark Alice in July 1903 for a voyage to Bristol, England, where, by their account, they arrived beaten and were discharged unpaid. Harry Olsen, a Savannah sailor runner, and Jack Johnson, his Black runner, were arrested that September, and in April 1904 a federal jury convicted Olsen, who was sentenced to five years. Papers likened the practice to peonage, and the Savannah Morning News called it the first shanghaiing case brought under the federal kidnapping statute.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Sour Lake, Texas
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black residents from Sour Lake, Texas, took place on July 9, 1903, when notices ordered Black people out of the oil town and a mob raided Black labor camps that night. It followed a report that a railroad brakeman had been shot by a Black man at Nome Junction. Fifty to two hundred people were reported driven out; within days Black workers were promised protection and began to return.

episodes.title: Vineland street fight of 1903
episodes.lead: The Vineland street fight of 1903 was a clash on the night of July 26, 1903, in Vineland, New Jersey, in which a crowd knocked down a Black police officer, John Shockley, and struck and chased a Black man named Thomas. No one was killed, and the officer, Thomas and a man named Tony Robinson were all arrested. The Bridgeton Pioneer reported it as a "race clash" that "nearly resulted in a riot."

episodes.title: Lynching of an unidentified Black man near Alto, Texas
episodes.lead: The lynching of an unidentified Black man near Alto, Texas, was reported on July 31, 1903, after a crowd took the man from a constable who had arrested him for allegedly cursing women and firing into their house. A Dallas News special carried by the Associated Press said he was lynched in the river bottom by a mob, while a report from Tyler said searching parties had not found his body. The item ran in at least seventeen white newspapers, several of which headlined the accusation as the reason for the killing.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black strangers from Vincennes, Indiana
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black strangers from Vincennes, Indiana, took place in July 1903, when city police were reported to be ordering all 'strange negroes' out of town after the Evansville race riot. The order was reported alongside the July 13 arrest of Henry Thomas, a Black man accused by a police commissioner of shouldering whites off a sidewalk. Only the Louisville Courier-Journal's correspondent reported the order directly, and Kentucky papers repeated it in short news notes.

episodes.title: Attempted expulsion of W. M. Grayor from Paducah
episodes.lead: The attempted expulsion of W. M. Grayor from Paducah was a failed effort on the night of July 8, 1903, by a group of Paducah residents to escort Grayor, a Black street preacher, out of the Kentucky city and warn him not to return. The group acted the day a special judge fined Grayor for speeches said to incite race trouble, but could not find him. The episode is known only from a single report in the Paducah Sun, which attributed it to unnamed "reports."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Everidge Williams and Walter Brown
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Everidge Williams and Walter Brown was an effort by United States soldiers from Fort Leavenworth and a number of citizens to lynch two Black men at their homes in Leavenworth, Kansas, on the night of Sunday, July 12, 1903. Armed police got both men to the police station before the crowd could act, and no one was killed. The soldiers' part drew editorial comment, and the Secretary of War later told a Black editor that the press account was not correct.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Riley and Andrew Kelly
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of William Riley and Andrew Kelly took place at Asbury Park, New Jersey, on the night of July 5, 1903, when citizens of nearby Eatontown set out to seize the two Black men from the Neptune township lockup after they were charged with running down a young white woman on a bicycle. The township police chief guarded the jail and moved the prisoners to the county jail at Freehold, and the crowd dispersed. Coming the same week as the Evansville riot, the case was cited in several editorials as proof that mob law had spread to the North.

episodes.title: Shooting of Willie Page
episodes.lead: The shooting of Willie Page took place on the Mobile, Alabama, river front, probably on 1 July 1903, when Special Policeman Jerry Lynch of the Louisville & Nashville Railroad fired into a crowd of Black boys and wounded 13-year-old Willie Page in the hip. The boy was treated and sent home, and the only report, in the Montgomery Advertiser, gave the officer's reason as an attempt to frighten two boys who were fighting.

episodes.title: West Sixty-second Street riot (New York, 1903)
episodes.lead: The West Sixty-second Street riot was a clash on the evening of Sunday, July 12, 1903, between New York policemen and Black residents of the tenement block on West Sixty-second Street between West End and Amsterdam avenues, set off by a patrolman's attempt to arrest a Black man. Bricks and shots were exchanged, reserves from three police stations cleared the street, and two Black men, William Johnson and William Brackett, were among those arrested; no deaths were reported. Wire services carried it nationally as a "race riot," and a report that white crowds had attacked Black people in the neighborhood drew Southern editorial comment.

episodes.title: Lynching of Amos Jones
episodes.lead: The lynching of Amos Jones took place at Hattiesburg, Mississippi, on the night of Saturday, August 8, 1903, when a mob broke into the jail, took Jones, a Black prisoner, from his cell, and hanged and shot him. Jones was accused of shooting the jailer, M. M. Sexton, during an attempt by prisoners to break jail. Wire reports of the jail break-in, carried from Massachusetts to Arizona, said the mob had tied up the sheriff and that the governor's order to protect Jones arrived too late.

episodes.title: Whipping of Annie Miller
episodes.lead: The whipping of Annie Miller was the public lashing of a young Black woman at or near Vanceville, Bossier Parish, Louisiana, in mid-August 1903, after she confessed to writing a threatening letter to a white planter over a Black man's name. Her confession came while that man and her father were jailed and reportedly about to be lynched; the men were released, and residents had her whipped and ordered her out of the parish.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Bert Hazelock
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Bert Hazelock was an assault by a white crowd on a Black man in Albany, New York, on the afternoon of August 2, 1903, after he was accused of cutting a white man with a razor during a street fight. The crowd chased him through the streets, and a thrown paving stone broke his arm before he took refuge in a house that the crowd surrounded. A policeman, John Begley, held the crowd back with a drawn revolver until other officers arrived and took Hazelock to the station house. New York and Washington papers reported it the next day as an attempted lynching, and weekly news digests repeated it.

episodes.title: Averted lynching of Bill Slaton
episodes.lead: The averted lynching of Bill Slaton took place near Lithia Springs, Georgia, on August 20, 1903, when a posse of citizens captured Slaton, a Black man accused of assaulting eighteen-year-old Emma Strickland, and threatened to lynch him. Wire reports credited the young woman's father, Isaac Strickland, with saving Slaton by pleading that the law take its course, and the sheriff later moved him to Atlanta because of rumors of a mob.

episodes.title: Biltmore militia blanket-tossing
episodes.lead: The Biltmore militia blanket-tossing was an assault on Black residents of Biltmore, North Carolina, on the evening of August 24, 1903, by soldiers of the First Regiment of the North Carolina National Guard. Several Black people were tossed in blankets or chased from the railway yards, and a Black brakeman who drew a revolver was arrested. Governor Aycock, who had reviewed the regiment that day, later called it a prank if it happened at all.

episodes.title: Bristol State Street disturbance (1903)
episodes.lead: The Bristol State Street disturbance was a confrontation on State Street in Bristol, Virginia, on the afternoon of Saturday, August 22, 1903, in which a white crowd cried "shoot" and "lynch" at two Black men. No one was reported killed, and the two men were "quickly hustled away to prevent violence"; a Richmond paper reported the incident under the headline "A Race Riot Was Imminent."

episodes.title: Whipping of Bun near Fender, Georgia
episodes.lead: The whipping of Bun near Fender, Georgia, was the reported flogging in late August 1903 of a 15-year-old Black youth accused of having been at a young white woman's bedside at night. Captured by local men who set out to take him to the jail at Tifton, he escaped before arriving, and rumor held that he had been severely flogged and told to leave the country.

episodes.title: Assault on Charles Collins
episodes.lead: The assault on Charles Collins was an attack by two white men on Collins, a Black saloon porter, in Minneapolis, Minnesota, on the night of 8 August 1903. Collins was badly bruised, and the attackers were not identified. The Saint Paul Globe reported it as one of several recent attacks on Black men in the city, which had prompted police orders to stop what its headline called a "race war."

episodes.title: Charley Hudson peonage case
episodes.lead: The Charley Hudson peonage case was a 1903 federal prosecution in Birmingham, Alabama, of members of the Dill family of Lamar County, accused of seizing Hudson, a Black man, on a public road, working him without pay, and having him whipped after he tried to escape. In November 1903 Marshall and Archie Dill were each fined $400, and the case against their father, Aaron Dill, was dropped. Papers outside Alabama carried the hearing testimony as a "flagrant case" and an instance of "modern slavery."

episodes.title: Whipping of Charlie Stark
episodes.lead: The whipping of Charlie Stark took place on Sunday, August 16, 1903, at Turkey Hill in Abbeville County, South Carolina, when a crowd of armed men seized a young Black man from Georgia accused of prowling at a young woman's window. Members of the crowd called for him to be lynched, but after a vote they flogged him and ordered him away. The local paper headed the story "Barely Escaped Lynching."

episodes.title: Attempted burning of the Richardson house in Clive, Iowa
episodes.lead: The attempted burning of the Richardson house in Clive, Iowa, was an arson attempt in about early August 1903 on the house where Chas. Richardson had lived and where his son Elmer still lived, in a village five miles west of Des Moines. Neighbors put out the fire, and no one was hurt. The Iowa State Bystander reported it as the first of a series of attacks that it attributed to "White Caps" seeking to drive colored residents from Clive.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black section hands near Corsicana, Texas
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black section hands near Corsicana, Texas, took place in August 1903, when Black men working on a section in the neighborhood were ordered to quit the vicinity. A telegraph brief gave their alleged thefts as the reason and said that they left; neither report named who gave the order.

episodes.title: Shooting of Andrew Crawford
episodes.lead: The shooting of Andrew Crawford took place in Parkersburg, West Virginia, in mid-August 1903, when officers and a crowd pursued Crawford, a Black hotel porter, and he was shot in the back. He was accused of threatening a hotel clerk with a revolver and of wounding Special Constable Perry Nolan, and the papers named different men as his shooter.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of David James
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of David James took place on August 7, 1903, in Camden, "just across the river from Philadelphia," when a crowd of about 500 pressed on a constable holding a Black man and called for the prisoner to be hanged. Officials held the crowd off, and James was sentenced the same day to thirty days in the county prison, a term the magistrate doubled. The episode drew notice mainly because the Alexandria Gazette used it to accuse Philadelphians of hypocrisy about lynching.

episodes.title: Killing of Trinnell Ellis
episodes.lead: The killing of Trinnell Ellis was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Julian Beckett, a member of a posse led by Marshal Tom Crawford, during a midnight raid on a gambling game at Thunderbolt, Georgia, on the night of August 22, 1903. A second Black man, Eddie West, was wounded in the arm by the marshal's fire and escaped. Recorder L. W. Nelson exonerated Beckett two days later, while the men caught in the house were bound over to the City Court for gambling. The Savannah Morning News told the story entirely from the posse's side.

episodes.title: Exclusion of Black horse handlers from the Elwood, Indiana, street fair
episodes.lead: The exclusion of Black horse handlers from the Elwood, Indiana, street fair took place in August 1903, when Black men caring for horses entered in the fair's horse show told their white employers they did not dare enter the town because they had been warned to stay away. Local authorities told the horsemen that no Black person had ever been allowed in Elwood, and the story spread through white newspapers as an example of a Northern town that barred Black people.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black railroad workers near Pennington Gap, Virginia
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black railroad workers near Pennington Gap was the forcing out of about 100 Black laborers from a railroad construction camp in Lee County, Virginia, by armed white men from Harlan County, Kentucky, in August 1903. The workers left after a display of firearms, and work at the camp was reported suspended. A short wire account ran in Virginia and New York papers, and both an Arizona daily and the St. Paul Appeal cited the episode as mob violence used to drive men from their work.

episodes.title: White Hall sawmill whitecapping
episodes.lead: The White Hall sawmill whitecapping was the expulsion of Black laborers from the Davis and Hodges sawmill at White Hall, Poinsett County, Arkansas, by a band of eleven white men on August 17, 1903. The men were arrested by a federal deputy marshal, and in March 1904 three of fifteen defendants were convicted in federal court at Helena and sentenced, two of them to the penitentiary. The Cleveland Gazette called it the first time white men in that section had been convicted in federal court of whitecapping Black people, and the defense appealed to the United States Supreme Court.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching in Henderson County, North Carolina (1903)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching in Henderson County, North Carolina, was an attack in August 1903 in which five or six white men nearly lynched an unnamed Black man after a row over a belt trade. Some men from Asheville arrived and rescued him almost at the last moment, and a Raleigh correspondent reported the incident beside the state's count of lynchings for the year.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Fletcher Hollis
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Fletcher Hollis was an armed manhunt near Smyrna, Delaware, in August 1903, in which posses hunted Hollis, a young Black man accused of shooting Constable James D. Wright at Clayton on August 3, and declared he would be shot if caught. Hollis escaped, Wright recovered, and Hollis was captured in Maryland in February 1904 and sentenced to five years, the pillory and a fine. Dispatches announced that Delaware was "on the eve of another lynching," and a Wilmington editorial tied the hunt to a recent burning in New Castle County.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Frank Jordan
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Frank Jordan took place near Beverly, New Jersey, on August 6, 1903, when farmers pursuing a Black man accused of robbing a house shot part of his ear off and nearly hanged him from a tree. He confessed to theft with the rope around his neck, was taken down, and was jailed in Beverly. An Associated Press dispatch carried the story to papers from New York to Salt Lake City and across the South, several of which headlined it as a near-lynching.

episodes.title: Shooting of Frank Wiley
episodes.lead: The shooting of Frank Wiley was the wounding of a Black man by Marshal Flanagan, the town marshal of Metropolis, Illinois, on or about August 16, 1903. Wiley was described as "seriously wounded," and the marshal was reported to have been "fully exonerated" on the claim that Wiley had been trying to assault him. The only known report is a short item in the Paducah Sun of Kentucky, which headlined it as a shooting in self-defense.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of French near Fort Logan
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of French took place near Fort Logan, outside Denver, Colorado, late on a Friday night in mid-August 1903, when soldiers seized a Black man named French accused of assaulting a white woman and would have lynched him had the county sheriff not arrived. French survived, and the only known account, in a western Colorado weekly, gives no outcome.

episodes.title: Hartford City lynch mob
episodes.lead: The Hartford City lynch mob was a manhunt and jail search in and near Hartford City, Indiana, on August 3, 1903, in which hundreds of men and boys hunted two unnamed Black men accused of mutilating George Hershey, a 19-year-old farm youth. The men were never found, and a crowd of about 500 at the county jail left peacefully after the sheriff let it search the building. Wire reports spread the story as a lynching in the making, while Indiana papers soon doubted the boy's account, which the Indianapolis Journal later called "altogether mythical."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of George Kenny
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of George Kenny took place at Elkhart, Texas, in August 1903, when a mob seized Kenny, a Black man, after he was accused of assaulting the young daughter of the white section foreman he worked under. The mob put a rope around his neck and fired at him as he broke away, and he came into the hands of Sheriff Henry Watts after a posse ran him down. A jury at Palestine sentenced him to death within days, and he was legally hanged on May 28, 1904; one wire story presented the verdict as proof that speedy trials could end lynching.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of George Wilson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of George Wilson took place in Birmingham, Alabama, at the end of August 1903, when several white men who had worked with the slain night foreman O. K. Waite twice went to the house of Wilson, a Black former assistant foreman, seeking to kill him. Wilson escaped both times and was then arrested by the police on suspicion of taking part in Waite's killing. The episode is known from a single Birmingham Age-Herald article, which treated it as the prelude to his arrest.

episodes.title: Union Station mob threat against Gordon Donaldson
episodes.lead: The Union Station mob threat against Gordon Donaldson took place on Sunday afternoon, 2 August 1903, when a crowd at Union Station in Indianapolis shouted "lynch him" at Donaldson, a Black special officer of the C., H. & D. Railroad. Police arrested him before he was harmed, and four days later a Police Court judge dismissed the charges against him.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Harry Bell and Fannie Shelby
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Harry Bell and Fannie Shelby took place at Batavia, Illinois, on the night of August 24, 1903, when a crowd of white townspeople surrounded the jail holding the two Black picnickers from Chicago and officers secretly moved them to the county jail at Geneva. The pair had been taken from a picnic train after picnickers were accused of beating a white woman and the city marshal. White papers across the country ran it as a lynching prevented, while the two Black papers that covered it did not mention the crowd at the jail.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Harry Irvin
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Harry Irvin took place at Monteith, Georgia, on 9 August 1903, when an armed mob pursued Irvin, a Black man accused of criminally assaulting an 11-year-old girl in Effingham County, and surrounded the house where he had taken refuge. Constable J. A. Northcutt persuaded the mob to let him take Irvin to Savannah, and the two left on a train that night. The Savannah Morning News reported the episode as a narrowly averted clash, noting that a crowd of Irvin's own relatives and friends later arrived to demand his release.

episodes.title: Whipping of Henry Carr
episodes.lead: The whipping of Henry Carr was an attack on a Black businessman in Alexandria, Louisiana, who was seized at the jail door by white men on the night of August 28, 1903, given fifty lashes on his bare back, and ordered to leave. The whipping followed Carr's forcing a white man, J. C. Mosely, at gunpoint to apologize to Carr's wife. The story ran in white papers from Texas to Ohio and in two Black weeklies, one of which, the Chicago Broad Ax, presented it as a case of a man punished for protecting his wife.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Henry Holloway
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Henry Holloway took place in Greene County, North Carolina, in August 1903, when a posse searched for Holloway, a Black farm laborer accused of burglary and an attempted assault on a white woman, and the sheriff hid him and took him to Goldsboro to keep him from being lynched. Holloway was convicted at Snow Hill in September and sentenced to hang, and in October he was again moved out of the county to avoid a lynching. Governor Charles B. Aycock commuted the sentence to life imprisonment in December because the identification rested entirely on the woman's recognition of his voice.

episodes.title: Resignation of mail clerk I. Bowman at Mansura, Louisiana
episodes.lead: The resignation of mail clerk I. Bowman at Mansura, Louisiana, took place in August 1903, when Bowman, a Black railway mail clerk in Avoyelles parish, quit after what he described as threats from a mob at Mansura. He gave up his post, saying it would be dangerous to remain in the service. Within a day the town marshal of Mansura denied the account, saying that he was the "mob" and that Bowman had fled an arrest.

episodes.title: Clive whitecap attacks
episodes.lead: The Clive whitecap attacks were night attacks and threats in August 1903 against the Black residents of Clive, Iowa, a village a few miles west of Des Moines, by unidentified men the press called whitecaps. After an attempt to burn a house and the dynamiting of Isaac Anderson's home, notices ordered Black residents to leave and warned white employers not to hire them. No one was reported hurt and no arrest appears in the coverage, but the story ran from New York to the Dakotas, and the Iowa State Bystander, a Black weekly, read it as a sign that lynching was spreading north.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Isom Strong
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Isom Strong took place at Henderson, Texas, on August 7, 1903, when a mob took Strong, a young Black prisoner, from a sheriff who had moved him out of town and prepared to lynch him. The mob gave him up after District Judge Levy promised that the grand jury would take up his case at once, and the next day Strong pleaded guilty and was sentenced to ninety-nine years in the penitentiary. White newspapers across the country carried the story as an example of a mob yielding to the law and of swift justice.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Brown and expulsion of Black residents from Whitesboro, Texas
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Brown and expulsion of Black residents from Whitesboro, Texas, took place in August 1903, when a white mob hanged a Black prisoner accused of attempting to assault a white woman and then drove much of the town's Black population out. Officers cut the man down alive, but the mob went on to whip men who stayed, and more than 100 Black residents were reported to have fled. In May 1904 the town's mayor was arrested on a federal indictment for conspiracy in the expulsion.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of James Hayes
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of James Hayes occurred in Minneapolis, Minnesota, in late August 1903, after Hayes, a Black man who worked at a Minneapolis barn, was arrested on a charge of carrying 13-year-old Ruby Steele from her bedroom and attempting to assault her. Talk of lynching was reported and police guarded him and moved him to the county jail, but no mob formed. The case drew attention in both the white dailies and the Black weeklies of the Twin Cities, where a mass meeting of Black residents and the resolutions it adopted became a subject of dispute.

episodes.title: Assault on Joe Hallier and B. L. Greer
episodes.lead: The assault on Joe Hallier and B. L. Greer was an attack on 11 August 1903 at Horse Creek, Walker County, Alabama, in which armed white men beat Greer, the Black vice president of the Alabama district of the United Mine Workers, and shot Hallier, the union's white district organizer, in the arm. Both survived; six men were prosecuted in federal court for conspiracy, but a U.S. commissioner released them in October 1903 and a federal judge dismissed later indictments in May 1904 as a state matter. It drew notice because a white and a Black union officer were attacked together and because the prosecution turned on Hallier's citizenship.

episodes.title: Killing of Joe Sanders
episodes.lead: The killing of Joe Sanders was the shooting of a Black man by a posse of citizens at Henderson, Texas, on August 22, 1903. Sanders had been accused of attempting a criminal assault on a young girl the night before, and the men who came to arrest him shot him to death at his door. An Associated Press dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, and the Cleveland Gazette reprinted it without comment.

episodes.title: Attack on Joe Williams and Earnest Griffin
episodes.lead: The attack on Joe Williams and Earnest Griffin took place on the night of August 12, 1903, near the Virginia City mines in southern Jefferson County, Alabama, when Williams, a Black man, was shot and seriously wounded and Griffin, also Black, was beaten into insensibility. The assault came during a United Mine Workers strike at the mines, and a dispatch to the New York Tribune described the attackers as a mob that included a white woman. Three white men were charged with assault with intent to murder and highway robbery, but within two weeks the cases were dropped and one defendant was acquitted.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John Black
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of John Black took place in South Carolina in late August 1903, when Black, a Black worker at the Haile Gold Mine arrested on a charge of poisoning his wife, faced "some threats of lynching" before police locked him in the guard house at Kershaw. He was not harmed and was held to be taken to the jail at Camden.

episodes.title: Tenderloin mob threat against John Brown (1903)
episodes.lead: The Tenderloin mob threat against John Brown occurred in the early morning of August 20, 1903, at Sixth Avenue and Thirtieth Street in New York City, when a street crowd cried for the lynching of Brown, a Black cabman, after he was charged with stabbing a white cabman, Michael Lynch. Police held Brown and stopped the crowd, and he was later held in $1,000 bail. New York papers headlined the lynching cries, and the story was reprinted in Savannah two weeks later.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Dixon
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Dixon took place at Sparta, Hancock County, Georgia, on August 3, 1903, when a mob gathered to kill Dixon, a young Black man accused of assaulting a white woman, and chased the sheriff who held him to the railroad depot. Sheriff Berry put Dixon on a train just before the mob's leaders arrived and lodged him in the Macon jail. A short Associated Press dispatch carried the story to white papers from Georgia to Massachusetts.

episodes.title: 1903 Bronx race riot
episodes.lead: The 1903 Bronx race riot was an outbreak of crowd violence against Black people near 155th Street and Washington Avenue in the Bronx, New York, on August 15, 1903, after a white man, John Finnessy, was stabbed outside a saloon, reportedly by a Black man who escaped. White men chased the assailant, and both reporting papers said four uninvolved Black men were attacked in the saloon until police rescued them.

episodes.title: Killing of Mrs. John Gundy
episodes.lead: The killing of Mrs. John Gundy took place in Amarillo, Texas, in 1903, when the house of John Gundy, a Black property owner who had been ordered to leave the town, was fired into and his wife was killed. The case is known only from a one-sentence news brief, which did not name the attackers or report any arrest.

episodes.title: Needmore whitecap raid
episodes.lead: The Needmore whitecap raid was a night attack by a masked band of fifteen to thirty "whitecaps" on the home of John Millikin, a Black preacher, at Needmore, a Black settlement near Lewisburg in Marshall County, Tennessee, after midnight on August 3–4, 1903. Millikin was shot dead as he fled, and his son-in-law John Hunter was shot in the back after the band forced him to join a search; Hunter was first reported mortally wounded and later as killed. No cause was known, the governor offered a $500 reward, and year-end chronologies in Black and white papers listed the case among the lynchings of 1903.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Jackson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Jackson took place at Zwolle, Louisiana, in August 1903, when a Black man accused of assaulting the wife of a local man was nearly lynched after his capture. A constable got Jackson to the parish prison, and the story ran in the New York Sun under the headline "Negro Saved From Lynching."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Thompson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Thompson took place on the night of August 11, 1903, at Passyunk square in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, when a crowd of several hundred people chased Thompson, a Black man accused of assaulting a white man, and besieged the trolley car in which he had taken refuge. Firemen from a nearby fire station fought through the crowd and rescued him before police arrived. Southern editors seized on the episode as evidence that Northern cities shared the mob spirit they condemned in the South.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John Wilson
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of John Wilson took place at Valparaiso, Indiana, in August 1903, when armed white farmers pursued a Black man accused of attacking a farmer's wife and then crowded the town's streets threatening to lynch him at the county jail. The sheriff guarded the jail, no attack was made, and Wilson was later sentenced to two to fourteen years in prison. The wire carried the story under headlines such as 'Indiana Farmers Thirst for Blood', and the hostility it stirred drove some Black residents from the town.

episodes.title: Beating of Joseph White
episodes.lead: The beating of Joseph White took place on August 11, 1903, near Newport, Delaware, when armed men pursued White, a Black man accused of robbing a family that had sheltered him, caught him in the woods, beat him and let him go. The Wilmington Evening Journal, the only paper found to report it, identified him as a cousin of George White, described as lynched for the murder of Helen Bishop.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Kay Woods
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Kay Woods took place in downtown Indianapolis, Indiana, on the morning of August 12, 1903, when a crowd of white men chased and shot at Woods, a Black man, after he and a white man, James Saunders, had exchanged pistol shots. Woods was wounded in the arm, and a patrolman named Dugan held off the crowd with a drawn revolver until other police arrived. Papers outside Indiana carried the story under headlines such as "Small Race Riot in Indianapolis" and "Lynching Is Prevented by Officer With a Gun," and the Indianapolis Journal praised the officer in an editorial.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of King Wrightman and Thompson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of King Wrightman and Thompson was a mob's pursuit, in August 1903, of a Black man, King Wrightman, and a white man named Thompson, who were accused of assaulting a white widow, Mrs. Mathis, at Hartsfield in Colquitt County, Georgia. An Albany dispatch of August 14 reported both men hanged together, but Albany officials denied it that night and said the two were in jail at Moultrie. Papers noticed the case because a white man and a Black man were said to have been lynched together, and some kept printing that version after the denial.

episodes.title: Killing of Knowles by an Atlanta bailiff
episodes.lead: The killing of Knowles by an Atlanta bailiff took place in Atlanta, Georgia, in about August 1903, when J. F. Wood, a justice court bailiff, went with a money lender to a Black family's house to collect a small debt and shot and killed the husband of the woman who owed it. Wood and the lender were indicted for murder in September, and Wood was later acquitted by a jury that deliberated about twenty minutes. The Cleveland Gazette reprinted the case under the headline "Deliberately Murdered" as an example of "Georgia justice."

episodes.title: Killing of L. A. Planving
episodes.lead: The killing of L. A. Planving was the ambush shooting of La Forest A. Planving, a Black minister and principal of the Pointe Coupee Industrial College, near Oscar, Louisiana, on a Sunday night at the end of August 1903. No arrest was reported, and accounts of who fired the shots differed. White dispatches tied the killing to his alleged "incendiary speeches," a charge the Black press and the American Missionary Association (AMA) rejected.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Jeanerette, Louisiana
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black residents from Jeanerette, Louisiana, took place in late August 1903, when white residents of the Iberia Parish town ordered dozens of Black people to leave after a Black barber, Louis Nicks, was accused of fatally shooting a white merchant, Joseph Sanders. Most of those ordered out left at once and were warned never to return, while a crowd searched the town's Black section and wire reports said Nicks would be lynched if caught. Deputies instead arrested Nicks at Baldwin on August 26, and he was lodged in the parish prison at New Iberia with no reported attempt on his life.

episodes.title: Whipping of Black brakemen at Lufkin, Texas
episodes.lead: The whipping of Black brakemen at Lufkin, Texas, was a mob attack in the summer of 1903 in which two Black brakemen of the Houston, East and West Texas Railroad were taken from a caboose and severely whipped, after which the mob fired into the car. No one was reported killed, and no arrests appear in the coverage. The episode drew notice outside Texas mainly because Lufkin's Commercial Club publicly condemned the mob and offered a reward, a response the New York Sun praised in an editorial that other papers reprinted.

episodes.title: West End mob letter to M. E. McKelley
episodes.lead: The West End mob letter to M. E. McKelley was an anonymous written order, dated August 23, 1903, telling the only Black family living on the West Side of Wichita, Kansas, to leave within ten days. McKelley decided, on the advice of local business men, not to move, and police detectives were reported searching for the writer.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Major Lee
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Major Lee took place at Moultrie, Georgia, in August 1903, when a Black prisoner accused of attempting to assault a young white girl was moved out of the Moultrie jail because a lynching had been arranged for him. Sheriff Murphy of Colquitt County sent him by train to the Thomasville jail, and no attack on him was reported. Dispatches from Moultrie gave the prisoner's name as Major Alexander.

episodes.title: Lynching of Manna Ponton
episodes.lead: The lynching of Manna Ponton took place at Halifax, North Carolina, on the night of August 20–21, 1903, when a crowd hanged a young Black man accused of assaulting and murdering Mary Jenkins, a white girl, and riddled his body with bullets. He was taken from the citizens and officers holding him within hours of the discovery of the girl's body. White North Carolina editors defended the killing, and a committee of Black residents of Halifax condemned the crime while saying they did not encourage lynching.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Maynard Hudson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Maynard Hudson took place early on August 8, 1903, when a mob of more than one hundred white men broke into the jail at Hillsboro, Ohio, to hang Hudson, a young Black man charged with attempting to assault a twelve-year-old white girl. The sheriff had secretly removed Hudson to Chillicothe shortly before, and the mob left after searching the jail, reportedly under orders to renew the hunt. A short dispatch about the attack ran in white papers across the country, several of which warned that a "race war" was feared in the town.

episodes.title: Minneapolis candy store assault
episodes.lead: The Minneapolis candy store assault was a street confrontation at about 2 a.m. on August 7, 1903, at First Avenue South and Third Street in Minneapolis, Minnesota, in which white men beat a Black man who had been eating ice cream with two white girls. A large crowd then gathered and talked of chasing the city's Black men "to cover" before police broke it up, and a second melee followed. The St. Paul Globe reported it as "something approaching a race riot," and the Minneapolis police were afterward ordered to suppress "demonstrations against colored men."

episodes.title: Moultrie depot whipping
episodes.lead: The Moultrie depot whipping was the beating of an unnamed Black railroad employee by two white men outside Moultrie, Georgia, on the night of Saturday, 29 August 1903. Freed on bond after being accused of kicking a white depot clerk, the man was marched beyond the city limits and, by report, whipped with a buggy trace; he was not seen again in the town.

episodes.title: Chanute Evergreen Park mass meeting against a Black homebuilder
episodes.lead: The Chanute Evergreen Park mass meeting was a night gathering of about 300 white residents of the Evergreen park second addition in Chanute, Kansas, on 12 August 1903, held at the partly built house of a Black woman, Mrs. Foster. The crowd, some of its members carrying clubs, resolved to press her to stop building and to tear the house down if she refused. The Topeka State Journal reprinted the Chanute Tribune's account under the headline "NEAR TO RACE WAR."

episodes.title: Mulberry railroad workers shooting incident
episodes.lead: The Mulberry railroad workers shooting incident was an episode in late August 1903 in which residents of Mulberry fired pistols to drive Black railroad construction workers out of the town and back to their cars. No one was reported killed or injured, and the local Van Buren Press, the only paper found to report it, said that rumors of a "wholesale slaughter of negroes" had been made "nearly out of whole cloth."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Frederick W. Williams
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Frederick W. Williams took place on the night of August 22, 1903, in Washington, D.C., when white men in the poolroom of James Stevens' saloon at Eighth and E Streets northwest seized Williams, a Black man accused of stabbing a white tinner, Nelson Pixton, while a crowd shouted for him to be lynched. The saloon's proprietor hid Williams in a back room until police arrived and arrested him, and he was later convicted of assault with a dangerous weapon, with a jury recommendation of mercy. Only The Washington Times reported the threat, under the deck "Lynching Was Threatened."

episodes.title: Norfolk road house shooting
episodes.lead: The Norfolk road house shooting was an exchange of gunfire in the early morning of August 18, 1903, between county constables and Black people attending a dance at a road house near Norfolk, Virginia. More than 150 shots were fired; one Black man was killed, two were wounded and twelve were arrested. The only account, an Associated Press dispatch from Norfolk carried by several Southern papers, gave the officers' version and dwelt on the weapons taken from those arrested.

episodes.title: Henrietta race riot
episodes.lead: The Henrietta race riot was a clash between white and Black residents of Henrietta, North Carolina, a cotton-mill town, on the night of August 6, 1903, after a number of white men and boys disturbed a Black church meeting. A Black man, Otis Bird, was badly cut and reported likely to die, while a separate report from Asheville said a white youth, Herbert Dubbs, had been stabbed to death and a Black man killed. Wire reports warned of an impending "race war," and every version said whites had started the trouble.

episodes.title: Pecaway shooting and attempted lynching
episodes.lead: The Pecaway shooting and attempted lynching took place on the night of Saturday, August 8, 1903, at Pecaway in Pittsylvania County, Virginia, when a white man named Joe Echols shot and wounded a Black man during a brawl at a political meeting. The wounded man's friends beat Echols, and a later effort to lynch the Black man was given up, so that no one was killed.

episodes.title: Stoning of Preston Bland
episodes.lead: The stoning of Preston Bland occurred on the night of Saturday, August 1, 1903, when a crowd on Manhattan's West Side threw stones at Bland, a Black longshoreman, as four policemen took him to the West Sixty-eighth street station after a shooting. Bland, accused of wounding a white passer-by, was held in $1,000 bail; the crowd episode is known only from a policeman's testimony as reported by the New York Sun.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of R. B. Williams
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of R. B. Williams occurred in Larned, Kansas, on the evening of August 1, 1903, after Williams, a Black tailor, shot and killed Clyde Langdon, a young white man, in his shop during a dispute over a suit of clothes. A mob formed with talk of lynching him, but officers took Williams by train to Hutchinson before any attack. A coroner's jury found that he had fired in self-defense, and by his own account he was released at his preliminary hearing.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Samuel Johnson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Samuel Johnson took place near Helena, Georgia, on Tuesday night, August 4, 1903, when a mob hanged Johnson, a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman, and left him for dead. Black passersby cut him down and revived him, and he was later found near Macon and jailed. Northern papers ran it under headlines such as "Lynched Negro Still Alive."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Shack Johnson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Shack Johnson took place in Winchester, Virginia, early on August 28, 1903, when a crowd beat Johnson, a Black man accused of assaulting councilman and night watchman James M. Haymaker, and tried to shoot him at the police station. An officer snatched the revolver away and Johnson was locked in a cell; less than a month later he was indicted, tried and sentenced to nine and a half years in the penitentiary within a few hours. White papers in Virginia, Washington and West Virginia treated it chiefly as an attack on a prominent citizen in which the accused "narrowly escaped lynching."

episodes.title: Booker murders and attempted lynching at Winchester, Tennessee
episodes.lead: The Booker murders and attempted lynching at Winchester, Tennessee, were the killing of Simon Booker and his wife at their Franklin County cabin on the night of August 4, 1903, and a mob's attempt six days later to lynch the three men charged with it. Sheriff Jim Stewart took the prisoners to Nashville before the mob reached the jail, and all three were later convicted and hanged at Winchester on May 5, 1904. Early dispatches called the killings moonshiners' revenge on informers, and one Alabama paper headlined the accused as "Three Negroes."

episodes.title: Pursuit of an unidentified Black man after the Hagan shooting, St. Paul (1903)
episodes.lead: On the night of August 23, 1903, several men in St. Paul, Minnesota, chased an unidentified Black man after Mary M. Hagan fired her revolver at him at the corner of Eighth and Sibley streets, saying he had grabbed her arm. The man escaped, and the Saint Paul Globe, the only paper found to report the incident, wrote that the pursuers "would have used summary methods had they overtaken him."

episodes.title: Killing of Thomas Williams
episodes.lead: The killing of Thomas Williams was the shooting death of a Black farmer near Ocklocknee, in Thomas County, Georgia, on the night of Friday, August 28, 1903, after unknown parties called him out of his house. A coroner's jury attributed his death to parties unknown, while his wife accused a young white man who was said to have an alibi. The Savannah Morning News reported the killing chiefly as the cause of a possible "race war" in the county.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Tom Clay from Muscatine
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Tom Clay from Muscatine took place on August 13, 1903, when Clay, a Black man described as a detective, was forced to leave the Iowa town minutes after a murder suspect he had helped identify was cleared. Wire briefs said Clay was "chased out of town," while a fuller Muscatine dispatch said the county attorney, the sheriff and a justice gave him until the next train to leave because local indignation against him was so intense.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Tom Fifer
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Tom Fifer took place near Brewton, Alabama, in August 1903, after Fifer, a young Black farm hand, was accused of poisoning the water of the farmer who employed him and striking the farmer with a rock. Threats of lynching were reported while a sheriff's posse hunted him, but he was arrested the next day and jailed at Brewton under guard.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John Wilson
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of John Wilson took place in Valparaiso, Indiana, on the night of August 8, 1903, when crowds of angry farmers gathered near the Porter County jail and talked of lynching Wilson, a Black man jailed that evening on a charge of attacking a farmer's wife. The sheriff doubled the guard, no attack was made, and Wilson was later sentenced to two to fourteen years in prison. The episode drew wider notice after a Chesterton editor, A. J. Bowser, cited it in starting a campaign against Black settlement in Porter County.

episodes.title: Attacks on Black miners at Virginia City, Alabama
episodes.lead: The attacks on Black miners at Virginia City, Alabama, were a series of shootings and beatings in August 1903 at a coal-mining camp in Jefferson County, where union miners were on strike. Striking miners were reported to have fired into the Black quarters at the mines on two nights, to have threatened a Black guard with lynching and shot him, and days later to have shot one Black man and beaten another on the road. No one was reported killed, and charges against three white men were dropped within two weeks.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of W. S. Sanders
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of W. S. Sanders occurred at Bunola, Pennsylvania, on Monday, August 17, 1903, when a crowd seized Sanders, a Black teamster accused of horsewhipping a white woman, and dragged him down the street amid cries of "Lynch him!" Officers rescued him and jailed him, and he was later reported to have pleaded guilty and been held for trial.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Walter Simmons
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Walter Simmons occurred on August 3, 1903, west of St. Louis, Missouri, when passengers of a derailed streetcar tried to lynch Simmons, a Black man they accused of causing the wreck. He was got away and handed to an officer, and the story ran as a short wire item the next day.

episodes.title: Orchard Park dynamiting
episodes.lead: The Orchard Park dynamiting was an attack early on August 8, 1903, in which a mob of "men and boys" dynamited and set fire to a house being built for a Black woman named Warner in Orchard Park, a suburb of Oklahoma City, Oklahoma Territory. It followed orders from armed, masked white men that the suburb's Black residents leave, and their refusal and arming led papers across the country to warn of a "race war." Black residents published an appeal for protection, and the Black press condemned the attack.

episodes.title: Waterloo "all-white city" report
episodes.lead: The Waterloo "all-white city" report was a widely published account, in late August and September 1903, that the citizens of Waterloo, Iowa, had ordered the town's Black residents to leave and that nearly all had gone. The story grew out of a Waterloo newspaper campaign for keeping the town "perfectly white," but Waterloo's mayor and local press denied that anyone had been driven out. Northern papers condemned the reported expulsion, while Southern papers cited it as proof that the North treated Black people no better than the South.

episodes.title: Ridgetop train hold-up
episodes.lead: The Ridgetop train hold-up took place on the night of August 29, 1903, when fifteen to twenty masked men stopped a Louisville & Nashville passenger train near Ridgetop, Tennessee, and searched it for Will Reed, a Black worker accused of shooting a construction foreman that day. Reed was not aboard, because officers had already taken him to Nashville by buggy, and a Kentucky paper judged that the band would otherwise have killed him.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Will Roseboro
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Will Roseboro took place at Statesville, Iredell County, North Carolina, on August 2, 1903, when crowds gathered to seize a Black prisoner accused of assaulting and murdering a white woman, Mrs. Dolph Beaver. Sheriff W. A. Summers kept him from the crowds and took him to Charlotte; Roseboro was later tried, convicted and hanged. Papers outside the state cited the sheriff's conduct as a sign of a "reaction against lynching," while a Raleigh correspondent reported that many leading citizens sympathized with the crowd.

episodes.title: Killing of Will Smith
episodes.lead: The killing of Will Smith was the fatal shooting of a Black chicken seller in Memphis, Tennessee, by grocer Lewis G. Slaughter on the morning of August 29, 1903, while Slaughter guarded him at the order of an off-duty patrolman. Patrolman A. S. Boyles had handed Slaughter his pistol with instructions to kill the prisoner if he tried to escape, and Smith died at the city hospital several days later. The case drew notice because the white Memphis Commercial Appeal investigated it, exposed Boyles's false first report, and denounced the killing as cold-blooded, coverage that was reprinted in both the white and the Black press.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Bradway
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of William Bradway took place on the night of 26 August 1903 in Salem, New Jersey, when a crowd of about 300 people tried to take Bradway, a young Black prisoner, from officers bringing him through the city. Bradway, charged with cutting two Black residents with a razor, was not taken and was held for trial. The only known report is a single sentence in a Salem County weekly.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Dorsey at Peach Bottom
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Dorsey at Peach Bottom took place in York County, Pennsylvania, on August 11, 1903, when a mob formed to lynch Dorsey and a second Black man after a fight at a hotel. The legal authorities jailed both men at York before the mob reached them, and Dorsey was later convicted of assault and sentenced to four years.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Nichols
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Nichols occurred on August 4, 1903, when about 200 people at the depot in Belle Centre, Ohio, called for Nichols, a Black prisoner accused of murder, to be shot or hanged as his train passed on the way to the Kenton jail. The train pulled out, a second crowd threatened him at Kenton, and the sheriff lodged him in jail unharmed. Papers across the country ran it as a lynching avoided; Nichols was electrocuted for the murder in December 1904.

episodes.title: Lynching of William (Bee) Washington
episodes.lead: The lynching of William (Bee) Washington took place on the night of Saturday, August 15, 1903, when a party of about seventy-five mounted men hanged a Black man to a tree just inside Mississippi, near the Louisiana line. Washington was accused of killing Stanley Wood, a young white clerk, and was tracked into Louisiana with bloodhounds and a hired river steamer before his capture at Red River Landing. A New Orleans report noted that the sheriff of West Feliciana Parish was present and did not stop it.

episodes.title: Wrightsville lynching threat (1903)
episodes.lead: The Wrightsville lynching threat was a threat by white citizens of Wrightsville, Pennsylvania, in August 1903 to lynch unidentified Black men accused of chasing white women on the town's streets at night. No one was reported caught or harmed, and the episode is known only from a single York dispatch carried by two Washington-area papers on August 15, 1903.

episodes.title: White Hall sawmill whitecapping
episodes.lead: The White Hall sawmill whitecapping was the driving out of the Black workforce of the Davis and Hodges sawmill at White Hall, Poinsett County, Arkansas, by a band of white men on the morning of August 17, 1903. Eleven men described as prominent planters were arrested on federal charges, and in March 1904 a federal jury at Helena convicted three of them of conspiracy to intimidate Black workmen. The Cleveland Gazette called it the first such federal conviction in that section, and the defense appealed to the Supreme Court.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Albert Going
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Albert Going took place at Rome, Georgia, on the night of September 18-19, 1903, when crowds gathered at the Floyd County jail threatening to take Going, a Black man charged with attempted criminal assault on a white girl. The sheriff refused to give him up, Governor Terrell sent militia to guard the jail, and Going was moved to Atlanta, later tried under military guard and sentenced to twenty years. The case drew notice as an instance of a Southern governor and sheriff turning back a mob, and some reports noted doubt about the charge itself.

episodes.title: Alexandria street assault of September 1903
episodes.lead: The Alexandria street assault of September 1903 was an attempted attack by two white men on an unnamed Black man on a street in Alexandria on the evening of Monday, 21 September 1903. One of the men struck at him, but he escaped, and no arrests were made. The incident is known only from a short item in the local news column of the Alexandria Gazette.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Alfred Daniels
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Alfred Daniels took place at Trenton, Jones County, North Carolina, on September 14, 1903, when a crowd at the county jail threatened to lynch Daniels, a Black man held for the killing of Farnifold G. Simmons, father of United States Senator F. M. Simmons. No attack was reported; Daniels was moved to New Bern the next morning, and he was later convicted and hanged at Trenton in May 1904. North Carolina papers held up the Senator's appeals as a lesson in restraint, while the Black press noticed the case mainly through an appeal against the exclusion of Black jurors.

episodes.title: Lynching of Allen Small
episodes.lead: The lynching of Allen Small was the killing of a Black prisoner by a mob of about 25 men who broke into the Moore County jail at Lynchburg, Tennessee, on the night of September 24, 1903. Small, charged with an attempted assault on a white woman, had been moved to Nashville in August after a judge warned he would be lynched at Lynchburg. A coroner's jury named 27 men and a grand jury indicted 22, which wire reports called probably the first indictment of white lynchers in the South; four defendants were acquitted in October 1904.

episodes.title: Armourdale mob chase and drowning
episodes.lead: The Armourdale mob chase and drowning took place on September 4, 1903, at Armourdale, Kansas, a suburb of Kansas City, when an unidentified Black man accused of choking a white widow, Margaret Gerahn, in her home was chased to the Kansas River by a crowd and drowned himself. According to the wire reports, he dived from a rowboat in midstream "rather than run the chances of being lynched," and his body was not recovered. The dispatch ran nationwide under headlines about escaping a mob, and the Montgomery Advertiser approved the outcome.

episodes.title: Killing of Bob Crouch
episodes.lead: The killing of Bob Crouch was the fatal shooting of a Black man on Main Street in Saluda, South Carolina, on the night of September 5, 1903. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of W. L. Rhoden, the sheriff of Saluda County, and Matt Berry, and the coroner arrested the sheriff. Papers treated the arrest of a sitting sheriff for murder as a rarity and followed his refusal to give up his office.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of two Black men in Pike County, Missouri (1903)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of two Black men in Pike County, Missouri, took place shortly before September 12, 1903, when crowds sought to hang two young men charged with attempted assault on a white woman. A constable spirited the men away from the first crowd, and the sheriff and his armed family turned back a second mob at the Bowling Green jail. Missouri papers told it as a story of the constable's "nerve."

episodes.title: Export Lumber Company strike assault, Brooklyn
episodes.lead: The Export Lumber Company strike assault was an attack in Brooklyn, New York, in about September 1903, in which white lumber handlers on strike threatened Black lumbermen hired to replace them and four of the strikers beat one of the Black workers. The four were arrested, and a magistrate fined one of them $2 and discharged the others after they said they objected to their jobs going to Black men. The case is known only from an Atlanta Constitution editorial that used it to taunt the Brooklyn minister Newell Dwight Hillis over Northern race prejudice.

episodes.title: Whipping of Buff Wright
episodes.lead: The whipping of Buff Wright was an attack in the late summer of 1903 in Warsaw, Benton County, Missouri, in which a group of white townsmen took a young Black man from the town jail, whipped him, and ordered him to leave town. The case reached print mainly through the damage suit Wright brought against several of his attackers with the help of P. D. Hastain of Sedalia, which white papers in Missouri and Kansas reported and a Black Sedalia weekly championed.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Peters
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Charles Peters took place in Reno, Nevada, in September 1903, after Peters, a Black man, was arrested on a charge of assaulting a white woman, Mrs. John Dotta. Fearing a lynching, police moved him to the county jail, and a night of rumors and street-corner gatherings ended without an attack. The story reached other Nevada papers through the Reno Journal, and one ran it under the headline "Should Have Lynched Him."

episodes.title: Beating of Daniel Allen at the Seamen's Union
