episodes.lead: The beating of Daniel Allen at the Seamen's Union was an assault on a West Indian Black seaman by a union agent and several white members at a West street branch in New York City on Tuesday, September 15, 1903. Black members drove the white men from the rooms, and no arrests were made. The New York Sun presented the fight as the outbreak of a growing split between white and Black union members over jobs.

episodes.title: Perry Hill church shooting
episodes.lead: The Perry Hill church shooting was a fight on a Sunday in September 1903 at the Perry Hill colored church near Bigbyville, Tennessee, in which a white vendor from Columbia, Tom McDonald, struck a Black man and fired into a crowd of Black churchgoers. Lewis Thompson was hit in the hand, and the Columbia Herald headlined the affair "SMALL RACE WAR."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Doc Bacon
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Doc Bacon took place at the jail in Boydton, Mecklenburg County, Virginia, on September 4, 1903, when a crowd from Chase City tried to stop the sheriff from removing Bacon, a Black man under sentence of death, after Governor Montague respited him for thirty days. An armed posse held the jail until Judge Homes persuaded the crowd to disperse, and Bacon was taken by special train to Petersburg. Papers across the country reported a narrow escape "both from the law and from a mob," and the Richmond Planet later printed an eyewitness account.

episodes.title: Police beating of Edward E. Wilson
episodes.lead: The police beating of Edward E. Wilson took place on Monday morning, 14 September 1903, at the Harrison Street police station in Chicago, where officers seized, struck and locked up Wilson, a lawyer, after he disobeyed an order to take a seat. Wilson, described as a "Neger" by the Polish-language Dziennik Chicagoski, sued the officers for $10,000.

episodes.title: Ordering out of Black railroad laborers near Sheridan, Arkansas
episodes.lead: The ordering out of Black railroad laborers near Sheridan, Arkansas, took place in 1903, shortly before September 1, when white laborers ordered Black workers grading the Pine Bluff and Western railroad to leave. No violence was reported, and an officer of the railroad company said the trouble was over and had never been serious. The episode drew notice chiefly because the Sheridan Headlight, edited by a state senator, publicly called the order a mistake.

episodes.title: Whitecap death notice to Garfield Williams
episodes.lead: The whitecap death notice to Garfield Williams was a written threat, dated September 7, 1903, ordering Williams, a Black tenant farmer near Linwood in Pike County, Alabama, to leave within five days or be killed. No harm to Williams is reported, but the notice became government evidence in a federal whitecapping prosecution of white men from the neighborhood. In January 1904 a federal grand jury indicted five of them for attempting to oppress Williams and nine other Black people because of their race.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Jones
episodes.lead: The lynching of George Jones was the killing of a Black prisoner by a masked mob that broke into the county jail at Mayersville, Mississippi, on the night of September 1, 1903. Jones had been arrested on a charge of arson, and the mob shot him so many times that his body was described as "literally riddled with bullets." The killing drew only brief notice, though an Atlanta editorial against lynching soon cited a Mississippi lynching over arson as proof that mobs no longer acted only to punish rape.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of George and Charles Pittman
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of George and Charles Pittman took place at Monticello, Lawrence County, Mississippi, in September 1903, when a mob twice sought to take the two Black brothers from the county jail. Officers removed the prisoners to Jackson for safekeeping, and no one was killed. Papers tied the mob's anger to the killing of J. L. Nelson near Brookhaven, of which Charles Pittman was suspected, though the Brookhaven Leader later reported that the witness said he was not the man.

episodes.title: Central Park incident in Henderson, Kentucky
episodes.lead: The Central Park incident in Henderson, Kentucky, was a confrontation on a Sunday night in September 1903 in which a white man struck a Black woman and other whites then drove the Black people present out of the town's Central Park. The local Henderson Journal described it as "a small touch of race war fever," and the item was reprinted by the Louisville Courier-Journal and, with ironic comment, by the Salt Lake Herald.

episodes.title: Manhunt for Harry Thomas (1903)
episodes.lead: The manhunt for Harry Thomas was an armed search in Clarke County, Virginia, in early September 1903 for a Black man accused of taking part in an assault on Capt. James M. Haymaker, a Winchester councilman and night watchman. On September 5 a party of armed men led by Winchester's police chief found Thomas in a corn field near the Shenandoah River, but he escaped, and a further search by a constable and deputized citizens also failed. Thomas was caught in Pennsylvania months later and sentenced to seven years in the penitentiary in February 1904.

episodes.title: Hoisington warning notices (1903)
episodes.lead: The Hoisington warning notices were typewritten notices posted around Hoisington, Kansas, one night in late September or early October 1903, warning the town's Black residents to leave. A rumored attempt to enforce them on the following Monday night passed without any disturbance, and the episode is known from a single local news item.

episodes.title: New Orleans riverfront lockout violence (September 1903)
episodes.lead: The New Orleans riverfront lockout violence of September 16, 1903, was a series of confrontations in which striking longshoremen drove Black longshoremen from a wharf and white union men threatened to lynch J. B. Williams, president of the colored longshoremen's union. Police broke up the crowd at the wharf after a riot call, and no injuries were reported.

episodes.title: Red Oak cotton pickers' cabin shooting
episodes.lead: The Red Oak cotton pickers' cabin shooting was an attack in September 1903 in which unknown assailants fired a volley of shots into a cabin of Black cotton pickers on a farm near Red Oak, Texas. A Texas dispatch reported two men, George Hill and Jess Bruce, wounded but not seriously, while a Houston wire carried in Northern papers reported two men killed and two women wounded. No assailant was identified.

episodes.title: Killing of Jim Nichols
episodes.lead: The killing of Jim Nichols was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Constable Hugo Schultz at a cabin in Oldham County, Kentucky, on or about September 6, 1903, during an attempt to arrest his brother Will. Nichols died twelve days later; the Louisville Courier-Journal reported that a posse had threatened "mob violence" against his brother.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Brinkley
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Brinkley took place in Chicago on the night of September 8, 1903, when a crowd chased, held and whipped Brinkley, a Black watchman, minutes after, according to the Associated Press, he had shot and killed a plasterer, Charles McCarthy. Four policemen fought through a shower of bricks and stones to carry Brinkley to a police station alive, and none of the crowd was arrested. The wire story ran across the country, and the Black weekly Professional World called it the first Chicago case in which police were "hardly able" to save a prisoner from a mob.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Griffin and attack on Black residents of Shawneetown
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Griffin and attack on Black residents of Shawneetown took place in Shawneetown, Illinois, between August 31 and September 3, 1903, when a masked mob tried to take Griffin, a Black prisoner accused of an attempted assault on a white woman, from the jail, and whites then stoned Black homes and gathering places. The jailer held off the mob and the sheriff moved Griffin to the jail at Carmi; no one was reported killed or hurt, but at least fifty Black residents left the town within two days. Wire stories carried the episode to white papers from Virginia to Wyoming and to two Black weeklies.

episodes.title: Whitecapping of John Lee
episodes.lead: The whitecapping of John Lee was a reported attack by whitecaps on John Lee, a Black teamster in Virginia and a prospective defense witness for the condemned Doc Bacon, on the night of Saturday, September 12, 1903. Lee was not seen afterward and was supposed to have left the county. The report reached the Richmond Times-Dispatch through Bacon's brother, Charles Bacon, who said that witnesses useful to the defense were being driven out of the county.

episodes.title: Bridgeville mob attack
episodes.lead: The Bridgeville mob attack was an assault by an armed white mob on Joseph Andrews, a Black man, and on several Black men who came to his aid in Bridgeville, Delaware, around midnight on Saturday, September 5, 1903. The mob, which sought Andrews after he was accused of stabbing a white man, wrecked the store where he had taken refuge and fired on him, but he escaped. A Wilmington paper reported it as a riot between "Whites and Blacks," and Southern weeklies later reduced it to a one-line "race riot" item.

episodes.title: Drowning of an unidentified Black man in the Kansas River at Armourdale
episodes.lead: On September 4, 1903, an unidentified Black man drowned in the Kansas River at Armourdale, Kansas, a suburb of Kansas City, after a crowd chased him from the home of a white widow he was accused of choking. He leaped from a hired rowboat in midstream as the crowd called the boat back to shore, and his body was not recovered. Newspapers across the country carried the Kansas City dispatch as a story of a man who chose drowning over lynching.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Law Young and William Murphey
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Law Young and William Murphey took place at Gladstone, Nelson County, Virginia, on September 11, 1903, when a crowd of several hundred gathered to await two Black men arrested on suspicion of killing a white man on a freight train. Authorities at Lynchburg, where the two were held, declined to send them to Gladstone, and no harm to them was reported. Another Black man, Frank Bradley, was later charged with the killing, convicted, and hanged.

episodes.title: Monessen saloon riot
episodes.lead: The Monessen saloon riot was a fight between white and Black coal miners in a saloon at Monessen, Pennsylvania, late on the night of September 7, 1903, in which a white miner, Lemuel Gilmore, was fatally shot. George Williams, a Black miner reported as the shooter, escaped with another Black man, William Griffey, and a crowd of white miners pursued them intending to lynch Williams. The pursuers did not catch him, and a Pittsburg dispatch about the "race riot" ran in papers from Georgia to Kansas.

episodes.title: Shooting of M. Carter
episodes.lead: The shooting of M. Carter took place early on September 22, 1903, when a posse with bloodhounds hunting a Black man accused of firing on a white man broke into Carter's house two miles from Shelby, Mississippi, and fatally wounded him. Carter was taken to Shelby, and the reports said he would be lynched if he showed signs of recovery.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching in South Memphis, Tennessee (1903)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching in South Memphis took place on the night of September 6, 1903, when a Black man accused of attacking a woman in her Memphis home was captured and a mob formed against him. He broke away before police sent to protect him arrived, and a dispatch predicted that he would probably be lynched; no later report of his fate was found.

episodes.title: Hanging of a Black man at Mer Rouge, Louisiana (1903)
episodes.lead: The hanging of a Black man at Mer Rouge, Louisiana, was reported in September 1903, when a state news column said that a man it called a "bad negro who tried to run the town" had been "strung up to a limb" there. The single report gave no name, date, or account of who hanged him, and it did not say whether he died.

episodes.title: Stoning of the Lincoln School teachers' home, Meridian, Mississippi
episodes.lead: The stoning of the Lincoln School teachers' home was a mob attack on the night of Thursday, September 10, 1903, on the house occupied by the teachers of Lincoln school, a school for Black children in Meridian, Mississippi. Stones smashed several shutters and windows while the principal, Mrs. H. I. Miller of Topeka, Kansas, stayed inside, and no one was reported hurt. Kansas papers carried the story because of Miller's Topeka ties, linking the attack to a Meridian Star editorial and to President Roosevelt's friendship with Booker T. Washington.

episodes.title: Assault on Mingo Hamilton
episodes.lead: The assault on Mingo Hamilton was an attack by a group of young men on Hamilton, a Black man, on the stoop of his home at 512 West Fifty-fifth Street in New York on the night of Saturday, September 19, 1903. Hamilton was struck with an ash can and cut or stabbed, and three days later Charles Kiernan was arrested and held in $500 bail on a charge of striking him. The two New York papers that covered the case disagreed over whether Hamilton's Black neighbors then fought Kiernan and his friends in a street riot.

episodes.title: Monroe excursion blockade (1903)
episodes.lead: The Monroe excursion blockade was an episode in late September 1903 in which armed white citizens and plantation overseers at Monroe, Louisiana, stopped Black residents from boarding an excursion train to Pine Bluff, Arkansas. No one was reported hurt, and Pine Bluff papers presented it as planters holding on to Black labor during the cotton harvest.

episodes.title: Mob attack on a robbery victim at the American Tract Society Building
episodes.lead: The mob attack on a robbery victim at the American Tract Society Building was a street assault in downtown New York on Wednesday, 2 September 1903, in which a crowd beat a Black man who had just been robbed of his watch by two white men. Police clubbed the crowd apart, and the man left under police protection. The Boston Transcript's account, reprinted in Georgia and in the Black press, presented the attack as evidence of race prejudice in the North.

episodes.title: Newmarket hotel whipping
episodes.lead: The Newmarket hotel whipping was the flogging of two young Black men by a crowd of white men at Newmarket (also printed New Market), Alabama, in early September 1903, after the men walked into the dining room of the town's hotel and ordered supper. Each man was given fifty lashes, and one account says they were then run out of town. The item ran in at least five white newspapers within four days, and a Montgomery editor presented it as a lesson connected to a recent dining-room controversy at Hamlet, North Carolina.

episodes.title: Newport mob threat (1903)
episodes.lead: The Newport mob threat of 1903 was a threat by a "revenging mob" against the village of Newport on the Monday night after a death in a Black-run "joint" there in late September 1903. About 25 Black men left the village for the night, and no violence was reported. The only account came from the St. Louis Palladium's Newport correspondent, who used it to campaign against the joint.

episodes.title: Expulsion order against Black women in Spokane's "burnt district" (1903)
episodes.lead: The expulsion order against Black women in Spokane's "burnt district" was a September 1903 attempt by the Spokane, Washington, police to drive ten Black women out of the city's crib alleys and out of town. Women who refused to leave were arrested and fined for vagrancy, but their attorney charged the police with racial discrimination, and within a week the police commissioner told the chief not to repeat it. The Spokane Press followed the case for a week and returned to it in November.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Robert Bishop
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Robert Bishop occurred on the night of September 11, 1903, at a railroad graders' camp at Oakville, St. Louis County, Missouri, when fellow graders tried to hang Bishop, a Black worker accused of shooting two people. Bishop escaped, and a Ste. Genevieve County posse later shot a Black man taken for him who, the local paper said, proved to be the wrong man.

episodes.title: Ste. Genevieve posse shooting
episodes.lead: The Ste. Genevieve posse shooting occurred in September 1903, when Sheriff Berry of Ste. Genevieve County, Missouri, and a posse shot and wounded a Black man they took to be Robert Bishop, wanted for a shooting at Oakville. The local Fair Play later reported that the jailed man "proved to be the wrong man."

episodes.title: Assault on Robert Hamlin
episodes.lead: The assault on Robert Hamlin was an attack by striking teamsters on Robert J. Hamlin, a Black non-union coal-wagon driver, at Washington and Dey streets in New York City on September 9, 1903. Hamlin was beaten with a shovel and chased by a large crowd, and two members of the Teamsters' Union, Robert Nelligan and James O'Brien, were later convicted and sentenced to nine months in the penitentiary. The Sun followed it from the street to the sentence as a case of union violence against a man's right to work.

episodes.title: Sour Lake expulsion notices
episodes.lead: The Sour Lake expulsion notices were written notices posted in Sour Lake, Texas, on Wednesday, September 16, 1903, ordering the town's Black residents to leave. Many Black residents fled with their belongings, but a local judge swore in extra deputies, white residents promised them protection, and the town was reported quiet within two days. Two papers later reported that the notices, which claimed to come from a white committee, had been posted by a practical joker.

episodes.title: Stroud restaurant dynamiting
episodes.lead: The Stroud restaurant dynamiting was an attack in September 1903 in which unknown persons set off dynamite at the restaurant of James Wadkins, a Black man, in Stroud, Oklahoma Territory, while Black patrons were inside. The blast wrecked the floor or the whole building and broke windows; most reports said no one was hurt, and the suspects who were arrested were released. White papers in Oklahoma, Kansas, Missouri and Wyoming reported it as a sequel to the town's expulsion of its Black residents two years earlier.

episodes.title: Sulphur Springs whippings (1903)
episodes.lead: The Sulphur Springs whippings were the public whipping of a Black school-teacher and about twenty Black men by a party of whites at Sulphur Springs, Bowie county, on September 16, 1903. The teacher was whipped for reportedly making insulting remarks about a young white woman, and the others for protesting his whipping; they were then warned to go to work or leave town. The episode is known from a single New Orleans wire dispatch printed in the New York Sun.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Thomas Hargo
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Thomas Hargo took place in Columbus, Ohio, on or shortly before September 15, 1903, when a crowd of about five hundred people chased Hargo, a Black man, through the streets and produced a rope. Police arrived before he was hanged, and Hargo survived with bruises from thrown bricks. The only report found, a short Ohio news brief, gave as the reason that he had beaten his wife, whom it described as a white woman.

episodes.title: Killing of 'Uncle A.' Finney
episodes.lead: The killing of 'Uncle A.' Finney was the shooting of an elderly Black man, described as a former slave over ninety years old, at the door of his mountain cabin in Franklin County, Virginia, in early September 1903. Three men called him to his door at night and shot him, reportedly because neighbors believed he was a sorcerer who had cast a spell on a sick woman. A son of the sick woman was arrested and released for want of evidence, and a Fredericksburg paper denounced the killing as "barbarism" and a disgrace to Virginia.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black men from Walnut, Kansas
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black men from Walnut, Kansas, was a series of incidents in late summer 1903 in which four Black men were chased out of the town of Walnut, which reportedly refused to allow any Black person on its townsite. The episode is known only from a one-sentence item in the Topeka State Journal, which reported it without comment.

episodes.title: Death of Will Davis
episodes.lead: The death of Will Davis followed a fight on September 1, 1903, at a railroad construction camp near Trussville, Jefferson County, Alabama, in which Davis, a Black laborer, was accused of killing W. G. "Waites" McCaa, a white paymaster, with an ax. Davis fled wounded while posses searched for him, and reports from Trussville said he would be lynched if caught. A Birmingham dispatch of September 7 said citizens had run him down and shot him to death, but after his decomposed body was found near Argo a week later, Birmingham and Montgomery papers said he had died of a wound from McCaa's brother.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Williams
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Williams was the shooting of a Black labor agent by a crowd in Centerville, Mississippi, on September 15, 1903, shortly after he shot and killed James H. Germany, a white employee of the Robinson Mercantile Company. Wire reports put the mob at several hundred people. Mississippi papers treated the killing as an episode in a seasonal conflict over labor agents who drew Black workers away from local employers, while a Black weekly read it as punishment for encouraging Black workers to leave for better wages.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Williams
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Williams was the killing of a Black farm hand by a mob near Whigham, Decatur County, Georgia, on September 26, 1903. Williams was accused of attacking the seven-year-old daughter of his former employer that morning, and that day a mob of about seventy-five men took him from the men holding him and hanged and shot him. A coroner's jury found no evidence against any member of the mob. Early reports stressed that Whigham residents would give no names or particulars, and the story ran across the country only as a brief wire item.

episodes.title: Wellston church whitecapping
episodes.lead: The Wellston church whitecapping was a night attack in early October 1903 at Wellston, Oklahoma Territory, in which unidentified parties destroyed the tent of Albert Boyd, a Black man living on lots bought by the town's colored Baptists for a church. The attackers left a notice signed 'Citizens of Wellston' warning that no church for colored people would be allowed and threatening 'sterner measures' if building went on. No one was hurt, and the coverage reports no arrests.

episodes.title: Attack on the home of Andrew Cheney
episodes.lead: The attack on the home of Andrew Cheney was a midnight attempt in October 1903 by white men to break into the house of Cheney, a Black farmer near Americus, Georgia, and capture him after a quarrel with a white neighbor. Cheney fired on the attackers, badly wounding a white farmer, John Suggs, and the party withdrew. Cheney surrendered to the sheriff and asked for protection; the case drew wire coverage across the South, some of it headlined as a Black man shooting a "whitecap."

episodes.title: Henderson whitecapping shooting
episodes.lead: The Henderson whitecapping shooting took place late on the night of October 6, 1903, at Henderson, Texas, when Bob Willis, a Black man, fired on a party of young white men who had come to his home to flog him, killing one and wounding another. The dead man was Charles Brown, and the sheriff took Willis into custody. The story ran nationally, and the Salt Lake Herald and the Black weeklies Richmond Planet and Cleveland Gazette praised Willis for defending himself.

episodes.title: Brightwood Y.M.C.A. mob threat
episodes.lead: The Brightwood Y.M.C.A. mob threat was an episode on the night of Saturday, 17 October 1903, in which an unnamed Black man was stabbed in a fight at the Brightwood Railroad Y.M.C.A. building in Indiana and then pursued by a mob that threatened to lynch him. He escaped on a street car and was not seen again, and the episode is known from a single short item in the Indianapolis Journal.

episodes.title: Lock Street school race riot
episodes.lead: The Lock Street school race riot was a fight between about 500 white and 150 Black children at the Lock street public school in Cincinnati, Ohio, reported in early October 1903. Some of the Black children were badly beaten and fled to their homes, and the incident reached small-town Michigan papers as a three-sentence wire brief.

episodes.title: Clarksville circus tent shooting
episodes.lead: The Clarksville circus tent shooting was the killing of an unnamed Black man by Deputy Sheriff John Stephens inside a crowded circus tent at Clarksville, Texas, on October 30, 1903. According to the only report found, the man, described as drunk, shot the deputy first and was killed instantly when Stephens returned fire.

episodes.title: Dothan buggy attack
episodes.lead: The Dothan buggy attack was an assault by a white mob on a few Black men who were out riding in a buggy in Dothan, Alabama, on a Sunday in the autumn of 1903. The attackers broke down the buggy and drew pistols on the men, and the incident is known only from a Dothan correspondent's letter to the Colored American, which set it among several acts of violence against the town's Black residents.

episodes.title: Lynching of Ed McCollum
episodes.lead: The lynching of Ed McCollum took place in Sheridan, the county seat of Grant County, Arkansas, around midnight on the night of October 5, 1903, when a masked mob took McCollum, a Black man, from the county jail, tied him to a tree and shot him to death. He had been jailed after he was accused of shooting and wounding a constable who tried to arrest him on a charge of assaulting another Black man. The killing was reported in Arkansas papers and in a short wire dispatch printed across the country, and a Black weekly later counted it among the year's lynchings.

episodes.title: Whitecap notices to Black residents of Robertson County, Texas
episodes.lead: The whitecap notices to Black residents of Robertson County, Texas, were printed warnings, reported in an Austin dispatch of October 30, 1903, ordering the county's Black population to leave under threat of being "whitecapped." According to the dispatch, the Black residents were alarmed and many were leaving. The known coverage consists of one brief wire item reprinted by newspapers in North Dakota, South Dakota and Minnesota.

episodes.title: Fort Riley maneuvers clash between Texas militia and Black cavalrymen
episodes.lead: The Fort Riley maneuvers clash between Texas militia and Black cavalrymen was a series of confrontations in October 1903 at the army maneuvers camp at Fort Riley, Kansas, after members of a Texas National Guard regiment forbade Black troopers of the Tenth United States Cavalry to pass through their camp. Fist fights followed, and the troopers retaliated against the Texans, though a returning Texas company later denied that any clash took place. Wire reports carried the story nationally, and Black weeklies in Kansas and Iowa printed fuller accounts celebrating the Black soldiers.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Fortune Ellis
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Fortune Ellis took place in Lowndes County, Alabama, in October 1903, when a sheriff-led posse hunted Ellis, a Black man accused of shooting two white men in a dispute over cotton, while newspapers predicted he would be lynched. Ellis was captured and moved to the Montgomery County jail for fear of a mob, and no lynching was reported. The case drew a Birmingham Age-Herald editorial against 'a second lynching' that year, and in 1904 Ellis was fined $500 and given six months' hard labor.

episodes.title: Whitecapping of George and Amelia Guenther
episodes.lead: The whitecapping of George and Amelia Guenther was a night attack on 9 October 1903 in which about a dozen masked men fired into the farmhouse of George Guenther, a white farmer near Sandusky, Ohio, and his Black wife, whom he had recently married. One bullet wounded both, and in November a grand jury indicted five Perkins Township men. Papers nationwide presented the attack as neighbors punishing an interracial marriage, and Black weeklies condemned the attackers.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Kennedy
episodes.lead: The lynching of George Kennedy took place on the night of Sunday, October 18, 1903, when a mob hanged Kennedy, a Black man, to a tree near Taylortown in Bossier Parish, Louisiana. White papers said he had been captured at the Taylortown railroad depot with a pistol, waiting to kill Mercer Brittain, a conductor on the Red River Valley railroad. The story ran as a short wire item in papers as far away as New York and Minnesota, and an Oklahoma paper called the lynching of a man for a contemplated crime "a dangerous precedent."

episodes.title: Lynching at Hattiesburg, Mississippi (October 1903)
episodes.lead: The lynching at Hattiesburg, Mississippi, took place in the early morning of October 30, 1903, when a mob took an unnamed Black man from the town jail and hanged him to a tree. He had been charged with entering the house of H. T. Allen to assault a member of the family, and no report gives his name. The story ran as a wire brief in papers from Mississippi to Minnesota, and the Hattiesburg paper later reprinted a Vicksburg comment counting it among recent examples of "swift justice."

episodes.title: Littleton dance hall shooting
episodes.lead: The Littleton dance hall shooting was an attack on a Black dance in a town called Littleton, on a Saturday night shortly before mid-October 1903, in which a group of drunken white men fired on the dancers after Black women refused to dance with them. James Matthews was killed and several others were seriously wounded. The shooting is known from a short telegram in an Atlanta paper, which an Iowa editor reprinted to contrast the muted response with what the editor said would follow an attack by Black men on white dancers.

episodes.title: Killing of Jennie McCall
episodes.lead: The killing of Jennie McCall was the shooting death of a Black woman by a mob at her house near Jennings, Florida, on the night of Tuesday, October 27, 1903. The mob had come for her husband and, believing he was inside, fired a volley into the house. An Associated Press dispatch from Jacksonville carried the story to papers from Maine to Mississippi, and the St. Paul Appeal, a Black newspaper, reprinted a Chicago account in which she died defending her husband.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jesse Franklin and Jim Phillips
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jesse Franklin and Jim Phillips was the fatal whipping of two Black men by a band of white men in the Bunker Hill community of Rusk County, Texas, in early October 1903. Both men died, and four white men were reported arrested. The case became national news when Webster Flanagan, the federal internal revenue collector for the district, said local news of the attacks had been suppressed and asked Governor Lanham for protection.

episodes.title: Shooting of John Wells
episodes.lead: The shooting of John Wells was the wounding of a Black porter by Charles Highland, a merchant policeman, in Indianapolis, Indiana, on the night of October 14, 1903. Highland took Wells for a burglar and fired without warning, striking him twice in the right leg. The Indianapolis Journal reported the case as the shooting of "an Innocent Man" by an officer "too ready with a pistol."

episodes.title: Mob shooting of Len Beauchamps
episodes.lead: The mob shooting of Len Beauchamps was an attack on a Black man on the night of October 30, 1903, in which a mob took him from officers and shot him on suspicion of assaulting a white girl; the fullest dispatch placed it at Sedalia, Missouri, while others gave the place as "Vidalia." Beauchamps survived the shooting but was reported so badly hurt that he was not expected to recover, and evidence was then said to point to another Black man, who escaped the mob. Newspapers that carried the story presented it as a case of a mob attacking "the wrong negro."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Willis Martin
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Willis Martin occurred in October 1903 at DeKalb, Mississippi, when a crowd of masked men gathered at night to seize Martin, a Black prisoner held in the town jail after a cutting fight. The crowd dispersed on learning that Sheriff Hull had placed special deputies around the jail, and the next day the sheriff moved Martin to the jail at Macon. The episode is known from a single Kemper Herald item reprinted in the Macon Beacon.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Melved H. Rosier
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Melved H. Rosier was a failed attempt by masked men on the night of Saturday, October 3, 1903, to lynch a Black boy of about fifteen held in the county jail at La Plata, Charles County, Maryland. The jail officer took Rosier out of the jail shortly before the mob came, hid him in the woods overnight and moved him to a place of safety the next day. Two Washington-area papers reported the episode as a frustrated lynching on October 6.

episodes.title: Sixth Street mob beating, Minneapolis (1903)
episodes.lead: The Sixth Street mob beating was an attack on a Black man by a crowd of white bystanders on Sixth Street in Minneapolis, Minnesota, on the night of 2 October 1903. After a stabbing in a saloon, a crowd chased three Black men and beat the one it caught while a policeman held him, until he was found to be "the wrong man" and released. The Minneapolis Journal called the affair a "miniature race war" that police interference kept from becoming a lynching.

episodes.title: Lynching of Minor Long
episodes.lead: The lynching of Minor Long was the killing of a Black prisoner by masked men inside the parish jail at St. Francisville, Louisiana, on the night of October 5 or 6, 1903. After taking the keys from the jailer, the men shot Long to death in his cell when a rope they had called for did not arrive. A New York Sun dispatch about the killing was reprinted under the headline "Lynching Outrage" and condensed in rural and German-language papers.

episodes.title: Lynching of Mitchell Gilbert
episodes.lead: The lynching of Mitchell Gilbert took place near Cordele, Georgia, during the night of October 15–16, 1903, when a Black former farm hand was hanged from a tree beside a public road south of the town and his body riddled with bullets. Wire reports carried across the country described him only as "an unknown negro" and said neither the cause nor the killers were known, while a Georgia paper named him and reported that a posse had hanged him for writing a letter to a young woman. The Black weekly St. Paul Appeal cited the case as "the latest from Lynchland" and called it murder.

episodes.title: Nahunta swamp lynching
episodes.lead: The Nahunta swamp lynching was the reported killing in October 1903 of an unnamed Black man by a posse near Nahunta, after a justice of the peace had discharged him on a charge of attempted assault. According to the Dawson News, the posse took him to a swamp, where "it is said" they gave him a "new trial" from which "he never came clear." The episode is known from that single hearsay item, and the man's death is implied rather than stated.

episodes.title: Jeanerette acid-attack manhunt
episodes.lead: The Jeanerette acid-attack manhunt was a posse search in Jeanerette, Louisiana, on October 29, 1903, for an unidentified man believed to be Black who had thrown sulphuric acid in the face of an engineer, Norther Provost. Two Black men were arrested and released, the assailant was not caught, and the dispatch reported that he would be "summarily dealt with" if captured.

episodes.title: Oakwood handcar ambush
episodes.lead: The Oakwood handcar ambush took place about October 5, 1903, when a citizen posse at Oakwood, Illinois, derailed a handcar carrying three Black men accused of burglary and fired on them. The three men escaped after a running fight, and one member of the posse was grazed by a bullet. Danville dispatches reported it as a battle with "negro burglars."

episodes.title: Pecan Grove posse shooting
episodes.lead: The Pecan Grove posse shooting was a gunfight on October 19, 1903, near Pecan Grove plantation in St. Charles Parish, Louisiana, in which a constable's posse killed three Black railroad workers and wounded about seven others. The posse had gone out over charges that some of the men owed unpaid debts, and no member of it was hurt. White papers across the country ran the story as a battle with a band of Black men led by a white man, while the Richmond Planet called it 'another butchery'.

episodes.title: Killing of Raymond Sizer
episodes.lead: The killing of Raymond Sizer was the fatal shooting of Sizer, a young Black man, by seventeen-year-old Clarence M. Brooks, a white storekeeper's son, in the Brooks store at Vaughanville, Newberry County, South Carolina, on October 10, 1903. By the Brooks family's sworn account the quarrel began when Brooks demanded to be called "Mr. Brooks"; a coroner's jury found self-defense, and a jury acquitted him of murder on November 5. A week later about fifty armed white men gathered at Vaughanville and the Black Odd Fellows' hall burned, which the Newberry Herald and News said made the case "well-known throughout the State."

episodes.title: Whitecapping of Robinson's farm near Johnson Station
episodes.lead: The whitecapping of Robinson's farm near Johnson Station was a night raid in late September or early October 1903 in which whitecappers destroyed the fences and crops of Robinson, a Black landowner in Lincoln County, Mississippi. The same report said that Jim Williams, a Black man living just across the county line in Pike County, had his property treated in the same way. The Brookhaven Leader, which learned of the raid secondhand, treated it as 'another case' of whitecapping and condemned it as 'a disgrace to civilization'.

episodes.title: Assault on Roland Alston at the Columbian Institution for the Deaf and Dumb
episodes.lead: The assault on Roland Alston at the Columbian Institution for the Deaf and Dumb occurred about noon on October 19, 1903, in Washington, D.C., when about fifty students "rushed" Alston, a young Black assistant janitor. They grabbed him and threw him down, and the pursuit ended only after he picked up a kitchen knife; he then left his job. The Evening Star covered it after rumors spread that the students had meant to lynch him.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Sam Bailey
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Sam Bailey was an armed pursuit of a Black furnace worker by a crowd of white men at North Birmingham, Alabama, on 10 October 1903, after he resisted arrest by an officer. Bailey escaped into the woods after an exchange of gunfire, and no report of his capture was found. The Birmingham Age-Herald wrote that a lynching "was only averted by his escaping from the mob," and a wire dispatch carried the chase to papers from Georgia to Arizona.

episodes.title: Air-rifle shooting of a Black woman in Savannah (1903)
episodes.lead: The air-rifle shooting of a Black woman in Savannah took place in the autumn of 1903, when some white boys "seriously" shot an unnamed "colored lady" with an air rifle in the East Broad Street neighborhood of Savannah, Georgia. The only known report, a paragraph in the Black weekly Savannah Tribune, said no attempt was made to apprehend the shooter and cited the case as evidence that white offenders against Black residents went unpunished.

episodes.title: Mob pursuit of William Daniels
episodes.lead: The mob pursuit of William Daniels took place in October 1903 near the Tug River between West Virginia and Kentucky, when friends of a bartender named Trimble Sparks formed a mob to deal out "summary justice" to the Black man accused of shooting him. According to a dispatch from Inez, Kentucky, the man escaped by a roundabout route and asked for protection at Williamson, West Virginia. A wire report named him as William Daniels and said an armed posse was pursuing him; no report of his capture or trial appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Beating of a Pullman porter at Sterling, Georgia
episodes.lead: The beating of a Pullman porter at Sterling, Georgia, took place on about October 21, 1903, when an unnamed Black sleeping-car porter on Southern Railway train No. 14 was beaten by George H. Smith, treasurer of the city of Brunswick, and then put off the train in the woods. He was accused of speaking insolently to a woman passenger bound for Spartanburg, South Carolina. Several South Carolina weeklies reprinted the story as a lesson in manners under headlines such as 'It Pays to be Polite.'

episodes.title: Killing of Steve Williams
episodes.lead: The killing of Steve Williams was the fatal shooting of an elderly Black man by bailiff Alfred Moree in a field at Isabella, Georgia, about noon on October 14, 1903. The only known report, a dispatch in the Savannah Morning News, called the killing justifiable on the information then available and said no arrest had been made.

episodes.title: Kevil depot fight and expulsion of Black residents
episodes.lead: The Kevil depot fight and expulsion of Black residents was a clash between Black men and white youths at Kevil, an Illinois Central station in Ballard County, Kentucky, on October 11, 1903, followed by the flight of the area's Black residents from armed white neighbors. A white youth, Crockett Childress, was mortally wounded, and a Black man, Tom Hall, was shot in the arm, arrested, and on October 16 lynched at Wickliffe. White papers called it a "race riot," while the St. Paul Appeal blamed the separation of the platform by color.

episodes.title: Lynching of Tom Hall
episodes.lead: The lynching of Tom Hall was the hanging of a Black prisoner by a masked mob that took him from the jail at Wickliffe, Ballard County, Kentucky, at about 1 a.m. on October 16, 1903. Hall was accused of shooting Crockett Childress, a white youth, in a fight over the railroad platform at Kevil five nights earlier, a charge he denied. Papers across the country remarked on how quietly the mob had worked; no arrests were reported.

episodes.title: Toombsboro curfew shooting
episodes.lead: The Toombsboro curfew shooting was an exchange of gunfire on the night of October 4–5, 1903, in Toombsboro, Wilkinson County, Georgia, between the town marshal, later joined by a posse, and a group of Black men he had ordered off a street corner under a new curfew ordinance. About 100 shots were reportedly fired without anyone being hit, and five Black men were jailed to be tried for assault with intent to murder.

episodes.title: Vaughanville Odd Fellows hall burning
episodes.lead: The Vaughanville Odd Fellows hall burning was the destruction of a Black lodge hall at Vaughanville, Newberry County, South Carolina, on the night of October 16, 1903, while about fifty armed white men were gathered nearby. The white men had assembled on a rumor that lodge members had sent for arms and meant to confront Clarence M. Brooks, a white youth who had shot and killed a Black man, Raymond Sizer, the week before. No one was confirmed killed, and the only account found, in the Newberry Herald and News, said the cause of the fire was not known.

episodes.title: Expulsion of the Bushfield families from Vernon, Indiana
episodes.lead: The expulsion of the Bushfield families from Vernon, Indiana, took place around October 22, 1903, when a mob ordered four families named Bushfield out of the Jennings County town and burned their four houses. The families were sent south and told not to return. Wire reports said the mob was believed to resent the light sentence a court had just given a Bushfield charged with attempted murder, and the item ran in papers from Georgia to North Dakota.

episodes.title: Lynching of Walter Davis
episodes.lead: The lynching of Walter Davis took place on the night of October 1, 1903, in Marshall, Texas, when a mob of several hundred men broke into the city jail, took Davis, a Black prisoner, and hanged him to a tree. Davis had been arrested hours earlier, after a constable named Hayes was shot from ambush. The story ran across the country through a single wire dispatch, much of which stressed that the militia sent to guard the jail arrived too late.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Butler
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Butler occurred in New York City on October 4, 1903, after Butler, a Black man, was arrested for the fatal shooting of Dean Evans in a quarrel over a crap game. According to a wire dispatch, the policeman who caught Butler after chasing him in a commandeered electric car had to turn his revolver on an "immense crowd of excited men who wanted to lynch the prisoner." The two New York papers whose reports were found described the shooting and arrest but did not mention a crowd threat.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Mason and Thomas DeMoss
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Mason and Thomas DeMoss took place in Topeka, Kansas, on the night of October 19, 1903, when a crowd gathered at the city jail after the two Black men were arrested in the fatal shooting of Fred Tutcher, a liveryman. Sheriff A. T. Lucas had already moved the prisoners to Lawrence, and the crowd dispersed without violence. Wire reports described a lynching mob of 200 to 1,000, while the Topeka State Journal and the Black weekly Topeka Plaindealer called it a gathering of spectators.

episodes.title: Whitecapping of William Noblett
episodes.lead: The whitecapping of William Noblett was a whitecap raid near Farmington, Marshall County, Tennessee, in the autumn of 1903, in which a band of men badly beat Noblett, a Black man, and his wife. Seven men from neighboring Bedford County were arrested, and in November 1903 a Marshall County grand jury indicted them while the governor appointed a special assistant to the prosecution. A December 1904 report that five men with matching names had been sentenced to four months in jail for whitecapping indicates that the case ended in convictions.

episodes.title: Flushing tunnel fight
episodes.lead: The Flushing tunnel fight was an armed clash on the night of October 23, 1903, near Flushing, Belmont County, Ohio, between a town marshal's posse and Black laborers, in which Marshal John G. Elliott was killed and four Black men were wounded. A crowd then threatened to lynch the captured men, and officials moved the prisoners to the county jail at St. Clairsville. Within four days an autopsy led authorities to suspect one of the marshal's own deputies, John Wheeler, of firing the fatal shot, and an Ohio paper headlined that the Black men were "Innocent."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Adam Hunt
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Adam Hunt took place at Roxboro, Person County, North Carolina, on the night of November 15, 1903, when forty or fifty men demanded the jail keys from Sheriff Thompson in order to lynch Hunt, a Black sawmill worker accused of killing the merchant Fleet Wilkins. The sheriff convinced the crowd that he did not have the keys, and it left without Hunt. Hunt was convicted within days and, after the state Supreme Court affirmed the verdict, hanged at Roxboro on June 15, 1904, an outcome the Richmond Times-Dispatch held up as justice that prevented lynching.

episodes.title: Albany Elk pin incident
episodes.lead: The Albany Elk pin incident was a confrontation in Albany, Georgia, in late 1903 in which about ten white men made a Black member of the touring Black Patti Troubadours remove his Elk pin. No one was reported hurt, but the men had knives drawn when they began to cut the pin from his coat. The Indianapolis Freeman printed the account under the head "A Georgia Absurdity."

episodes.title: Killing of Albert Dennis
episodes.lead: The killing of Albert Dennis was the fatal shooting of a young Black man by Milan E. McNamara, a special policeman employed by the Great Northern theater in Chicago, outside the theater on the evening of Sunday, November 29, 1903. Dennis had just been ejected from the theater, and he died a short time later at the county hospital. White papers carried the shooting as a brief wire item, while the Chicago Broad Ax reported that Dennis's Knights of Pythias lodge had voted to pay for McNamara's prosecution.

episodes.title: Beating of Arthur Patterson and William Black
episodes.lead: The beating of Arthur Patterson and William Black was an attack by a crowd of white men on two Black men on the West Side of New York City on November 3, 1903, after a sixteen-year-old white boy, Jeremiah Healy, was shot in the street. Both men were beaten so badly that they were taken to Roosevelt Hospital, and the papers reported that only the arrival of police kept them from being killed. Patterson, charged with the shooting, denied it, and the attack was reported in two New York dailies and by wire across the country.

episodes.title: Stoning of the Masonic Temple on Courtland Street, Baltimore
episodes.lead: The stoning of the Masonic Temple on Courtland Street was an attack on a Black Masonic lodge hall in Baltimore, Maryland, on election night, Tuesday, November 3, 1903, and the following morning, by a crowd the Baltimore Afro-American put at more than two hundred white men and boys. No one was reported injured, but the front of the three-story building was left with hardly a pane of glass. The Afro-American presented the attack as the fruit of the Democratic campaign against "Negro domination" and faulted the police for their slow response.

episodes.title: Shooting of Ben Douglass
episodes.lead: The shooting of Ben Douglass was the wounding of a Black pool-room keeper by Deputy V. G. Richardson on Upper Front street in Newport, Arkansas, late on Tuesday, November 3, 1903, as officers tried to arrest him. The officer said Douglass moved to resist, while a Black bystander said the deputy fired first.

episodes.title: Harmony Grove assault on a Black woman (1903)
episodes.lead: The Harmony Grove assault on a Black woman was an attack on the night of Saturday, November 21, 1903, about three miles below Harmony Grove in Madison County, Georgia, in which three young white men named Chandler, McGinnis and Fitzpatrick broke into a Black home, carried off a young mother and assaulted her in a field. Warrants were issued for the three men, and one wire report said posses of Black and white men were hunting them with lynching openly promised. Black newspapers and at least one Northern white paper cited the case to answer the claim that sexual assault was a crime of Black men.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Smith
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Charles Smith took place on the night of November 13, 1903, in Washington, D.C., when a crowd that had chased Smith, a Black youth accused of robbing a cafe cashier and shooting two policemen, beat him and shouted for his lynching as he was captured in an alley off New York Avenue. Police held the crowd back until a patrol wagon arrived, and Smith was held for the grand jury. Out-of-town papers stressed that it happened within sight of the White House, and one wire version said a "race riot" had barely been averted.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Charles Young
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of Charles Young was a killing said to have taken place near Coal City, St. Clair County, Alabama, on the night of Saturday, November 7, 1903, after Young, a Black railroad construction worker, was accused of attempting to assault a white woman, Mrs. Barbour. The story, which came secondhand through Ragland, ran in papers from Maine to Montana in the following days. The Birmingham Age-Herald, however, stated that the St. Clair County lynching reported in distant papers never took place.

episodes.title: Sixth and Vine street attack, Cincinnati (1903)
episodes.lead: The Sixth and Vine street attack was an assault by a white crowd on three Black men at Sixth and Vine streets in central Cincinnati, Ohio, early on the morning of November 24, 1903, after the men were accused of insulting two white women. A white man, John McCarthy, was stabbed three times in the melee, and the three men were "roughly handled" before police kept the crowd from killing them. The story circulated as a short wire item headed "race war" and was reprinted in Midwestern and Dakota weeklies into December 1903.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Dick Thompson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Dick Thompson took place in Centralia, Missouri, on a Tuesday night in November 1903, when a crowd of about two hundred men gathered at the city hall where Thompson, a Black man accused of indecent conduct before schoolgirls, was being held. Officers and deputized citizens guarded him through the night, and he was afterward fined $100 and costs in a justice court. Two weeklies in Mexico, Missouri, reported the episode under the headlines "Lynching Averted" and "Almost a Lynching."

episodes.title: Whipping of Ed Williams
episodes.lead: The whipping of Ed Williams was a mob assault in Augusta, Kentucky, in November 1903, in which a group of local residents took Williams, a Black man, from the town jail at night and whipped him. He was accused of "impudence to young white ladies," and he left Augusta afterward. The only known report, a short item in the Maysville Daily Public Ledger, called the whipping "much-deserved."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Edward Green
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Edward Green took place in Bronxville, New York, in November 1903, when residents threatened to lynch Green, a Black man of Mount Vernon, after he was identified as the man who had attacked the private secretary of former state senator Isaac N. Mills. Officials guarded Green, and two days after his arrest he was acquitted on the alibi testimony of a former mayor of Mount Vernon. Wire reports carried the story nationally, first as a jail guarded against lynchers and then as the narrow escape of an innocent man.

episodes.title: Whitecap attack on the home of Eli Hilson
episodes.lead: The whitecap attack on the home of Eli Hilson was a night shooting in November 1903 in which a band of whitecaps fired into the house of Eli Hilson, a Black farmer living about seven miles from Brookhaven in Lincoln County, Mississippi, after he had ignored their warning to leave. No one was hit, although Hilson's wife had given birth only hours before. The papers reported it as part of a revival of whitecapping that within days killed another Black farmer, Henry Lisle, and recalled it when Hilson himself was shot dead the next month.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Scott and Smith counties, Mississippi
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black residents from Scott and Smith counties, Mississippi, was a campaign in the autumn of 1903 in which white residents whipped the occupants of numerous Black cabins, burned their homes and drove them out of the state. It is known only from a brief New Orleans wire dispatch of mid-November that described "race riots of large proportions" and was reprinted in a handful of papers outside the South.

episodes.title: Gillsburg lynching and reported riot
episodes.lead: The Gillsburg lynching and reported riot was the hanging of an unnamed Black man by a posse at Gillsburg, a small town twelve miles northeast of Kentwood, Louisiana, on Sunday, November 15, 1903, after he was accused of assaulting a white woman. A wire dispatch from Kentwood added that Black residents who gathered in anger were met in a fight in which eighteen of them were killed, a figure it said was only "reported here tonight." The story ran in a handful of white papers in South Carolina, Kansas and Missouri; no confirmation, names or follow-up appear in the coverage.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Johnson
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Johnson took place at Lake Village, Chicot County, Arkansas, on November 3, 1903, when a white crowd broke into the jail, took Johnson, a Black prisoner, from his cell and hanged him in the center of town. Johnson had been arrested after an early-morning saloon shooting in which Frank Anderson, a white man, was killed. The Associated Press reported it nationally as a "race riot" followed by a lynching, and the New York Sun called Johnson innocent, while papers near the scene held him responsible.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Liste
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Liste was the killing of a Black farmer by a band of whitecappers at his home in the Gum Grove neighborhood of Lincoln County, Mississippi, on the night of November 24, 1903. The riders had fired into his house and ordered him to leave about two weeks earlier, and they returned when he stayed. Newspapers treated the killing as evidence that whitecapping in the county, thought to have been suppressed, had revived in a worse form.

episodes.title: Killing of Herbert Clifton and manhunt for George Jenkins
episodes.lead: The killing of Herbert Clifton and manhunt for George Jenkins took place in Tunica County, Mississippi, where on the evening of November 29, 1903, Jenkins, a Black plantation laborer, was accused of shooting Clifton, a young white planter, at Banks station. Armed posses from Tunica and DeSoto counties hunted Jenkins with bloodhounds, and white papers reported as a certainty that he would be lynched if caught. The posses did not catch him; rewards reaching $1,300 followed, his father was jailed, and a man of his name was arrested in Louisiana in 1904.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Hugh Armstead
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Hugh Armstead took place on the evening of November 3, 1903, election day, in Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, when a crowd of 500 or more men chased Armstead, a Black man, to the Monongahela River crying "Lynch him" after he shot Patrick Butler, a watcher at the polls. Police fought the crowd for their prisoner and took him safely to jail. A single Associated Press dispatch about the case ran in papers across the country, in some of them among reports of election-day violence elsewhere, and the Richmond Planet reprinted it.

episodes.title: Whitecap attack on Isaiah Dillon's house
episodes.lead: The whitecap attack on Isaiah Dillon's house was a night shooting in Franklin County, Mississippi, in mid-November 1903, in which a band of whitecappers fired revolvers into the home of Isaiah Dillon, an elderly Black man. Several bullets passed through the cover of the bed in which Dillon was sleeping, but no injury was reported. Brought to Jackson by a Franklin County state senator, the shooting was reported as the sign of a renewed whitecap outbreak that was driving Black residents and laborers out of Amite, Franklin and Lincoln counties.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Nelson
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jim Nelson was the hanging of a Black farm laborer of about 19 by twenty or thirty mounted men on the road about three miles from Jefferson, Chesterfield County, South Carolina, on Saturday night, November 21, 1903. Nelson had been accused of attempting to assault the young daughter of his employer and was taken from two men who were carrying him to the sheriff. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of "parties unknown," and South Carolina papers noted that it was the county's first lynching.

episodes.title: Montevideo courthouse crowd (1903)
episodes.lead: The Montevideo courthouse crowd of November 1903 was a reported mob threat against Joe Scott, a Black prisoner, when he was brought to Montevideo, Minnesota, on November 24, 1903, to answer for an axe attack on Helen Olson at Watson the previous July. Scott pleaded guilty and was sentenced to thirty years, and the sheriff removed him from the town under guard. Whether a mob threatened him is disputed: the St. Paul Globe described a "threatening mob" that followed him to the train, while dispatches from Montevideo reported no disturbance.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Fogle
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Fogle took place early on November 28, 1903, near Ross, a small railway station in Dorchester County, South Carolina, when a mob hanged and shot a Black man of about thirty accused of attempting to assault a young white woman. Hunted overnight with bloodhounds, Fogle was taken before his accuser for identification and then strung to a tree and shot. The Associated Press reported it as the first lynching in the county's history, the angle many headlines took.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Joe Battle
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Joe Battle took place in Edgecombe County, North Carolina, in November 1903, when officers heard that people meant to seize Battle, a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman near Rocky Mount, and lynch him. A deputy sheriff drove him to the Wake County jail in Raleigh on November 14 by a roundabout route, and he was held there until his return to Tarboro for trial in March 1904. North Carolina and Richmond papers followed the case through Battle's escape from the Raleigh jail, his recapture and his identification by the woman.

episodes.title: Mob attack on Leslie Triplett
episodes.lead: The mob attack on Leslie Triplett was an assault by white men on Leslie Triplett, a Black performer with the touring Black Patti Troubadours, at West Point, Mississippi, on November 12, 1903. Triplett was still suffering from his injuries a week later, and a Columbus, Mississippi, paper said a "scrap in West Point" had cost the company several performers.

episodes.title: 1903 Morgan Park lynching attempt and expulsion order
episodes.lead: The 1903 Morgan Park lynching attempt and expulsion order was an attack by a white mob on Black prisoners in the village lockup of Morgan Park, Illinois, a suburb of Chicago, on November 1, 1903, followed by placards ordering all Black residents to leave. The prisoners, accused of killing police chief George A. Airey on Halloween, were rescued by Chicago police; after the placards several Black families left.

episodes.title: Killing of Rafe Harvey
episodes.lead: The killing of Rafe Harvey was the shooting and beating of a Black man by police officers and citizens in Savannah, Georgia, early on November 15, 1903, after he had wounded two officers and a railroad engineer while resisting arrest. Patrolman Harmon Miller shot him twice, and officers and citizens clubbed him before he was taken prisoner. Harvey died in the jail hospital two weeks later, and the only coverage found, in the Savannah Morning News, told the story entirely from the police side.

episodes.title: Raleigh street car seat incident (1903)
episodes.lead: The Raleigh street car seat incident took place in Raleigh, North Carolina, around 2 November 1903, when white men seized two Black passengers on a street car at the Fair Grounds and pulled them from their seats after they refused to give the seats up to white college girls. No one was reported hurt, and the only account, in the Raleigh News & Observer, was written to deny a rumor that several Black passengers had been pushed off the car.

episodes.title: Lynching of Phil Davis, Walter Carter and Clint Thomas
episodes.lead: The lynching of Phil Davis, Walter Carter and Clint Thomas was the hanging of three Black men near Belcher, Caddo Parish, Louisiana, on November 30, 1903, before a crowd reported at about 1,200 people. The men were accused of taking part in the shooting of Robert Adger, a white planter and merchant who died a week later. Papers across the country noted that Black residents had joined the hunt and that whites gave one of them a $100 purse, a detail the Black press condemned.

episodes.title: Killing of Robert E. Banks
episodes.lead: The killing of Robert E. Banks was the fatal shooting of an 18-year-old youth by a gang of white boys and men on Josephine street near Howard in New Orleans on the evening of November 6, 1903. Three white boys were arrested, and a white man, Gus Drew, later surrendered saying he had fired in self defense. The case is known from a New Orleans correspondent's letter to the Richmond Planet, which called it an "unprovoked murder."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Rufus Martin
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Rufus Martin was an unsuccessful effort, reported from Fort Worth, Texas, to lynch a Black man accused of killing a farmer in early November 1903. Martin survived, and on November 10 a jury sentenced him to death, a verdict carried by wire to papers in Nebraska and Wyoming.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sam Adams
episodes.lead: The lynching of Sam Adams was the hanging of a young Black man by residents of Pass Christian, Mississippi, on the night of November 5, 1903, after he was accused of assaulting Mrs. Peter Labouisse, a white woman, that afternoon. He was taken from officers who were moving him from the jail, and a coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of "male citizens, both white and colored," organized to kill him. The case drew national notice because Mrs. Labouisse had been a New York society figure.

episodes.title: Hurlock election riot
episodes.lead: The Hurlock election riot was an exchange of gunfire between Black and white men in Hurlock, Dorchester County, Maryland, on the night of November 3, 1903, the state's election day. Three or four white men and at least one Black man were wounded, and a sheriff's party with a posse arrested fourteen Black men and took them to the jail at Cambridge. Black men were afterward indicted for rioting, and in December John Brown and six others were acquitted on the court's instruction.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Taylor Gibbs
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Taylor Gibbs took place at Lancaster, Garrard County, Kentucky, on 25 November 1903, when crowds of local citizens sought to hang Gibbs, a Black man accused of attempting to assault two white women on the road to Kirksville. County Attorney James Hamilton persuaded the crowd at the jail to disperse by promising an immediate indictment and trial. Gibbs was indicted two days later and sentenced to seven years in the penitentiary, and the wire reports presented the episode as a lynching prevented by the prosecutor's plea.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Hardy
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Hardy took place at Baconton, Mitchell County, Georgia, on November 22, 1903, after Hardy, a Black man, shot a member of a posse sent to arrest him. Posse gunfire wounded Hardy, and officers moved him to the Albany jail as a mob organized to lynch him. The posse member, Raymond Mullins, the mayor's son, died the next day, and Hardy was tried within eight days and hanged at Camilla on December 22.

episodes.title: Yorktown, Indiana, mob pursuit of a Black man (1903)
episodes.lead: The Yorktown mob pursuit was the chase of an unnamed Black man by a mob of twenty-five men at Yorktown, Indiana, six miles west of Muncie, reported in a dispatch dated November 2, 1903. The man escaped by jumping into the river and swimming across, and no one was reported hurt. The report was notable for stating the motive plainly: "Colored men are unpopular in the village Yorktown."

episodes.title: Berkley poll-tax riot
episodes.lead: The Berkley poll-tax riot took place on the night of December 8, 1903, when about 300 armed white "straightout" Democrats in Berkley, Norfolk County, Virginia, drove county officials and a group of Black men from an office where the men had come to pay their poll taxes. The crowd kicked County Treasurer Samuel W. Lyons down a flight of stairs and choked County Clerk Alvah H. Martin, the Fusionist leader; shots were fired, but no one was reported hit. The Richmond Times-Dispatch called it a "Party Riot," and the Richmond Planet condemned it as a "high-handed proceeding" against Black taxpayers.

episodes.title: Lynching of Arthur Stewart
episodes.lead: The lynching of Arthur Stewart was the killing of a Black prisoner in the town calaboose at Pineapple, Wilcox County, Alabama, early on December 26, 1903, by a mob that struck him on the head, poured kerosene over him and set the building on fire. The fire spread through the business district, and although a coroner's jury charged five men with murder, a grand jury found no true bill. Alabama and Black papers alike stressed that Stewart had not done the shooting that prompted the attack.

episodes.title: Barney shooting and race-riot scare
episodes.lead: The Barney shooting and race-riot scare took place on Christmas Day 1903 at Barney, Georgia, a village near Quitman, when a white man, Perry Peeples, shot and killed an unnamed Black man and Black residents were reported to have "took up the fight." The sheriff took an armed posse to the village by special train, found it quiet, and returned the same night. White newspapers in Georgia and beyond headlined the episode as a feared "race riot" among Black residents rather than as a killing.

episodes.title: Whitecapping threat against an interracial couple at Puncheon Run, Delaware
episodes.lead: The whitecapping threat at Puncheon Run was an episode in December 1903 near Dover, Delaware, in which local citizens threatened to whitecap a white woman, Bertie Fleming, and a Black man named Smith who were living together. Rather than act against those making the threats, the sheriff and three officers arrested the couple on December 22 as "suspicious characters."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Berry Henry
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Berry Henry took place in Bartow, Polk County, Florida, on the night of December 24, 1903, when 25 to 35 armed men marched to the jail and demanded Henry, a Black prisoner suspected of shooting Colonel John Beatty and his wife that morning. Sheriff J. D. Tillis refused to give up the prisoner and threatened to fire, and the men dispersed; Henry was then moved to Tampa. Headlines praised the sheriff for saving his prisoner from a mob.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Bynum
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Charles Bynum took place near Driver, in Nansemond County, Virginia, in the early morning of December 19, 1903, when a crowd threatened the life of Bynum, a Black man accused of burning the barn and stables of his landlord, John L. Bond. To keep him from the crowd, Justice Morris held a preliminary hearing at about 3 a.m. by the light of the fire, held Bynum for court, and had him taken to jail. The image of a night court lit by the burning barn carried the story into papers across the country.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Clarendon, Arkansas (1903)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching at Clarendon, Arkansas, was a mob's effort on the night of December 3, 1903, to lynch an unnamed Black prisoner who was on trial in the town. The sheriff protected the prisoner, and the only report of the mob said it was expected to return the following night.

episodes.title: Expulsion notice to the Dabney brothers at Port Royal, Virginia
episodes.lead: The expulsion notice to the Dabney brothers was an order given in December 1903 by citizens of Port Royal, Caroline County, Virginia, that a Black man named Dabney and his brothers leave the county within twenty-four hours, after they fell under suspicion in a night attack on a young physician, Dr. Lloyd Norland. The men disappeared, and within about two weeks three brothers named Walker, reported as the suspected attackers, had been arrested, jailed at Bowling Green and sent on to a grand jury. Fredericksburg and Richmond papers mentioned the notice in a single sentence, as a step the citizens took because no direct evidence could be found.

episodes.title: Whitecap notice to Dennis Powell
episodes.lead: The whitecap notice to Dennis Powell was a death threat posted at the gate of a Black landowner about two miles southwest of Brookhaven, Mississippi, in early December 1903. The typewritten notice ordered Powell to leave or suffer death, and the men who left it fired shots near his house; no one was reported hurt. The Brookhaven Leader reported it as a local item, and a Black correspondent at Brookhaven soon described a white-cap notice there, possibly the same one.

episodes.title: Killing of Eli Hilson
episodes.lead: The killing of Eli Hilson was the ambush shooting of a Black farmer near Brookhaven, Lincoln County, Mississippi, on the evening of December 19, 1903, after he refused a whitecap order to leave his land. Papers in Mississippi and beyond reported him as the second Black man murdered by whitecaps in that part of the county within a month. Nearly a year later Oscar Franklin, charged by the Lincoln County Law and Order League, pleaded guilty to the murder and was sentenced to life imprisonment.

episodes.title: Manchester Avenue police siege and killing of Elmer Chambliss
episodes.lead: The Manchester Avenue police siege took place on the afternoon of December 25, 1903, in St. Louis, Missouri, when five policemen exchanged fire for about two hours with David W. Ellington, a Black man barricaded in his house, and Elmer Chambliss, a Black prisoner in police custody, was shot dead. A patrolman was wounded, a crowd made threats of lynching that the police quieted, and Ellington was later charged with Chambliss's murder on the statement of one of the officers.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Neely Zimmerman and George Williams
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Neely Zimmerman and George Williams took place in Council Bluffs, Iowa, on the night of 28-29 December 1903, when a crowd broke down the door of the Pottawattamie county jail to seize two Black men charged with robbing and attempting to assault two white women. Deputy sheriffs turned the crowd back, Congressman Walter I. Smith persuaded it to disperse, and the men were moved to the penitentiary at Fort Madison the next day. The wire carried it nationally as a lynching narrowly averted, and Black papers praised Smith for upholding the law.

episodes.title: Hahira near-riot of 1903
episodes.lead: The Hahira near-riot of 1903 was an armed standoff between about twenty white men and as many Black men at Hahira, Lowndes County, Georgia, on the night of December 23, 1903. The sheriff asked Governor Terrell for troops, and the crowds dispersed once the request became known, with no deaths reported. Wire services carried it as a "race riot" narrowly averted, and papers from Texas to Minnesota printed the story.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Isaac Adkins
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Isaac Adkins took place at Fishkill, Dutchess County, New York, in December 1903, when a crowd of citizens prepared to hang Adkins, a 35-year-old Black man accused of attacking a 17-year-old white girl. The crowd bought a rope, tied a hangman's knot and chose a place of execution, but Justice Norris had Adkins taken secretly to the county jail at Poughkeepsie. Papers stressed that the attempt came within 60 miles of New York City, and one editorial cited it as proof that the North was as ready to lynch as the South.

episodes.title: Attacks on Black Western Union messengers in Richmond, 1903
episodes.lead: The attacks on Black Western Union messengers in Richmond took place on December 2, 1903, when white boys described as strikers or strike sympathizers stabbed a Black messenger, James Randolph, in the shoulder and drove a second Black messenger from his bicycle with bricks during a strike of white messenger boys against a pay cut and the hiring of Black replacements. No arrests for either attack were reported, and the Richmond Times-Dispatch wrote that public sentiment was 'largely with the boys.' The story ran widely, while the Richmond Planet, a Black weekly, later wrote that the new messengers had met 'brutal treatment' without quailing.

episodes.title: Shooting of Jesse Bagents
episodes.lead: The shooting of Jesse Bagents was an ambush on the night of December 26, 1903, in which three white men fired a shotgun at Bagents, a Black man, and his younger brother on the Monticello road about four miles from Brookhaven, in Lincoln County, Mississippi. Bagents was hit in the back and left for dead, but the county coroner found him alive the next morning and judged him likely to recover. State papers counted the attack among the Lincoln County whitecap outrages, and a widely reprinted paragraph in January 1904 reported it as "another murder by whitecaps."

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Carr
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jim Carr took place in Hancock County, Mississippi, in late December 1903, when a mob took Carr, a Black man held for shooting Deputy Marshal Cobb at Saucier, from the officer who was moving him at night to the county jail at McHenry, and killed him. Accounts differed on whether he was hanged or shot to death, and on whether the shooting of Cobb happened on Christmas Day or the day after. The case ran as a short item in white newspapers from New York to Nevada and South Carolina, most of them carrying a New Orleans wire dispatch that called Carr "Cobb's slayer."

episodes.title: Lynching of Joe Drake
episodes.lead: The lynching of Joe Drake took place on the night of December 18, 1903, when a mob of about 100 men took Drake, a young Black prisoner, from the Lauderdale County jail at Ripley, Tennessee, and hanged him to a tree near the jail. Drake had been arrested on the accusation of killing Chester Conner, a young white man, at Ashport that day. The mob shot the body many times, and white papers from Tennessee to Washington state carried the news as a murder avenged.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Joseph Erwin
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Joseph Erwin took place in East St. Louis, Illinois, on the afternoon of December 7, 1903, when a crowd of several hundred chased Erwin, a Black man accused of robbing and shooting a white man, and tried to seize him from a policeman. Policeman P. J. Mulqueeny held the crowd back with drawn revolvers until a patrol wagon took Erwin to the police station unharmed. Newspapers across the country carried the episode as a rescue of a man from a mob, and Erwin was later held for murder after the wounded man died.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Joe Minor
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Joe Minor took place in December 1903, when laborers at a camp near Wellsville, Montgomery County, Missouri, were reported to have threatened to lynch Minor, a Black man accused of killing a fellow camp worker. Montgomery County's sheriff brought Minor back from St. Louis, where he had been arrested, and said he would protect him; no attempt on Minor is reported.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Keys and Joe Tyler
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Keys and Joe Tyler took place in Hagerstown, Maryland, in early December 1903, when townspeople openly advocated lynching two Black men accused in a sex scandal involving white girls. A gang of white men organized to tar and feather them, and the two were warned to leave town, but no attack was reported.
